attribution.title: Marble Skill Taxonomy (v1)
attribution.standards: Curriculum standards referenced by the taxonomy have their own upstream licences (see PROVENANCE.md in that repository).
attribution.note: This is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Ages are approximate and the taxonomy is not written for learners with additional needs. Treat prerequisite links as a starting point and use professional judgement.

topics.ds: Step-by-step instructions for everyday tasks (making a sandwich, brushing teeth); that if instructions are wrong or missing, things go wrong; computers follow instructions exactly
topics.p: If {{name}} had to write instructions for making a jam sandwich so precise that even a robot could follow them, could they include every single step?

topics.ds: Follow and describe algorithms that include a sequence of steps, branching (a decision such as 'if it is raining, take an umbrella') and iteration (repeating steps, such as 'hop 3 times')
topics.p: In a game like 'If I clap, jump; if I stomp, sit — repeat 5 times', can {{name}} follow the rules and explain the 'if' part and the 'repeat' part?

topics.ds: Use input (key presses, mouse clicks, sensors or typed answers) and branching blocks (if ... then, if ... then ... else) with comparison operators to make a visual program respond to the user
topics.p: Can {{name}} make a simple game in a coding app where pressing the arrow keys moves a character, or a quiz that says 'Correct' or 'Try again'?

topics.ds: Use repeat (loop) blocks in a visual program to repeat actions a set number of times or forever, and identify where a loop makes a program shorter
topics.p: In a coding app, can {{name}} use a 'repeat' block to make a character draw a square or dance — instead of dragging the same blocks over and over?

topics.ds: Implement a simple algorithm as a visual (block-based) program — a start event, a sequence of blocks, run and observe — in an environment such as Scratch, ScratchJr or a programmable robot app
topics.p: Has {{name}} used a block-coding app like Scratch to make a character move and talk — and can they explain what happens if they swap the order of the blocks?

topics.ds: Test visual programs by predicting what should happen, running them, finding where the behaviour differs (bugs) and fixing them one change at a time
topics.p: When {{name}}'s coding project doesn't work the way they wanted, do they test it, hunt for the 'bug' and fix it step by step rather than starting over?

topics.ds: Implement a designed algorithm as a visual program combining control structures (sequence, multiple branches with if ... else, repeat until), variables and user input, and test it with planned test cases, refining it until it works for all of them
topics.p: Has {{name}} built a complete game or quiz in a coding app — planning it first, testing it with tricky answers, and improving it until it works properly?

topics.ds: Create and use variables in visual programs to store and change values — such as a score, a timer, a counter or a user's answer — and use them in conditions
topics.p: In a game {{name}} made with block coding, can they make a score that goes up each time the player wins a point, and end the game when the lives run out?

topics.ds: Spotting AI in daily life: face unlock on a phone, video recommendations, spelling auto-correct, automatic doors that detect people; technology that seems to 'know' things
topics.p: Could {{name}} point out several things they use every day — like auto-correct or face unlock — and explain that these are examples of AI?

topics.ds: What a robot really is — not the sci-fi version; robots in factories, robot vacuum cleaners, robot arms in surgery; that robots follow instructions given by people
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a robot vacuum cleaner, could they explain how it's different from a person cleaning — that it follows instructions rather than thinking for itself?

topics.ds: Sorting objects into 'smart' (can sense and respond) and 'not smart' (just sits there); a toaster vs a smart speaker; introduction to the idea that some machines can sense and respond to the world
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain the difference between a normal light switch and one that turns on automatically when you walk into a room?

topics.n: Voice Assistants and How They Work
topics.ds: What happens when you talk to Alexa, Siri, or Google Assistant; they listen, try to understand, look up answers; sometimes they get it wrong; they are tools, not alive
topics.p: If {{name}} asked Alexa or Siri a question and got a wrong answer, could they explain why the voice assistant sometimes makes mistakes?

topics.ds: How recommendation systems work: YouTube, Netflix, and shop websites track what you click and find patterns; filter bubbles; the difference between helpful suggestions and manipulation
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand why YouTube keeps suggesting similar videos to ones they've watched, and could they explain how the recommendation system works?

topics.ds: How computer game characters 'decide' what to do; simple rule-based AI vs learning AI; NPCs, difficulty adjustment; AI as the opponent in chess or board games
topics.p: When {{name}} plays a video game against the computer, could they explain how the game's characters 'decide' what to do?

topics.ds: Machines make mistakes; they only know what they've been shown; bad training data leads to bad results; AI is not magic — just maths on data; showing edge cases and failures
topics.p: If an AI incorrectly identified a picture of a muffin as a chihuahua, could {{name}} explain why that kind of mistake happens?

topics.ds: Comparing human and machine capabilities: creativity, empathy, common sense vs speed, memory, repetition; the Turing Test (simplified); what makes humans unique
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain what humans are still better at than computers and what computers can do that humans can't?

topics.ds: How machine learning works at a conceptual level: show the computer many examples, it finds patterns, then it makes predictions about new things; hands-on experience with Teachable Machine or similar tool
topics.p: Could {{name}} describe how you teach a computer to recognise something — by showing it lots of examples until it spots the pattern?

topics.ds: Humans are great at spotting patterns; computers can learn to spot patterns too, but they need lots of examples; sorting and classification activities as the basis of machine learning
topics.p: If you showed {{name}} pictures of cats and dogs, could they explain how a computer could learn to tell them apart — and why it would need many more pictures than a person would?

topics.ds: What data AI systems collect about you; who has it and why it matters; cookies, tracking, smart speakers always listening; your data is valuable
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that apps and websites collect information about what they do online, and could they explain why that matters?

topics.ds: Deepfakes, AI-generated images and text; how to spot them and why they matter; the importance of checking sources; not everything online is real
topics.p: If {{name}} saw an amazing photo online, would they think to question whether it might have been created by AI rather than captured by a camera?

topics.ds: Whether AI should make important decisions about people: jobs, loans, justice; who is responsible when AI makes unfair decisions; introduction to algorithmic fairness
topics.p: If {{name}} learned that a computer program was deciding who gets a job interview, could they explain why that might be unfair and who should be responsible?

topics.ds: AI needs huge amounts of energy and water to train; data centres and their environmental cost; but AI can also help — predicting weather, monitoring deforestation, optimising energy; trade-offs
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain that AI needs a lot of energy to work but can also be used to help protect the environment, and discuss whether the trade-off is worth it?

topics.n: AI and the Future of Work
topics.ds: How AI is changing the world of work: some jobs disappear, new ones are created, many change; jobs AI can't do (yet); what skills matter in an AI world
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain how AI might change the way people work in the future and which human skills will still be important?

topics.ds: If training data is biased, AI will be biased; examples: facial recognition working better for some skin tones, translation assuming gender; where bias comes from and whether we can fix it
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why an AI trained mostly on photos of light-skinned faces might not work as well for people with darker skin?

topics.ds: Design thinking applied to AI ethics: if you were designing an AI system, what rules would you give it? Who should it help? What should it not be allowed to do?
topics.p: If {{name}} was designing an AI assistant for their school, could they think of rules to make sure it was fair and helpful for everyone?

topics.ds: What AI might do in 10 years; what we want it to do and what we're worried about; children as future designers and decision-makers about AI; hopeful, empowered framing
topics.p: Could {{name}} have a thoughtful conversation about what they'd want AI to do in the future and what they'd be worried about?

topics.ds: What data is: information that computers use — numbers, words, pictures, sounds; everything a computer knows comes from data that people give it
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain what 'data' means and give examples of data they create every time they use a phone or computer?

topics.ds: Explain how digital systems represent all data — text, images and sound — using numbers: each pixel's colour is stored as numbers, each letter has a number code and sound is stored as a series of number samples
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that a photo on your phone is really stored as numbers — and could they turn a list of numbers into a picture on squared paper?

topics.ds: Explore how digital systems represent data using two states — on and off, written as 1 and 0 — called bits, and use binary numbers to represent whole numbers and letters
topics.p: Playing with 'binary cards' or light switches, could {{name}} show how on and off (1 and 0) can make any number — like making 5 with 101?

topics.ds: Discuss how existing digital systems satisfy the identified needs of known users: what the user needs, which features help and what does not work well for them
topics.p: Could {{name}} look at a learning app a younger cousin uses and explain what makes it good for a little kid — like big buttons and sounds — and what could be better?

topics.ds: Investigate simple problems for people they know (classmates, family, the teacher) and suggest how a digital system could help solve them
topics.p: Can {{name}} notice a problem someone in the family has — like Grandma missing them — and suggest a device or app that would help, like a video call?

topics.ds: Discuss how existing digital solutions and their own digital solutions satisfy the design criteria and user stories, using evidence from trying them out
topics.p: After making a game or animation, can {{name}} check it against the goals they set — like 'it must have 3 levels' — and say what still needs fixing?

topics.ds: Define a problem to be solved with a digital solution using given design criteria, and co-create user stories in the form 'As a ..., I want ..., so that ...' to describe what users need
topics.p: If {{name}} was helping design a game for younger kids, could they write a 'user story' like 'As a 6-year-old, I want big buttons so that I can tap them easily'?

topics.ds: Generate, communicate and compare designs for a digital solution — sketching or storyboarding the screens, inputs, outputs and steps of a game, app or program — and choose the design that best meets the criteria
topics.p: Before coding a game, does {{name}} sketch out the screens and what happens when you press each button — and compare a couple of ideas to pick the best?

topics.ds: Design a user interface for a digital system — the layout of screens, buttons, menus and navigation — applying principles such as consistency, readability and accessibility for the intended users
topics.p: If {{name}} designed the screens for an app, would they think about where the buttons go, how users move between screens and whether it's easy for everyone to use?

topics.ds: Evaluate existing digital solutions and their own against design criteria and user stories, and consider their broader community impact: who benefits, who might be excluded, and effects on privacy, safety, wellbeing and the environment
topics.p: Can {{name}} judge an app — their own or a real one — against the goals it was meant to meet, and think about who in the community it helps or leaves out?

topics.ds: Generate, modify, communicate and evaluate designs for digital solutions — algorithms, flowcharts, storyboards and wireframes — refining them in response to feedback and testing
topics.p: When {{name}} plans a digital project, do they share their design, take on feedback and improve it — explaining why the new version is better?

topics.ds: Define problems for digital solutions by creating their own user stories for different users and co-developing measurable design criteria from them
topics.p: Before making an app or game, could {{name}} talk to the people who'll use it and turn what they need into clear goals the design must meet?

topics.ds: Identifying computers in everyday life — not just laptops but phones, tablets, smart speakers, traffic lights, washing machines; what makes something a computer
topics.p: Could {{name}} look around your home and point out at least five things that have a computer inside them, including ones that don't look like traditional computers?

topics.ds: Recognise that digital systems are made of hardware (the parts you can touch, such as the screen, buttons and camera) and software (the apps and programs that tell the hardware what to do), and explore a device or app to achieve a simple purpose
topics.p: When {{name}} uses a tablet, can they tell you which parts are hardware they can touch (like the screen or camera) and which are apps — and use one app to do something, like take a photo?

topics.ds: Identify the components of common digital systems — screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, touchscreen, speakers, microphone and camera — and explore what each is used for, telling parts that put information in (input) from parts that give information out (output)
topics.p: Can {{name}} name the parts of a laptop or tablet — keyboard, screen, camera, microphone, speaker — and say which one they'd use to record a message for Grandma?

topics.ds: Explore and describe a range of digital systems (computers, tablets, game consoles, smart watches, robots) and the peripherals that connect to them — printers, scanners, headphones, game controllers, external drives, digital microscopes and sensors — and choose peripherals for different purposes
topics.p: If the family wanted to record a podcast or print photos, could {{name}} explain which devices and add-ons you'd need — like a microphone, headphones or a printer — and why?

topics.ds: Explore how different types of data — text, images, sound and video — are transmitted between digital systems by cable or wirelessly (e.g. Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, mobile networks), noticing that larger files such as videos take longer to send
topics.p: When {{name}} sends a photo or video to a relative, can they explain how it gets there — by cable, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi — and why a video takes longer to send than a message?

topics.ds: Examine how digital systems connect to form networks — wired and wireless connections, routers and servers in a home or school network — so they can share data and resources such as printers, files and the internet
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how all the devices at home connect through the Wi-Fi router — and why you can print from any computer in the house?

topics.ds: Explain that the internet is a network of networks and that data is broken into small packets, addressed, sent along different routes and reassembled at its destination
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why a video call sometimes freezes — that the internet chops data into little packets that travel separately and are put back together?

topics.ds: Investigate the main internal components of common digital systems — processor (CPU), memory (RAM), storage, circuit board, battery or power supply and wireless adaptor — and explain the function of each
topics.p: Looking at the specs of a new tablet or laptop, could {{name}} explain what the processor, memory and storage each do — and why more storage means more room for photos and games?

topics.ds: Use the basic features of common digital tools to share content and work together — posting a drawing or recording to a class space, adding to a shared class book or slideshow, giving kind comments — following agreed behaviours with guidance from trusted adults
topics.p: With a teacher or parent helping, can {{name}} add their page to a shared class book or post a drawing online — and leave a kind comment on someone else's work?

topics.ds: Use the core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate — co-editing a shared document or slideshow, using comments and a shared task list — following agreed behaviours with support from trusted adults
topics.p: Has {{name}} worked on a shared document or slideshow with classmates — each doing their own part and leaving comments rather than deleting others' work?

topics.ds: Save, name and organise digital files in folders following agreed conventions, so that work can be found, shared and reopened
topics.p: Can {{name}} save their school work with a sensible file name in the right folder — and find it again the next week?

topics.ds: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to create, locate and communicate content — choosing between word processing, presentation, spreadsheet, graphics, video and search tools for a task, using their digital-specific features and applying common conventions
topics.p: When {{name}} has a school project, do they pick the right tool — slides for a talk, a spreadsheet for numbers, a video app for a how-to — and use its features well?

topics.ds: Select and use appropriate digital tools to share content online, plan tasks and collaborate on projects — task boards, shared calendars, co-edited documents, version history and video calls — demonstrating agreed behaviours
topics.p: For a group project, can {{name}} choose sensible online tools — a shared document, a to-do board, a video call — and use them to plan who does what and keep track?

topics.ds: Identify some data that is personal and belongs to them — their name, age, birthday, address, photos and videos of themselves, voice recordings and drawings — and know to ask a trusted adult before sharing it
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that their name, birthday, address and photos are their own information — and that they should ask you before sharing them in a tablet game?

topics.ds: Discuss that some websites and apps store their personal data online — names, photos, voice recordings, game scores and location — so the information stays there and may be seen by others
topics.p: When a game or app asks for {{name}}'s name, photo or location, do they understand it gets saved online somewhere — and check with you before typing it in?

topics.ds: Access their school or learning account using a recorded username and password (e.g. from a login card), log out when finished, and keep the password private except from trusted adults
topics.p: Can {{name}} log in to their school learning app using the username and password on their card, and log out when they're finished?

topics.ds: Access their school account using a memorised password and explain why a good password is easy for them to remember but hard for others to guess, avoiding names, birthdays and simple patterns
topics.p: Can {{name}} log in to their school account from memory — and explain why their pet's name or birthday would make a bad password?

topics.ds: Identify what personal data is stored and shared in their own online accounts (e.g. a school learning account or a game) — profile name, photo, age, location, contacts and work — who can see it, and discuss the associated risks
topics.p: Looking at {{name}}'s game or school account together, could they tell you what personal information it stores, who can see it and what the risks might be?

topics.ds: Explain how their digital footprint is created — posts, photos, comments, searches and data collected by apps — and why it can be permanent, because content can be copied, shared and stored even after it is deleted
topics.p: Before posting something online, does {{name}} think about the fact that it could be copied and stay around for years — even if they delete it?

topics.ds: Consider privacy when collecting data from users: collect only the data needed, tell people why it is collected, ask permission, avoid identifying details where possible, and store and share results safely
topics.p: If {{name}} made an online survey for their class, would they only ask for what they need, explain why, and keep people's answers private?

topics.ds: Access multiple personal accounts using a unique passphrase for each, and explain the risks of reusing passwords: if one account is breached, every account with the same password is exposed
topics.p: Does {{name}} use a different passphrase for each of their accounts — and can they explain why reusing one password is risky if a website gets hacked?

topics.ds: Understand that reading is about making meaning, not just saying words correctly — a text that can be decoded but not understood has not been read
topics.p: If {{name}} reads something aloud correctly but then can't tell you what it was about, do they recognise that reading means understanding — not just saying the words?

topics.ds: Notice the difference between decoding words and actually understanding them — recognise when you've read the words but not grasped the meaning, and do something about it
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a paragraph or listens to an explanation, do they notice when they haven't really understood it — rather than just carrying on as if they had?

topics.ds: Recognise how an author's deliberate choices — of words, structure, tone, and perspective — create particular effects on you as a reader
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a book or article, do they ever notice and comment on why the author chose to write it a certain way — and what effect that has on them as a reader?

topics.ds: Distinguish between what a text explicitly says and what you have inferred, assumed, or read in — knowing which is which is fundamental to honest comprehension
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a story or article, can they tell you which parts they actually read in the text and which parts they worked out or assumed for themselves?

topics.ds: Monitor your own vocabulary gaps — notice words you half-know, distinguish confident from uncertain knowledge, and develop strategies to resolve the uncertainty
topics.p: When {{name}} comes across a word they half-know — where they can guess the meaning but aren't sure — do they notice that gap and do something about it, like looking it up or asking?

topics.ds: Evaluate whether your own writing achieves the effect you intended on a reader — go beyond checking for correctness to asking whether it actually works
topics.p: After {{name}} writes something — a story, a letter, a persuasive piece — do they think about whether it would have the effect they wanted on a reader, not just whether the spelling is right?

topics.ds: Reflect on yourself as a language user — how your reading, writing, and speaking shift across audiences, purposes, and contexts, and where you want to develop further
topics.p: Does {{name}} notice how they communicate differently in different situations — writing for school versus texting a friend, or speaking in a debate versus chatting at home — and can they explain why those differences matter?

topics.ds: Understand that words combine to make sentences — a sentence expresses a complete thought; produce and expand complete sentences in speech and writing
topics.p: If {{name}} says something like "The dog", can they tell you that's not a complete sentence — and add words to make it say something like "The dog ran fast"?

topics.ds: Separate words with spaces in writing; understand that spaces mark word boundaries in print
topics.p: If {{name}} is writing a short message, can they leave a space between each word — so the reader can tell where one word ends and the next begins?

topics.ds: Use frequently occurring nouns (people, places, things) and verbs (action words) appropriately in speech and writing
topics.p: When {{name}} talks or writes about everyday things — like "the dog runs" or "Mum cooks dinner" — do they use the right kind of words for things (nouns) and actions (verbs) without mixing them up?

topics.n: Capitals for Names, Days and I
topics.ds: Use capital letters for proper nouns (names of people, places) the days of the week, and the personal pronoun 'I'
topics.p: If {{name}} is writing their friend's name or the name of a town, do they automatically start it with a capital letter — and do they write the word 'I' with a capital when talking about themselves?

topics.ds: Use basic grammatical terminology when discussing reading and writing: letter, capital letter, word, singular, plural, sentence, punctuation, full stop, question mark, exclamation mark
topics.p: If you point to a full stop or a question mark in a book, can {{name}} tell you what it's called and what it's for — and do they know the difference between a word and a sentence?

topics.ds: Join words and clauses using the conjunction 'and' to create longer sentences
topics.p: When {{name}} is telling you about their day, can they write two ideas joined together with the word 'and' — like "I had lunch and then we played outside"?

topics.ds: Understand and use the most frequently occurring prepositions of location and direction (e.g. to, from, in, out, on, off, for, by, with)
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to describe where something is — like where the cup is on the table — can they use little words like "on", "under", "next to", or "by" correctly?

topics.ds: Understand and use question words (who, what, where, when, why, how) to form and answer questions
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to find out something — like where you put their shoes or why the sky is blue — can they start their question with the right word, like "where" or "why"?

topics.ds: Form and use regular plural nouns orally and in writing by adding -s or -es; understand that plural means more than one
topics.p: If you point to a picture of one cat and then several cats, can {{name}} tell you the correct word for more than one — and write it with the right ending, like "cats" or "boxes"?

topics.ds: Begin sentences with a capital letter and end them with the appropriate mark (full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark); recognise and name end punctuation
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a sentence like "the cat sat on the mat", do they remember to use a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end — without needing a reminder?

topics.ds: Use apostrophes in writing for both contraction (marking omitted letters) and singular possession, distinguishing the two uses
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a word like "don't" or "it's", do they put the apostrophe in the right place — and can they also write something like "the dog's bowl" to show the bowl belongs to the dog?

topics.ds: Use commas to separate items in a list within a sentence (e.g., 'I bought apples, bananas, and oranges')
topics.p: If {{name}} writes a sentence listing three or more things — like the items they'd pack for a picnic — do they put commas between each item in the list?

topics.ds: Use determiners (articles a/an/the and demonstratives this/that/these/those) correctly before nouns
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about something nearby versus something far away, do they use the right word — saying "this book" for one in their hand and "that book" for one across the room?

topics.ds: Use expanded noun phrases to describe and specify, adding adjectives and other modifiers before a noun (e.g., 'the blue butterfly', 'the old, creaky door')
topics.p: When {{name}} describes something in writing — like a pet or a toy — do they add extra describing words, such as "the small, fluffy rabbit" rather than just "the rabbit"?

topics.ds: Understand and use the four sentence types — statement, question, exclamation, and command — recognising how grammatical patterns indicate sentence function
topics.p: Can {{name}} spot the difference between a question ("Are you hungry?") and a command ("Eat your dinner!") — and write each type of sentence using the right punctuation at the end?

topics.n: Grammar Terms: Nouns, Verbs and Tense
topics.ds: Use and understand Year 2 grammatical terminology in discussion: noun, noun phrase, statement, question, exclamation, command, compound, suffix, adjective, adverb, verb, tense (past/present), apostrophe, comma
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to point out a noun, a verb, or an adjective in a sentence from their reading book, can they find one and explain what it does in the sentence?

topics.ds: Use verbs to convey past and present tense correctly and consistently, including the progressive form (e.g., she is drumming, he was shouting), understanding how tense indicates time
topics.p: If {{name}} is writing about something that happened yesterday versus something happening right now, do they change the verb — for example, writing "she jumped" for the past and "she is jumping" for right now?

topics.ds: Use personal, possessive, and indefinite pronouns correctly (e.g., I/me/my, they/them/their, anyone/everything), replacing nouns to avoid repetition
topics.p: When {{name}} retells a story or describes what a friend did, do they use words like "he", "she", "they", or "his" correctly — instead of repeating the person's name every single time?

topics.ds: Understand that a simple sentence is a single independent clause expressing one event or idea, usually built around one verb, and tell it apart from a sentence that joins two ideas
topics.p: When {{name}} writes, can they write a short sentence about one thing happening — like 'The dog barked.' — and split a long joined-up sentence into two?

topics.ds: Use singular and plural nouns with matching verbs in sentences, maintaining subject-verb agreement (e.g., 'He hops' vs 'We hop')
topics.p: If {{name}} writes "she hop" or "we hops", do they catch the mistake — and can they fix it to "she hops" and "we hop" so the subject and verb match?

topics.ds: Use subordination (when, if, that, because) and co-ordination (or, and, but) to join clauses and create compound and complex sentences
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story or a message, can they join two ideas with words like "because", "but", "when", or "if" — rather than writing every thought as a short separate sentence?

topics.ds: Use adjectives and adverbs correctly, choosing between them depending on whether a noun or verb/adjective is being modified (e.g., 'She ran quickly' vs 'She is quick')
topics.p: If {{name}} writes "she ran quick" instead of "she ran quickly", can they spot that they need an adverb to describe the running — and fix it themselves?

topics.ds: Recognise and use capital letters in titles of books, stories, films and headings, alongside commas to separate items in lists
topics.p: When {{name}} writes the name of a favourite book or movie, do they start it — and its important words — with capital letters?

topics.ds: Use the correct form of the indefinite article — 'a' before words beginning with a consonant sound and 'an' before words beginning with a vowel sound (e.g., a rock, an open box, an hour, a unicorn)
topics.p: When {{name}} writes, do they automatically choose "a" before a word that starts with a consonant sound and "an" before a vowel sound — like "a cat" but "an apple" or "an hour"?

topics.ds: Use conjunctions (when, before, after, while, so, because), adverbs (then, next, soon, therefore) and prepositions (before, after, during, in, because of) to express time, place and cause within and across sentences
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they use time words like "after", "while", or "soon" to show the order things happened — rather than starting every sentence with "then"?

topics.ds: Use and understand Year 3 grammatical terminology accurately when discussing reading and writing: preposition, conjunction, word family, prefix, clause, subordinate clause, direct speech, consonant letter, vowel letter, inverted commas/speech marks
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to find a "subordinate clause" or a "preposition" in a sentence from their book, can they point one out and explain what it means?

topics.ds: Form and use the past tense of frequently occurring irregular verbs correctly (e.g., sat, hid, told, went, came, ran), recognising that these do not follow the regular -ed pattern
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about something that happened in the past with an irregular verb — like "run" or "sit" — do they write "ran" and "sat" rather than "runned" and "sitted"?

topics.ds: Form and use irregular plural nouns (e.g., children, teeth, mice, geese) in addition to regular plurals, recognising that some nouns have irregular plural forms that do not follow the -s/-es pattern
topics.p: If you point to a picture of several mice or a group of children, can {{name}} write the correct plural — knowing it's "mice" not "mouses" and "children" not "childs"?

topics.ds: Understand that texts are made cohesive by using personal and possessive pronouns and by leaving out (omitting) words the reader can work out from earlier in the text (ellipsis)
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about a day out, do they avoid repeating the same words — using 'he' or 'she' and leaving out words the reader already knows?

topics.ds: Choose pronouns for clarity and cohesion, avoiding ambiguity and repetition; use reflexive pronouns correctly (e.g., myself, ourselves, himself)
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a paragraph about two people — like two characters in a story — do they use "he", "she", and "they" clearly enough that you always know who is being talked about?

topics.ds: Punctuate direct speech using inverted commas (speech marks), understanding that direct speech records the exact words spoken and must be enclosed in punctuation marks
topics.p: When {{name}} writes down something a character said in a story, do they put speech marks around the exact words — like "Come here," she called — and use the correct punctuation inside?

topics.ds: Use the present perfect form of verbs in contrast to the simple past tense, understanding how the present perfect indicates an action completed at an unspecified time or with ongoing relevance (e.g., 'He has gone out' vs 'He went out')
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the difference between "I ate breakfast" (simple past) and "I have eaten breakfast" (present perfect) — knowing one means a finished action and the other links the past to right now?

topics.ds: Understand and use abstract nouns to name ideas, qualities, and states that cannot be perceived by the senses
topics.p: Can {{name}} write a sentence using an abstract word like "kindness", "freedom", or "happiness" — knowing these are nouns even though you can't touch or see them?

topics.ds: Ensure subject-verb agreement and pronoun-antecedent agreement within and across sentences
topics.p: If {{name}} writes "Each of the players have their own locker", can they spot the error and fix it to "has their own locker" — making sure the verb matches the subject?

topics.ds: Form and use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs, choosing correctly between them
topics.p: If {{name}} is comparing three things — like three books they've read — can they correctly say one is "good", another is "better", and the best one is "the best"?

topics.ds: Understand how verbs represent different processes: doing (action), feeling and thinking (sensing), saying, and relating (being and having)
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell the difference between action words like 'ran', thinking or feeling words like 'wondered', saying words like 'whispered', and 'being' words like 'is' and 'has'?

topics.ds: Expand noun phrases with modifying adjectives, nouns, and preposition phrases to add detail
topics.p: When {{name}} describes something in a piece of writing, do they build up a rich description — like "the tall man with the grey coat" rather than just "the man"?

topics.ds: Use fronted adverbials to vary sentence openings and punctuate them with commas
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story or a report, do they sometimes start a sentence with a phrase like "After lunch," or "Quietly, the fox moved closer," — and put a comma after that opening phrase?

topics.ds: Know and use Year 4 grammar terminology including determiner, pronoun, possessive pronoun, and adverbial
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to find a "determiner" or a "possessive pronoun" in a sentence, can they point one out and explain what job it does?

topics.ds: Understand and use modal verbs (can, may, must, might, shall, will, could, should, would) and modal adverbs (perhaps, surely, certainly) to indicate degrees of possibility, necessity, and permission
topics.p: When {{name}} writes, do they choose between words like "must", "might", "could", and "should" to show whether something is certain, possible, or just an idea — rather than treating every action as definite?

topics.ds: Distinguish between the plural -s suffix and the possessive -'s suffix in nouns
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell the difference between "the girls' coats" (belonging to many girls) and "the girls are coming" (just a plural) — and write each one correctly without mixing up the apostrophe?

topics.ds: Form and use the simple past, present, and future verb tenses consistently in writing
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about something that happened yesterday, something happening now, and something that will happen tomorrow, do they change the verb correctly for each time — like "I walked", "I walk", and "I will walk"?

topics.ds: Use Standard English verb inflections in place of non-standard local forms
topics.p: If {{name}} sometimes says "we was" or "they done it" in conversation, do they know to write "we were" and "they did it" in their schoolwork — using standard written English?

topics.ds: Order adjectives within sentences according to conventional English patterns (opinion-size-age-shape-colour-origin-material-purpose) to produce natural-sounding descriptions
topics.p: When {{name}} uses several describing words together — like "a tiny old wooden box" — does the order sound natural, or do they mix up the adjectives so it sounds odd?

topics.ds: Use brackets, dashes, and commas to indicate parenthesis — additional information inserted into a sentence that could be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning
topics.p: When {{name}} adds a little extra detail inside a sentence — like "The teacher, who is very strict, gave us homework" — do they correctly use brackets, dashes, or commas around that added bit?

topics.ds: Use cohesive devices within a paragraph — including pronouns, adverbials (then, after that, firstly), and synonyms — to link sentences and build a coherent flow of ideas
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a paragraph, do the sentences flow together smoothly — using words like "however", "after this", or "in contrast" to link ideas, rather than every sentence starting with "And then"?

topics.ds: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet) when joining two independent clauses in a compound sentence
topics.p: When {{name}} joins two complete thoughts with a word like "but" or "so" — like "I wanted to go, but it was raining" — do they put a comma before that joining word?

topics.ds: Use commas to clarify meaning and avoid ambiguity in sentences where the absence of a comma could cause misreading
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why "Let's eat, Grandma" and "Let's eat Grandma" mean very different things — and use that kind of comma in their own writing to avoid confusion?

topics.ds: Convert nouns and adjectives into verbs by adding suffixes -ate, -ise (-ize), and -ify, understanding how word class changes affect sentence construction
topics.p: Can {{name}} take a word like "active" or "sharp" and turn it into a verb by adding a suffix — knowing that "activate" and "sharpen" are the verb forms?

topics.ds: Form and use prepositional phrases (preposition + noun phrase) to add detail about time, location, or direction within sentences, recognising how they function as adjective or adverb phrases
topics.p: When {{name}} writes directions or descriptions of a place — like "behind the old tree" or "near the top of the hill" — do they use prepositional phrases naturally to show where or when something is?

topics.ds: Recognise and correct sentence fragments (incomplete sentences lacking a subject or predicate) and run-on sentences (two or more independent clauses joined without proper punctuation or conjunctions)
topics.p: If {{name}}'s writing has a sentence like "Running down the street." or two ideas jammed together without any punctuation, can they spot that something's wrong and fix it?

topics.n: Grammar Terms: Modal Verbs and Clauses
topics.ds: Know and use Year 5 grammar terminology accurately when discussing reading and writing: modal verb, relative pronoun, relative clause, parenthesis, bracket, dash, cohesion, ambiguity
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} what a "modal verb" or a "relative clause" is, can they give you a clear explanation and point to an example in a sentence?

topics.ds: Link ideas across paragraphs using adverbials of time (later, meanwhile, after a while), place (nearby, far away, beyond the wall), and number (secondly, finally, in addition) to guide the reader through a multi-paragraph text
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a multi-paragraph story or report, do they use linking phrases — like "Meanwhile, far away…" or "By the following morning…" — to guide the reader smoothly from one section to the next?

topics.ds: Form and use the progressive (continuous) verb tenses — past progressive (was walking), present progressive (am walking), and future progressive (will be walking) — to convey ongoing actions at different times
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to describe an action that was happening over a period of time in the past — like "I was reading when the phone rang" — can they write the verb in the right ongoing-past form?

topics.ds: Investigate how quoted (direct) and reported (indirect) speech are used, and change between them by adjusting pronouns, tense and punctuation
topics.p: Can {{name}} retell what someone said in their own words — like 'Mia said that she was tired' — as well as writing the exact words in speech marks?

topics.ds: Form and use relative clauses beginning with relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that) and relative adverbs (where, when, why) to add detail, qualify nouns, and create complex sentences
topics.p: When {{name}} writes to add detail about a noun — like describing a friend "who loves football" or a place "where we always go on holiday" — do they build that into the same sentence using a relative clause?

topics.ds: Use verb prefixes (dis-, de-, mis-, over-, re-) to change verb meaning, understanding how each prefix modifies the action expressed by the root verb
topics.p: If you give {{name}} a verb like "appear" and ask them to use a prefix to change its meaning, can they produce words like "disappear", "reappear", or "misrepresent" and explain what the prefix does?

topics.ds: Use the passive voice to shift focus from the agent to the action or recipient, understanding how passive constructions affect the presentation of information in formal and objective writing
topics.p: When {{name}} wants to write about something without saying who did it — like in a science report — can they switch the sentence round to say "The experiment was carried out" instead of "We carried out the experiment"?

topics.ds: Use apostrophes correctly where there is multiple possession — joint possession (an apostrophe on the last owner only) and separate possession (an apostrophe on each owner) — alongside commas after introductory prepositional phrases
topics.p: When writing about two people who share something, does {{name}} know to write 'Sam and Ali's house' — but 'Sam's and Ali's bikes' when they each have their own?

topics.ds: Punctuate bullet points consistently to list information clearly, applying conventions for capitalisation, end punctuation, and parallel structure across items
topics.p: When {{name}} uses bullet points to list information — like in a school project — are all the bullets punctuated the same way, with matching capitalisation and consistent end punctuation?

topics.ds: Use verb tense to convey various times, sequences, states, and conditions, selecting tenses deliberately to express the precise timing and nature of actions and events
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story that jumps between past events and present thoughts, do they shift verb tenses deliberately and accurately — so the reader always knows exactly when each event is happening?

topics.ds: Use a colon to introduce a list and semi-colons to separate items within lists, particularly when list items contain internal commas or are complex phrases
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a list of things that are themselves quite long or contain commas — like a list of ingredients with measurements — do they use a colon to introduce it and semi-colons to separate the items?

topics.ds: Use a comma to separate an introductory element from the rest of the sentence, including introductory words, phrases, and clauses
topics.p: When {{name}} begins a sentence with a phrase or clause — like "Despite the rain," or "If you look closely," — do they put a comma after that opening part before the main sentence begins?

topics.n: Commas with yes, no, and names
topics.ds: Use commas to set off the words yes and no, to set off tag questions, and to indicate direct address in sentences
topics.p: When {{name}} writes dialogue or a letter and addresses someone by name — like "Yes, Mum, I did tidy my room" — do they use commas correctly around the name and around words like "yes" or "no"?

topics.ds: Explain the function of conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections in general and in particular sentences, understanding how each word class contributes to meaning
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} what the word "although" or "ouch!" does in a sentence, can they explain one is a conjunction that joins ideas and the other is an interjection that expresses feeling?

topics.ds: Recognise and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense within and across sentences and paragraphs, maintaining consistency unless a shift is required by meaning
topics.p: If you read back a paragraph {{name}} has written and it unexpectedly switches from past tense to present tense mid-way through, can they spot the shift and correct it so the tense stays consistent?

topics.ds: Use correlative conjunctions correctly in sentences, pairing words such as either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also, and whether/or
topics.p: When {{name}} wants to say that two things are equally true — like "both cats and dogs make good pets" — do they know to use "both…and" together, rather than just "and" on its own?

topics.ds: Know and use Year 6 grammatical terminology accurately: subject, object, active voice, passive voice, synonym, antonym, ellipsis, hyphen, colon, semi-colon, bullet points
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to find the "subject" and "object" in a sentence, or to explain what a "semi-colon" or "ellipsis" does, can they give you a confident and accurate answer?

topics.ds: Use hyphens to avoid ambiguity in compound modifiers and prefixed words, distinguishing between meanings that change based on hyphen placement
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why "a man-eating shark" and "a man eating shark" mean completely different things — and use a hyphen correctly in their own writing to avoid that kind of confusion?

topics.ds: Link ideas across paragraphs using a wider range of cohesive devices including word repetition, grammatical connections such as adverbials, and ellipsis to create coherent extended texts
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a long piece across several paragraphs, do the sections feel connected — with repeated key words, linking phrases, and occasional gaps (ellipsis) used deliberately to hold the whole text together?

topics.ds: Use semi-colons, colons, and dashes to mark boundaries between independent clauses, choosing the appropriate punctuation based on the relationship between the clauses
topics.p: When {{name}} writes two closely related sentences, can they join them with a semi-colon or colon — like "It was late; the streets were empty" — rather than always using a full stop or "and"?

topics.ds: Use underlining, quotation marks, or italics to indicate titles of works, applying conventions for different types of works such as books, stories, poems, songs, and articles
topics.p: When {{name}} refers to a book title or a film name in their writing, do they know to put it in inverted commas or italics — like writing *Charlotte's Web* or "Charlotte's Web" — rather than just leaving it as plain text?

topics.ds: Use the subjunctive form in formal writing and speech to express wishes, demands, suggestions, or hypothetical situations (e.g., 'If I were you', 'I suggest that he go', 'Were they to arrive')
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a formal letter or a persuasive essay, can they use phrases like "If I were in charge…" or "The school suggests that every pupil attend…" to sound more formal and precise?

topics.ds: Expand, combine, and reduce sentences for meaning, reader interest, and style, using techniques such as embedding clauses, using appositives, and varying sentence length
topics.p: When {{name}} revises their writing, can they take a very long sentence and split it up, or take three short choppy sentences and combine them into one — choosing the version that reads best for the audience?

topics.ds: Use punctuation confidently and accurately for effect and clarity — including semicolons to link related clauses, colons to introduce lists or explanations, dashes and parentheses for parenthetical information, ellipsis for omission or suspense, and commas for coordinate adjectives and nonrestrictive elements
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a complex piece — like an essay or a detailed story — do they use advanced punctuation like semi-colons, colons, dashes, and ellipses confidently and accurately to shape meaning and style?

topics.ds: Analyse the effectiveness and impact of grammatical features in texts read — understanding how authors make deliberate grammatical choices (sentence length, passive voice, fronted adverbials, listing) to create specific effects on the reader
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a piece of writing they admire, can they point to specific grammatical choices the author made — like very short sentences for tension, or a list of three for rhythm — and explain why those choices work?

topics.ds: Discuss reading, writing, and spoken language with precise and confident use of linguistic and literary terminology — including terms for word classes, sentence types, clause types, literary devices, and text-level features
topics.p: When {{name}} discusses a book or piece of writing with a teacher, do they use precise language — like "the author uses a compound-complex sentence here" or "that's a non-restrictive relative clause" — rather than just saying "this bit is good"?

topics.ds: Understand and analyse the function of phrases (noun, verb, adjectival, adverbial, prepositional) and clauses (main, subordinate, relative) in general and in specific sentences, including recognising and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers
topics.p: If {{name}} reads a sentence like "Walking home from school, the rain soaked her backpack" and something feels grammatically off, can they identify the dangling modifier and explain how to rewrite it correctly?

topics.ds: Know and understand the differences between spoken and written language — including differences in formality, register, grammar, and vocabulary — and between Standard English and other varieties of English, using Standard English confidently in writing and speech
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that the way they speak with friends is different from how they should write in school — and can they adjust their language for formal situations, using standard grammar and vocabulary?

topics.ds: Choose among and construct simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex sentences to signal different relationships among ideas, varying sentence patterns deliberately for meaning, interest, and style
topics.p: When {{name}} is writing for effect — like building tension in a story or structuring an argument — do they deliberately vary their sentence types, mixing short punchy sentences with longer, more complex ones?

topics.ds: Understand and use active and passive voice deliberately, and recognise verb moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, conditional) and their effects — choosing the appropriate voice and mood for purpose and audience
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a formal report or analysis, can they choose between active and passive voice deliberately — for example, using passive voice in a science write-up to sound objective and impersonal?

topics.ds: Sit correctly at a table holding a pencil comfortably and correctly; form lower-case letters in the correct direction starting and finishing in the right place
topics.p: When {{name}} sits down to write, do they hold their pencil comfortably and form each letter the right way — starting from the right place and going in the right direction?

topics.ds: Form capital letters correctly; print many upper- and lowercase letters legibly
topics.p: Can {{name}} write all the capital letters clearly and legibly so that someone reading their work can easily tell which letter is which?

topics.ds: Understand which letters belong to which handwriting families based on similar formation patterns and practise letters in groups
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that certain letters are formed in similar ways — for example, "c," "a," "d," and "g" all start with the same curved stroke — and practise those families together?

topics.ds: Form digits 0-9 correctly and legibly
topics.p: When {{name}} writes numbers like 3, 5, and 7, are they formed the right way and clearly readable — not reversed or written in an unusual direction?

topics.ds: Begin to join letters using diagonal and horizontal strokes, understanding which letter pairs are best left unjoined, forming letters of correct size relative to one another
topics.p: Is {{name}} starting to join up their letters when writing, so that their handwriting flows more smoothly rather than each letter standing completely separate?

topics.ds: Write words legibly and with growing fluency (speed and ease) using correctly formed unjoined upper- and lower-case letters
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a birthday card or a short note, can they write neatly at a steady pace without stopping to think how each letter goes?

topics.ds: Write words using clearly formed joined letters with developing fluency and automaticity, keeping handwriting legible when writing at pace
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a page of homework in joined-up writing, can they keep up a good speed without their writing becoming hard to read?

topics.ds: Apply phonic knowledge to blend sounds in unfamiliar words containing taught grapheme-phoneme correspondences; respond speedily to graphemes for all 40+ phonemes
topics.p: When {{name}} comes across a word they haven't seen before, can they sound it out bit by bit and blend the parts together to read it — even if it takes a moment?

topics.ds: Read and spell words containing consonant digraphs and less common consonant spellings (ch, sh, th, ck, tch, ng, ph, wh, k for /k/)
topics.p: When {{name}} sees words like 'shop', 'chip', 'ring', or 'photo', can they spot that two letters together make one sound and read the whole word correctly?

topics.ds: Recognise and name all uppercase and lowercase letters of the alphabet; name the letters in order and use letter names to distinguish between alternative spellings
topics.p: Can {{name}} point to any letter — capital or small — and tell you its name? And can they say the alphabet in order from A to Z?

topics.ds: Blend and segment onsets and rimes in single-syllable words; isolate and pronounce individual phonemes (initial, medial, final) in CVC words; add or substitute phonemes to make new words
topics.p: If you slowly say the sounds '/d/ /o/ /g/', can {{name}} blend them together and say 'dog'? And if you say 'cat', can they tell you the three separate sounds: /k/ /a/ /t/?

topics.ds: Recognise and produce rhyming words; join in with predictable phrases and rhymes in stories and poems; learn to appreciate and recite poems by heart
topics.p: When you read a rhyming book to {{name}}, do they join in and predict the rhyming words — and can they come up with their own rhyme for a simple word like 'cat'?

topics.ds: Know the primary sound for each consonant and the short and long sounds for the five major vowels; respond speedily to single-letter graphemes
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a letter and quickly say its sound — like 's' makes /s/, 'a' can make a short /a/ as in 'apple' or a long /ā/ as in 'cake'?

topics.ds: Demonstrate understanding that print carries meaning, follows left-to-right top-to-bottom directionality, and is organised page by page in books
topics.p: When {{name}} looks at a page in a picture book, do they know to start at the top-left and follow the words left to right, then move down to the next line?

topics.ds: Read and spell words containing common vowel digraphs (ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, oe, oo, oi, oy) including where a digraph can represent more than one sound
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a word like 'rain', 'boat', or 'moon', can they recognise the vowel pair that makes a special sound and read the whole word correctly?

topics.ds: Recognise and spell compound words by identifying the two component words that combine to form a single word
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a word like 'sunshine' or 'football' and spot the two smaller words hiding inside it?

topics.ds: Segment spoken sentences into individual words by clapping, tapping or moving a counter for each word heard (phonological awareness)
topics.p: If you say a short sentence like 'The big dog ran', can {{name}} clap once for each word and tell you how many words there were?

topics.ds: Read and spell words containing diphthongs and complex vowel patterns (ow, ou, ew, ue, ie, aw, au) and words ending in -y as a vowel sound
topics.p: Can {{name}} read words like 'town', 'cloud', 'flew', 'claw', or 'pie' — spotting the special vowel combinations and saying the right sound for each one?

topics.ds: Read and spell words containing r-controlled vowels (ar, er, ir, ur, or, ore) and vowel-r patterns where 'r' modifies the vowel sound
topics.p: When {{name}} reads words like 'car', 'bird', 'nurse', or 'fork', can they recognise that the 'r' after the vowel changes its sound, and read the word correctly?

topics.ds: Read and understand contractions with apostrophes, knowing the apostrophe represents omitted letters
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that 'can't' means 'cannot' and 'it's' means 'it is' — knowing the apostrophe stands for the missing letter or letters?

topics.ds: Read aloud books matched to phonic ability accurately and with growing fluency; reread familiar texts to build confidence, speed, and expression
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a book aloud at their level, can they get through most words without stumbling — sounding less like they're decoding and more like they're telling a story?

topics.ds: Read common high-frequency and exception words automatically by sight, including words with irregular spelling patterns
topics.p: Can {{name}} instantly recognise everyday words like 'said', 'was', 'they', 'come', and 'because' without needing to sound them out every time?

topics.ds: Read words containing taught GPCs with common inflectional endings (-s, -es, -ing, -ed, -er, -est) and the prefix un-; read multi-syllable words with taught patterns
topics.p: When {{name}} sees familiar words with different endings — like 'jumped', 'running', 'biggest', or 'unhappy' — can they spot the root word and read the whole thing correctly?

topics.ds: Read and spell words containing split digraphs (a-e, e-e, i-e, o-e, u-e) where a final 'e' makes the preceding vowel long
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that the 'e' at the end of words like 'cake', 'bike', or 'home' changes the vowel sound in the middle — making it say its name instead of its short sound?

topics.ds: Recognise and generate alliteration — words close together that start with the same sound — in spoken phrases, names and tongue twisters (phonological awareness)
topics.p: Can {{name}} make up a fun name where the words start with the same sound — like 'Bouncy Ben' — and spot the repeated sound in a tongue twister?

topics.ds: Count, blend, and segment syllables in spoken words; divide written words into syllables as an aid to reading and spelling
topics.p: Can {{name}} clap out the syllables in words — two claps for 'pen-cil' or three for 'com-pu-ter' — and split a spoken word into its parts?

topics.ds: Read and spell words containing trigraphs — three-letter graphemes representing a single sound (igh, air, ear, are)
topics.p: Can {{name}} recognise three-letter combinations like 'igh' in 'night', 'air' in 'chair', and 'ear' in 'hear' — knowing that all three letters together make just one sound?

topics.ds: Orally manipulate phonemes in spoken words by adding, deleting and substituting initial, medial and final phonemes to make new words (phonological awareness)
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to say 'slip' without the 's', or to change the middle sound of 'pin' to make 'pan', can they do it out loud?

topics.ds: Recognise alternative grapheme-phoneme correspondences for known phonemes (e.g., /dʒ/ as ge/dge/g, /s/ as c, /n/ as kn/gn, /r/ as wr, /ʒ/ as s), reading words with less common spellings for familiar sounds
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that the /j/ sound can be spelled different ways — like in 'jump', 'cage', and 'bridge' — and can they read words with these less common spellings?

topics.ds: Use consonant blends (clusters) together with short vowels, common long vowels and digraphs to write words, and blend them to read one- and two-syllable words
topics.p: When reading, can {{name}} sound out words like 'frog', 'jump' and 'blanket' — and spell them without leaving out a sound?

topics.ds: Read aloud with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression (prosody), re-reading familiar texts to build fluency and confidence, and using context to self-correct
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story aloud, do they vary their voice to match the mood — pausing at punctuation, slowing for sad parts, speeding up for excitement?

topics.ds: Orally segment spoken words into separate phonemes, including consonant blends (clusters) at the beginnings and ends of words, saying each consonant sound in the cluster separately (phonological awareness)
topics.p: If you say a word like 'jump' or 'stop', can {{name}} say each sound separately — j-u-m-p — without missing the sounds that are squashed together?

topics.ds: Decode words of two or more syllables by breaking them into syllable chunks, applying knowledge that every syllable must contain a vowel sound, and blending the parts together
topics.p: When {{name}} encounters a long word like 'fantastic' or 'umbrella', can they break it into syllables and blend the parts together to read the whole word?

topics.ds: Read Y3-4 exception words with unusual spelling-sound correspondences, applying growing knowledge of morphology and etymology to decode unfamiliar exception words
topics.p: Can {{name}} read trickier exception words — like 'ordinary', 'promise', 'recent', or 'island' — without being thrown off by the parts that don't follow the usual spelling rules?

topics.ds: Read words containing common prefixes and suffixes from the Y3-4 programme, applying knowledge of root words, prefixes and suffixes (morphology and etymology) to read aloud and understand new words
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a word like 'disappear' or 'comfortable', can they spot the root word and figure out what the prefix or suffix is adding to its meaning?

topics.ds: Manipulate more complex sounds in spoken words, including consonant clusters and the single sounds represented by digraphs (e.g. /ʃ/ spelt sh, /tʃ/ spelt ch), and use blending, segmenting, phoneme deletion and phoneme substitution to read and write words
topics.p: Can {{name}} play sound games like 'say black without the l' or 'change the ch in chop to sh' — and use the same trick to write new words?

topics.ds: Use phoneme–grapheme matches for consonant clusters, including three-letter clusters, when reading and writing words of one or more syllables and compound words, distinguishing letters from sounds: spl, str, scr and spr each represent three consonant phonemes, while thr and shr combine a digraph (th, sh) with r and represent only two consonant phonemes
topics.p: When reading, can {{name}} sound out tricky words like 'string', 'splash' or 'starfish' — and spell them with all the consonant sounds in place?

topics.ds: Predict what might happen next in a story based on what has been read so far; discuss the significance of titles and events
topics.p: When you stop midway through a story, can {{name}} make a reasonable guess about what might happen next — and explain why they think so based on what's happened so far?

topics.ds: Identify front cover, back cover, and title page of a book; identify the reasons an author gives to support points in informational text
topics.p: Can {{name}} find the contents page or index in a non-fiction book and use it to locate specific information — and do they understand why the author included those features?

topics.ds: Identify characters, settings, and major events in stories; become familiar with key stories, fairy tales, and traditional tales and retell them with key details in sequence
topics.p: After reading a fairy tale or story together, can {{name}} retell it to you in order — saying who was in it, where it happened, and what the main events were?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the adventures and experiences of characters in familiar stories; identify similarities and differences between two texts on the same topic
topics.p: If {{name}} has read two stories with similar themes — like two tales about a brave hero — can they tell you what was the same and what was different between them?

topics.ds: Link what is read or heard to own experiences; draw on background knowledge and vocabulary to support understanding of texts
topics.p: When {{name}} hears or reads a story about something familiar — like going to school or visiting a grandparent — do they connect it to their own life and use that to help understand what's happening?

topics.ds: Recognise common types of texts (storybooks, poems, non-fiction); name the author and illustrator and define the role of each in telling or presenting a text
topics.p: When you hand {{name}} a book, can they tell you whether it's a story or a fact book — and point out the author's name on the cover?

topics.ds: Participate in discussions about what is read, taking turns and listening to others; explain understanding clearly; actively engage in group reading activities
topics.p: When {{name}}'s class discusses a book they've all read, does {{name}} join in — sharing their own ideas and listening to what others think, even if their view is different?

topics.ds: Listen to and discuss poems, stories, and non-fiction at a level beyond independent reading; confirm understanding of texts read aloud by asking and answering questions about key details
topics.p: After you read a story aloud to {{name}}, can they answer questions about what happened — like who the main character was, where the story took place, and what the problem was?

topics.ds: Identify the main topic and retell key details of informational texts; describe connections between individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a short fact book — like one about animals or space — can they tell you what the main topic was and give you a few key facts they learned from it?

topics.ds: Describe the relationship between illustrations and the text in which they appear; use pictures to support and extend comprehension
topics.p: When {{name}} is reading a picture book, do they look at the illustrations to help them understand what's happening in the story — and can they explain how a picture connects to the words on the page?

topics.ds: Explore and compare how images contribute to meaning in different types of texts: illustrations that show characters and events in stories, and photographs, labelled diagrams and captions that give facts in informative texts
topics.p: When reading a book about animals with {{name}}, can they tell you what a photo or label shows — and how it's different from the drawings in a storybook?

topics.ds: Use visualising (making pictures in the mind from the words) and simple summarising to understand texts listened to, viewed or read: picturing what the words describe and telling what a text was mostly about
topics.p: When you read {{name}} a story without showing the pictures, can they describe or draw what they imagined — and tell you in a sentence what it was mostly about?

topics.ds: Ask and answer questions about key details in literary and informational texts; make simple inferences based on what characters say and do
topics.p: While reading a story, can {{name}} answer questions like "Why did the character do that?" or "How do you think they felt?" — using clues from the text rather than just guessing?

topics.ds: Understand the conventions of simple digital texts: swiping or tapping arrows to turn pages, scrolling, using home and back icons, and reading screen text top to bottom and left to right as in print
topics.p: When {{name}} uses a story app on a tablet, can they swipe to turn the page, scroll down, and use the back or home button to find their way?

topics.ds: Retell stories including key details in sequence, describe characters, settings, and major events using evidence from the text, and describe the overall structure of a story (beginning, middle, ending)
topics.p: After reading a story, can {{name}} describe the main character — including what kind of person they are, what they wanted, and how they felt at the end — using details from the book?

topics.ds: Explore and replicate the rhythms and sound patterns of nursery rhymes, chants and songs by clapping or tapping the beat and joining in with repeated sound patterns
topics.p: When you sing or say a nursery rhyme together, can {{name}} clap along to the beat and join in with the repeated sounds?

topics.ds: Check that text makes sense while reading and self-correct inaccurate reading by re-reading or using context
topics.p: When {{name}} is reading and something doesn't quite make sense, do they go back and re-read that part — or use the surrounding words to work out what a tricky word or sentence means?

topics.ds: Share ideas about stories, poems and images by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators, reflecting on experiences that are similar to or different from their own
topics.p: After hearing a picture book by an Australian or First Nations author, does {{name}} share what they thought — like how a character's life is the same as or different from theirs?

topics.ds: Understand that texts come in many forms — signs, labels, books, cards and digital texts on tablets or screens — and that each carries a message to be read
topics.p: When you're out walking, does {{name}} point to signs like STOP or the toilet sign and understand they are 'texts' with a message, just like books?

topics.ds: Identify familiar texts such as stories, information books, lists and recipes and say their purpose: to entertain, to give information or to tell us what to do
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to find out what koalas eat, do they know to pick an information book rather than a storybook — and can they say what each kind of book is for?

topics.ds: Discuss how authors' words and illustrators' images create characters, settings and events in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators
topics.p: When reading an Australian picture book, can {{name}} point to the words and pictures that show what a character or place is like?

topics.ds: Identify and compare characters' points of view, recognise who is narrating a story, describe how characters respond to events and challenges, and compare characters' experiences across different stories or versions of the same story
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story told from one character's point of view, can they think about how a different character in the same story might have seen events differently?

topics.ds: Recognise recurring literary language in stories and poetry, identify words and phrases that suggest feelings or appeal to the senses, and discuss favourite words and phrases
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a poem or a story with vivid language, can they pick out a phrase they really liked — and tell you why it works well or how it made them feel?

topics.ds: Explore how texts are organised in stages according to purpose: a recount (orientation, events in order, personal comment), a report (topic opener, facts grouped by feature) and a simple explanation (what happens and why, in steps)
topics.p: After a family outing, can {{name}} tell you about it in order — who was there, what happened first, next and last — and finish with what they thought of it?

topics.ds: Identify the main topic of a multi-paragraph informational text, determine the focus of specific paragraphs, and explain how key details support the main idea
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a multi-page article — like a school text about a historical event — can they tell you the main idea and then explain what each section was specifically about?

topics.ds: Use visualising as a comprehension strategy when listening, viewing and reading: building and revising a mental picture from descriptive words to support literal and inferred meaning
topics.p: When reading a chapter book with no pictures, can {{name}} describe or draw the picture in their head — and change it when new details come up?

topics.ds: Navigate print and screen texts using chapters, tables of contents, indexes, side-bar menus, drop-down menus and links to find information
topics.p: When looking something up on a kids' website, can {{name}} use the menu down the side or a drop-down list, and click links to find what they need?

topics.ds: Understand how screen texts are organised and navigated using navigation buttons, swipe screens, links, images and voice commands, alongside print features such as page numbers, contents and headings
topics.p: When using a kids' website or e-book, can {{name}} tap the buttons or links to find what they want — and get back to where they started?

topics.ds: Recognise different non-fiction text structures and features (headings, contents, glossary, index), understanding how texts are organised to present information
topics.p: When {{name}} is using a non-fiction book for a school project, do they know how to use the headings, contents page, and index to find what they need quickly?

topics.ds: Describe similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, including simple persuasive texts such as posters, ads and letters that try to get the reader to do or think something
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a toy ad or a poster for an event, can they tell it's trying to convince them — and how that's different from a storybook or a fact book?

topics.ds: Discuss the sequence of events in narrative texts and how items of information are related in non-fiction, retelling stories including key details and demonstrating understanding of central message or lesson
topics.p: After {{name}} finishes a chapter book, can they explain the beginning, middle, and end in their own words — and describe what the story was really about at its heart?

topics.ds: Explore how repeated lines, rhyming words and a steady rhythm link the parts of simple poems, chants and songs so that they hang together (cohesion) and are easy to remember
topics.p: When {{name}} sings a favourite song or chant, do they notice the line that keeps repeating and the rhyming words that make it easy to remember?

topics.ds: Recognise different forms of poetry (free verse, narrative poetry, haiku) and discuss their features; prepare poems and play scripts to read aloud and perform with understanding through intonation, tone, volume and action
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a poem aloud, do they change their voice to match the mood — reading excitedly for a lively poem or quietly for a sad one — rather than reading it flat?

topics.ds: Discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators — how a place shapes what characters do and feel, and how characters belong to or change a place
topics.p: When reading a story set in the Australian bush or by the sea, can {{name}} explain how the place affects what the characters do or feel?

topics.ds: Identify and describe how texts across the curriculum — such as science procedures, maths word problems, history recounts and health posters — are organised differently and use language features suited to their purposes
topics.p: When {{name}} does homework, do they notice that a science experiment sheet, a maths word problem and a history story are set out differently — and why?

topics.ds: Draw inferences from independently-read texts, such as inferring characters' feelings, thoughts and motives from their actions, and justifying inferences with evidence from the text
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a chapter of a novel, can they explain how a character was feeling and why — pointing to something the character said or did as their evidence?

topics.ds: Identify main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph and summarise them; retrieve and record information from non-fiction texts using notes, tables or other methods
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a long non-fiction article or chapter, can they pull out the most important points and write them as a short summary — rather than just copying chunks of text?

topics.ds: Identify how similar topics and information are presented in different types of texts, such as a poem, an information report, a website and a picture book about the same subject
