topics.p: If {{name}} reads a poem and a fact book about the same thing — say, the ocean — can they tell you how each one shares information differently?

topics.ds: Determine the central message, lesson, or moral of a story, fable, or folktale, explaining what the story teaches the reader and supporting the interpretation with key details from the text
topics.p: After reading a fable like "The Tortoise and the Hare", can {{name}} tell you the lesson the story is teaching — and point to a moment in the story that shows that lesson?

topics.ds: Identify how language choices, text structure and presentational features (illustrations, diagrams, bold print, layout) contribute to the overall meaning and effect of a text
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a page with headings, diagrams, or bold words, can they explain how those features help — like "the diagram shows the water cycle because the words alone are hard to picture"?

topics.ds: Identify recurring themes (good vs evil, friendship, bravery) and conventions (once upon a time, moral at the end, hero's journey) across a wide range of books including fairy stories, myths, legends and traditional tales
topics.p: After reading a few different fairy tales or myths, can {{name}} spot patterns — like "the hero always faces three challenges" or "good always wins in the end" — across the different stories?

topics.ds: Identify the purpose and intended audience of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, using clues such as topic, words, pictures and where the text appears
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a school newsletter, a toddler's book or a toy ad, can they say who it's meant for and point to a clue?

topics.ds: Distinguish one's own point of view from that of the author of an informational text and identify the author's purpose
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a fact book or an article, can they tell you what the author's purpose was — like whether they were trying to inform, persuade, or entertain — and whether they agree with the author's viewpoint?

topics.ds: Discuss characters and settings across a range of texts and identify how language — adjectives, verbs, dialogue and descriptive phrases — presents them in different ways
topics.p: Can {{name}} point to the words in a story that show a character is grumpy or kind — like 'stomped' or 'giggled'?

topics.ds: Analyse character traits, motivations, and feelings using text evidence, and distinguish one's own point of view from that of the narrator or characters
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story, can they describe why a character made a particular choice — explaining their motivations — and also say whether they personally agree with what the character did?

topics.ds: Identify the audience and purpose of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts through their use of language features and images
topics.p: When {{name}} looks at a poster or ad, can they use the pictures and words to tell who it's for and what it's trying to do?

topics.ds: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably, combining and comparing what each source contributes
topics.p: If {{name}} is researching a topic using two different books or articles, can they combine the information they've gathered from both to talk or write about the subject more fully than either source alone?

topics.ds: Describe connections between events, ideas, or concepts in informational text using time, sequence, cause-and-effect, and comparison language, and identify logical connections between sentences and paragraphs
topics.p: After reading a non-fiction passage — like one about climate or history — can {{name}} explain what caused something to happen, what the effect was, and how the author linked those ideas together?

topics.ds: Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story or drama, drawing on specific details from the text such as a character's thoughts, words, actions, and interactions
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a chapter where an important event happens, can they write or talk about it in detail — describing what the character thought, said, and did, using specific words and moments from the text?

topics.ds: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively in informational texts (e.g., charts, graphs, diagrams, timelines, animations) and explain how it contributes to understanding the text
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a non-fiction article that includes a chart or timeline, can they explain what extra information those visuals add — beyond what the written text says?

topics.ds: Identify the purpose of layout features in print and digital texts (headings, columns, banners, sidebars, text boxes, icons) and the words used for navigation such as home, back, menu, search and next
topics.p: On a website, does {{name}} know what 'home', 'back', 'menu' and 'search' do — and use them to find what they need?

topics.n: Morals in Fables, Folktales and Myths
topics.ds: Explain how the central message, lesson, or moral of a story is conveyed through key details across diverse text types including fables, folktales, and myths
topics.p: After reading a myth or folktale from another culture, can {{name}} explain what lesson or value it was teaching — and say which details in the story showed that?

topics.ds: Discuss the effects of literary devices such as rhythm and onomatopoeia in poetry and prose: how they enhance meaning and shape the reader's reaction
topics.p: When reading a poem or story with 'sound words' like 'crash' or 'sizzle', can {{name}} explain how they help them hear or feel what's happening?

topics.ds: Recognise how texts with similar purposes are created differently for different audiences, by comparing word choice, sentence length, images and layout
topics.p: If {{name}} sees two ads or books on the same topic — one for little kids and one for grown-ups — can they spot how they're written differently?

topics.ds: Discuss characters, events and settings in different contexts (places, times, cultures) in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators
topics.p: When reading a story set somewhere very different — the outback, a big city, or long ago — can {{name}} explain how the place and time shape what happens to the characters?

topics.ds: Use structural terminology (chapter, scene, stanza) to refer to parts of literary texts and describe how each successive part builds on earlier sections
topics.p: When {{name}} talks about a book they're reading, do they use words like "chapter", "stanza", or "scene" correctly — and can they explain how a later chapter builds on what happened earlier?

topics.ds: Describe the overall structure of an informational text (chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) and explain how the author's chosen structure helps convey information and ideas
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a non-fiction text, can they identify how it's organised — for example, "this one is structured as a problem and solution" or "this one goes through events in time order" — and explain why that structure works?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the treatment of similar themes, topics, and story patterns (e.g., good vs evil, quest narratives, trickster tales) in stories, myths, and traditional literature from different cultures
topics.p: If {{name}} has read two quest stories from different cultures — like a Greek myth and a West African folktale — can they compare how each treats the hero's journey and what values each story prizes?

topics.ds: Use comprehension strategies when listening to and viewing texts (films, videos, podcasts, multimodal texts) to build literal and inferred meaning, and begin to evaluate texts using knowledge of context, structure and language features
topics.p: After watching a short film or kids' documentary, can {{name}} tell you what happened, why a character acted that way, and whether they thought it was good — with a reason?

topics.ds: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as used in literary texts, including understanding references to mythology and cultural allusions (e.g., Herculean, Achilles' heel)
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story that mentions something like "a Herculean task" or "an Achilles heel", can they work out what it means — or look it up and explain the mythological reference behind it?

topics.ds: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in an informational text, including what happened and why, by citing specific textual evidence about causes, effects, and steps in a process
topics.p: After reading a non-fiction article that explains how something works — like how volcanoes form — can {{name}} write down the main steps or causes in their own words, citing the specific evidence the author used?

topics.ds: Distinguish between statements of fact and statements of opinion in texts, recognising how authors blend factual information with subjective viewpoints
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a newspaper article or non-fiction text, can they point out which parts are facts and which parts are the author's opinions — and explain how they can tell the difference?

topics.ds: Determine the theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text, and provide an objective summary that captures the key events without personal opinions
topics.p: After reading a novel or a poem, can {{name}} explain the theme — like "it's about not giving up" — and then write a brief summary of the plot without mixing it up with their own opinions?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast a firsthand account (autobiography, diary, letter) with a secondhand account (biography, textbook, news report) of the same event or topic, identifying differences in focus and information provided
topics.p: If {{name}} reads both a diary entry by someone who was at a historical event and a textbook account of the same event, can they explain what's different about the two — like what details each one includes and why?

topics.ds: Identify text navigation features of online texts that enhance readability, including headlines, drop-down menus, links, graphics and layout, and explain how each helps the reader
topics.p: When reading a kids' news site, can {{name}} use the headlines, menus and links to find a story — and say what makes one website easier to read than another?

topics.ds: Explain how an author of an informational text uses reasons and evidence to support particular points, evaluating whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient
topics.p: After reading a persuasive article — like one arguing for or against something — can {{name}} identify the reasons the author gives and say whether each one is convincing and well-supported?

topics.ds: Explore the effect of choices in framing (close-up, mid shot, long shot), placement of elements and salience (what stands out through size, colour, light or position) on the composition of still and moving images in texts
topics.p: When looking at a picture book or a movie scene, can {{name}} explain why the illustrator zoomed in close, or made one thing bigger or brighter than the rest?

topics.n: How Language Choices Affect the Reader
topics.ds: Evaluate how authors use language including figurative language, considering the impact of word choices, imagery, and literary devices on the reader
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a descriptive passage with figurative language — like "the sun was a burning eye" — can they explain what image or feeling the author was creating and whether it was effective?

topics.n: How Parts Build a Whole Text
topics.ds: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to provide the overall structure of a story, drama, or poem, analysing how each part contributes to the whole
topics.p: After finishing a novel, can {{name}} explain how each chapter contributed to the whole — like how an early chapter introduced a tension that wasn't resolved until much later?

topics.ds: Provide reasoned justifications for views about texts, supporting interpretations and opinions with evidence and logical arguments
topics.p: When {{name}} shares an opinion about a book — like "I think the villain had a point" — can they back it up with specific quotes or events from the text, rather than just saying how they feel?

topics.ds: Analyse multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent
topics.p: If {{name}} reads two different accounts of the same event — like two news articles covering the same story — can they explain what each account emphasises, what each leaves out, and why the perspectives differ?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrated, including distinguishing between first-person and third-person narration and explaining how the narrator's perspective shapes the reader's understanding
topics.p: After reading a story written in first person, can {{name}} explain how the story might feel different if it were told by a different character or by a narrator watching from the outside?

topics.ds: Compare texts from different times with similar purposes and audiences (e.g. an older and a modern news report, school reader or advertisement) to identify similarities and differences in how they depict events
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at an old newspaper or ad and a modern one about the same kind of thing, can they spot how the language and pictures have changed?

topics.ds: Explain major differences between poems, drama, and prose, identifying structural elements unique to each form: verse, rhythm, and meter in poetry; cast of characters, dialogue, and stage directions in drama; chapters and paragraphs in prose
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a poem, a play, and a chapter from a novel and explain how each is laid out differently — for example, that a play has stage directions and a poem has verses?

topics.ds: Examine the use of literary devices and deliberate word play in literary texts, including poetry, to shape meaning: puns, invented words, double meanings and nonsense verse
topics.p: Does {{name}} get the joke in a pun or a silly made-up word in a poem — and can they explain the double meaning?

topics.ds: Recommend books to peers, giving reasons for choices based on knowledge of a wide range of genres, authors, and themes, and making comparisons within and across books
topics.p: When {{name}} recommends a book to a friend, can they explain clearly why they think that person would enjoy it — mentioning the genre, characters, and themes rather than just saying "it's good"?

topics.ds: Recognise similar storylines, ideas and relationships in different contexts in literary texts by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors
topics.p: When reading, does {{name}} notice when two stories from different places — like an Australian story and a fairytale from overseas — have a similar plot or message?

topics.ds: Identify how texts across the curriculum have different language features and are typically organised into characteristic stages depending on purpose (e.g. procedure: goal, materials, steps; explanation: phenomenon, sequence of causes; report: classification, description; recount: orientation, events, reorientation)
topics.p: When {{name}} writes for science or history, do they know how that kind of text is usually set out — like the steps of an experiment or the stages of a recount?

topics.ds: Make connections between the text of a story or drama and a visual or oral presentation of the text, identifying where each version reflects specific descriptions and directions from the text
topics.p: If {{name}} has read a book and then seen a film version, can they compare the two — pointing out moments where the film showed something differently from how the book described it?

topics.ds: Use visualising together with other comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning, expand topic knowledge and evaluate texts
topics.p: After reading a chapter, can {{name}} describe the scene they pictured — using the author's words — and say whether the movie version matched the book?

topics.ds: Make comparisons within and across books, identifying similarities and differences in themes, characters, settings, and authorial choices across multiple texts
topics.p: After reading a few books by the same author or in the same genre, can {{name}} compare them — discussing what themes, styles, or character types the author tends to use?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details about how characters interact, settings influence action, or events connect
topics.p: After reading a novel with several main characters, can {{name}} compare two of them in detail — explaining how their personalities, experiences, and relationships are both similar and different?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more informational texts, identifying patterns such as chronology, comparison, cause/effect, or problem/solution
topics.p: If {{name}} reads two non-fiction texts about the same topic that are organised differently — one in time order and one comparing two sides — can they describe those structural differences and explain how each one shapes the reader's experience?

topics.ds: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described, recognising the difference between limited and omniscient narration and how perspective shapes storytelling
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how a story told by an all-knowing narrator feels different from one told by a single character who only knows their own side — and give an example of how that changes what the reader knows?

topics.ds: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in historical, scientific, or technical texts based on specific information
topics.p: After reading a history or science text about how two events or discoveries were connected, can {{name}} explain that relationship clearly — describing how one thing led to or influenced the other?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre on their approaches to similar themes and topics, identifying how different authors treat common ideas
topics.p: After reading two adventure stories in the same genre, can {{name}} compare how each author handled similar elements — like the hero's challenge or the resolution — and say which approach they preferred and why?

topics.ds: Explain how the sequence of images in print, digital and film texts (picture-book spreads, comic panels, slideshow images, film shots) affects meaning, pacing and the reader's or viewer's response
topics.p: When reading a comic or watching a movie scene, can {{name}} explain how the order of the pictures or shots builds suspense or tells the story?

topics.ds: Analyse how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text such as graphic novels, multimedia presentations, or illustrated editions of fiction and poetry
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a graphic novel or illustrated book, can they explain how the pictures and layout — not just the words — help tell the story or create a particular mood?

topics.ds: Examine the effects of imagery, including simile, metaphor and personification, and of sound devices such as alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia and rhyme in narratives, poetry and songs
topics.p: When listening to a song or poem, can {{name}} notice when the writer makes the wind 'howl' like a person, or repeats sounds — and say what feeling that creates?

topics.ds: Quote accurately from literary and informational texts when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences, using quotation marks and citations correctly
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about a book or article for school, do they quote from the text directly — putting the exact words in speech marks — to support their points?

topics.ds: Identify aspects of literary texts that represent details or information about historical, social and cultural contexts, in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story set in the past or in another culture, can they point out the details — clothes, jobs, rules, events — that show what life was like then and there?

topics.ds: Navigate and read texts for specific purposes, monitoring meaning using the strategies of skimming (for gist), scanning (for specific details) and confirming (re-reading to check information)
topics.p: When {{name}} needs a fact for homework, can they quickly skim a page for the main idea, scan for the exact detail, and then re-read to check they got it right?

topics.ds: Describe how spoken, written and multimodal texts use language features and are organised into characteristic stages and phases depending on purpose (e.g. a speech's introduction, points and conclusion; a documentary's hook, explanation and summary; a podcast interview's introduction, questions and sign-off)
topics.p: When watching a kids' documentary or listening to a podcast, can {{name}} notice how it's structured — the hook at the start, the main parts, and the wrap-up?

topics.ds: Determine two or more main ideas of an informational text and explain how they are supported by key details, then summarise the text without personal opinions
topics.p: After reading a long non-fiction article, can {{name}} identify two or three main ideas it covers and write a brief summary that captures all of them — without adding their own opinions?

topics.ds: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which specific points
topics.p: After reading a persuasive text, can {{name}} map out which reasons the author uses to support which specific points — showing that they understand the structure of the argument, not just the conclusion?

topics.ds: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably, combining information without plagiarising
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a school report using several sources, do they bring together information from all of them into their own words — rather than just quoting or copying from one source at a time?

topics.ds: Describe the ways in which a text reflects the time and place in which it was created, through its language, values, references, technology and images
topics.p: When {{name}} reads an old poem or watches an old ad, can they spot the clues — words, ideas or technology — that show when and where it was made?

topics.ds: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or solve a problem efficiently
topics.p: When {{name}} needs to answer a research question for school, can they search across several books or websites to find the relevant information quickly — rather than reading every source from start to finish?

topics.ds: Use visualising with other comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning from complex literary and informative texts, to evaluate information and ideas, and to connect and compare content across sources
topics.p: When {{name}} reads about something complicated — like how a volcano erupts — can they picture it in their head or sketch it to check they understand?

topics.ds: Analyse how a text's structure — including its overall organisation, use of chapters, stanzas, scenes, paragraphs, or sections — contributes to its meaning, style, and development of ideas
topics.p: When {{name}} analyses a poem or novel, can they explain how the author's structural choices — like starting in the middle of the action, or ending with a repeated image — shape the overall meaning of the text?

topics.ds: Explain how texts across the curriculum are organised into characteristic stages and phases depending on purpose, and recognise how authors adapt or blend text structures and language features (e.g. a narrative used to inform in science, a persuasive information text, a historical diary used to recount)
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a science book written like a story, or a campaign website that mixes facts and persuasion, can they explain how the author blended text types — and why?

topics.ds: Make critical comparisons across texts — comparing themes, characters, settings, styles, or arguments in two or more works, including texts from different periods, genres, or cultures
topics.p: After reading texts from very different times or cultures, can {{name}} compare them thoughtfully — noting not just surface similarities but deeper differences in values, style, and what the author assumed about their reader?

topics.ds: Evaluate arguments and claims in non-fiction texts — assess whether reasoning is sound, evidence is relevant and sufficient, distinguish between fact and opinion, and recognise bias, propaganda, and rhetorical techniques
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a persuasive piece — like an editorial or a speech — can they identify the rhetorical techniques being used, evaluate whether the argument is logically sound, and explain what might be biased or misleading?

topics.ds: Determine the meaning of figurative and connotative language in context, analyse the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, and identify literary devices such as metaphor, simile, personification, allusion, and irony
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a passage containing a metaphor, irony, or allusion, can they explain what the author really meant — going beyond the literal words to describe the effect that device creates for the reader?

topics.ds: Identify responses to characters and events in literary texts that are drawn from historical, social or cultural contexts, in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors, including how readers' own contexts shape their responses
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story about the past or another culture, can they explain why people from different backgrounds might feel differently about a character or event?

topics.ds: Examine texts, including media texts (news reports, ads, social media posts, documentaries), that represent ideas and events, and identify how they reflect the context — time, place, culture and audience — in which they were created
topics.p: When watching the news or an ad, can {{name}} explain how it reflects the time, place and people it was made for — and how it might look different elsewhere?

topics.ds: Analyse point of view and narrative perspective — including first person, third person limited and omniscient, and unreliable narrator — and how the author's or narrator's perspective shapes the reader's understanding and creates effects such as suspense, irony, or humour
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story with an unreliable narrator — where the person telling the story isn't fully trustworthy — can they spot the clues that suggest the narrator isn't giving the full picture?

topics.ds: Analyse how plot structure unfolds through episodes or key events, and how characters develop, respond to challenges, and change over the course of a narrative — including the relationship between character, setting, and plot
topics.p: After reading a novel, can {{name}} explain how the main character changed from the beginning to the end — pointing to specific events that caused that change and how the setting shaped who they became?

topics.ds: Recognise and understand poetic conventions — including form (sonnet, ballad, free verse), metre, rhyme scheme, stanza structure, imagery, and sound devices (alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia) — and analyse how poets use them for effect
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a poem, can they identify its form — like a sonnet or a ballad — and explain how the poet's use of rhyme, rhythm, and imagery contributes to the poem's meaning or emotional impact?

topics.ds: Identify the purpose, audience, and context of a text and use this knowledge to support comprehension — recognising how writing aimed at different audiences (academic, popular, persuasive) uses different conventions, register, and tone
topics.p: When {{name}} reads something written for a very different audience — like a scientific journal article versus a children's book on the same topic — can they explain how the purpose and audience shaped the language, tone, and structure?

topics.ds: Identify and explain the characteristics that define an author's individual style — recurring themes, sentence patterns, vocabulary, humour, narrative voice, structures such as twist endings, and illustration style
topics.p: After reading several books by a favourite author, can {{name}} describe what makes that author's writing recognisable — like their twist endings or kind of humour?

topics.ds: Explain the way authors use sound devices (alliteration, assonance, rhythm, rhyme, onomatopoeia) together with imagery to create meaning and effect in poetry
topics.p: When reading a poem aloud, can {{name}} explain how its rhythm and repeated sounds help create a feeling — like the galloping beat of a horse-riding poem?

topics.ds: Determine and analyse the theme or central idea of a text, trace how it develops across the text through key details and events, and provide an objective summary distinct from personal opinion
topics.p: After reading a novel or long poem, can {{name}} explain what it was really about at its deepest level — the central idea or theme — and trace how that idea developed through key moments in the text?

topics.ds: Understand how dramatists communicate meaning through performance — including staging, direction, set design, lighting, and actors' choices — and how different productions can interpret the same script differently
topics.p: After watching a stage or film production of a play they've read, can {{name}} discuss how specific choices — like the lighting, the actor's tone, or the set design — interpreted the script, and whether they agreed with those choices?

topics.ds: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of what a text says explicitly and what can be inferred, distinguishing between strong and weak evidence and explaining how the evidence supports a point
topics.p: When {{name}} makes a point about a text in class or in writing, do they back it up with a specific quote or reference — and can they explain whether that evidence strongly supports their point or only weakly?

topics.ds: Read widely and independently across fiction and non-fiction — including whole novels, short stories, plays, poetry, and non-fiction from different genres, periods, and cultures — building stamina, breadth, and personal taste as a reader
topics.p: Does {{name}} read for pleasure across a wide range of books — fiction, non-fiction, poetry, plays — and can they talk enthusiastically about authors, genres, or themes they've discovered on their own?

topics.ds: Ask relevant questions to extend understanding; ask and answer questions to seek help, get information, or clarify something not understood
topics.p: If {{name}} doesn't understand something — like instructions for a game or an explanation from a teacher — do they ask a question to find out more rather than just guessing?

topics.ds: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events with detail; speak audibly and express thoughts, feelings, and ideas clearly; give well-structured descriptions and explanations
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you about something that happened — like a trip or a film — in enough detail that you could really picture it, speaking clearly so you can follow along?

topics.ds: Use spoken language to develop understanding through speculating, hypothesising, imagining, and exploring ideas; use strategies to build vocabulary through talk
topics.p: When {{name}} is trying to figure something out — like why something happened in a story or how something works — do they talk through their ideas out loud and explore possibilities before settling on an answer?

topics.ds: Articulate and justify answers, arguments, and opinions; participate in discussions, presentations, performances, role play, and debates
topics.p: When {{name}} disagrees with something or has an opinion, can they say why they think that and back it up with a reason rather than just saying "because I just do"?

topics.ds: Participate actively in collaborative conversations staying on topic; continue a conversation through multiple exchanges; maintain attention in discussions
topics.p: When {{name}} is chatting with a friend or taking part in a group activity, can they keep a conversation going back and forth — listening, responding, and building on what the other person said?

topics.ds: Listen and respond appropriately to adults and peers; follow agreed-upon rules for discussion such as listening to others and taking turns speaking
topics.p: When {{name}} is in a group conversation at school or at the dinner table, do they listen while others are talking and wait for their turn before speaking?

topics.ds: Explore how the words and greetings people use change between home and school depending on the relationship with the person they are talking to (family, friends, teacher, principal, visitor)
topics.p: When {{name}} talks to their teacher, do they notice they speak a bit differently than with family at home — like saying 'Good morning, Ms Lee' instead of 'Hi'?

topics.ds: Understand how language, facial expressions and gestures work together when asking for and giving information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands
topics.p: When {{name}} wants something at the dinner table, do they ask with polite words and a friendly face — and can they offer things to others, like 'Would you like some?'

topics.ds: Learn poems by heart and recite with appropriate intonation, adding visual displays to descriptions when appropriate, and producing complete sentences in spoken presentations
topics.p: Can {{name}} memorise a short poem and recite it with expression — changing their voice to match the mood of the words?

topics.ds: Create and deliver short oral and multimodal presentations on personal and learnt topics with an opening statement, middle details and a concluding statement, using some topic words and appropriate gesture, volume and pace
topics.p: When {{name}} does show-and-tell, do they start by saying what they'll talk about, give a couple of details, and finish with a closing sentence — at a good pace?

topics.ds: Gain, maintain and monitor the interest of listeners when speaking; consider and evaluate different viewpoints, attending to and building on others' contributions; begin to select appropriate language for different situations
topics.p: When {{name}} is talking in a group, do they notice if people are losing interest and adjust how they're speaking — or pick up on what others have said and add to it thoughtfully?

topics.ds: Use interaction skills to receive and give spoken instructions: listening for each step, asking to clarify, and giving clear, ordered instructions to others
topics.p: If you give {{name}} three or four steps — like 'get your shoes, then your hat, then wait at the door' — can they follow them in order, and give clear instructions to someone else?

topics.ds: Investigate how interpersonal language choices change with the context and the role taken in an interaction, such as leader, helper, host, guest, customer or shopkeeper
topics.p: When {{name}} plays shop or has a friend over, do they change how they talk to suit their role — like 'How can I help you?' as the shopkeeper or 'Thanks for having me' as a guest?

topics.ds: Report on a topic or recount an experience with organised facts and descriptive details, speaking clearly at an understandable pace
topics.p: Can {{name}} give a short talk about a topic they've researched — presenting the key facts in a logical order and speaking clearly enough for others to follow?

topics.ds: Plan, rehearse and deliver short presentations that use topic-specific and precise vocabulary to inform, express opinions or tell stories
topics.p: When {{name}} gives a talk or explains a school topic, do they use the proper words — like 'tadpole' or 'metamorphosis' — instead of 'thing' or 'stuff'?

topics.n: Preparing for and Explaining in Discussions
topics.ds: Come to discussions prepared, draw on preparation and known information, and explain ideas in light of the discussion
topics.p: If {{name}} knows they're going to discuss a topic in class, do they think about it beforehand and come ready with ideas or facts to share?

topics.ds: Pose and respond to specific questions in discussions, making comments that contribute to the discussion and elaborate on the remarks of others
topics.p: In a class discussion, does {{name}} ask questions that move the conversation forward and add comments that build on what others have said rather than just repeating the same ideas?

topics.n: Identifying Reasons Behind a Speaker's Points
topics.ds: Identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points, evaluating whether the reasoning is logical and the evidence is relevant
topics.p: When {{name}} listens to someone making an argument or giving reasons for something, can they tell you whether the reasons given actually support what the person is claiming?

topics.ds: Explore language used to develop and maintain relationships in formal and informal situations: greetings, compliments, inclusive language ('we', 'let's'), encouragement, apologies and thanks
topics.p: When {{name}} works with friends or writes a thank-you note, do they use words that build friendships — like 'Let's try your idea' or 'Thanks so much for...'?

topics.ds: Paraphrase portions of a text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats, capturing the key ideas accurately in one's own words
topics.p: If {{name}} listens to a short talk or watches a video clip about a topic, can they explain the main points back to you in their own words?

topics.ds: Plan, rehearse and deliver a structured spoken argument using subjective language for opinion and objective language for facts, complex sentences, visual features and deliberate control of tone, pitch, pace and volume
topics.p: Could {{name}} stand up and argue for something they believe in — like a longer lunch break — giving reasons, a fact or two, and a strong ending?

topics.ds: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, using formal English when appropriate to task and situation while adjusting tone, vocabulary, and style for different audiences
topics.p: Does {{name}} naturally speak differently depending on who they're talking to — for example, more formally with a teacher than with a friend at the playground?

topics.ds: Review the key ideas expressed in discussions and draw conclusions in light of information and knowledge gained from the discussion
topics.p: After a group discussion, can {{name}} pull together the main points that were made and explain what conclusion the group reached?

topics.ds: Summarise the points a speaker makes and explain how each claim is supported by reasons and evidence, evaluating the logic and relevance of the support
topics.p: When {{name}} listens to a speaker making a case for something, can they explain back to you both what the speaker claimed and the reasons and evidence they gave to back it up?

topics.ds: Understand that language is selected for social contexts and signals social roles and relationships, and that it becomes more formal and impersonal as formality and social distance (how well people know each other) increase
topics.p: Does {{name}} change how they write or speak depending on who it's for — chatting with a friend versus emailing someone they've never met — and can they explain why?

topics.ds: Include multimedia components and visual displays in presentations when appropriate to enhance the development of main ideas or themes
topics.p: When {{name}} gives a presentation at school, do they think about including things like diagrams, slides, or pictures to help make their points clearer for the audience?

topics.ds: Summarise a written text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats including visually, quantitatively, and orally
topics.p: After listening to a talk or watching an informational video, can {{name}} give you a spoken summary of what the main message was in their own words?

topics.ds: Plan, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that sequence elaborated ideas using complex sentences and specialist and technical vocabulary, with visual and digital features and deliberate use of pitch, tone, pace and volume
topics.p: When {{name}} presents a project, do they use the proper technical words — like 'evaporation' or 'condensation' — and explain ideas with linked sentences like 'When... it...'?

topics.ds: Improvise, rehearse, and perform play scripts and poetry — using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness, and action to generate language, explore meaning, and add impact to performance
topics.p: When {{name}} performs in a play or reads aloud from a script, do they use their voice — volume, pace, and expression — to bring the character or poem to life?

topics.ds: Plan, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that include information, arguments and details that develop a theme or idea, organised with precise topic-specific and technical vocabulary and with visual and digital features
topics.p: Could {{name}} give a presentation where every point builds one big idea — like 'small actions can protect our oceans' — with slides to back up each point?

topics.ds: Use Standard English confidently in formal and informal spoken contexts — give short speeches and presentations expressing own ideas clearly, keeping to the point, and adapting register and vocabulary to the audience
topics.p: Can {{name}} give a short prepared speech or presentation in Standard English — staying on point and adjusting their vocabulary to suit the audience?

topics.ds: Participate in formal debates and structured discussions — presenting a position with supporting evidence, responding to others’ points, summarising and building on what has been said, and following rules of discussion
topics.p: Has {{name}} taken part in a school debate where they had to argue a position with evidence, respond to the other side's points, and keep to the rules of formal discussion?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of phonics and word structure — phoneme, grapheme, GPC (grapheme-phoneme correspondence), blend, segment, digraph, CVC, vowel, consonant, syllable, root word, suffix, prefix, and homophone — and understand that these words describe the building blocks that phonics instruction is built on
topics.p: When {{name}}'s teacher asks them to 'segment a word into phonemes' or spot a 'digraph', do they understand what those words mean and can they do the task without looking confused?

topics.ds: Segment spoken words into phonemes and spell CVC and simple phonetically regular words by writing a letter or letters for each sound
topics.p: Can {{name}} listen to a simple word like "cat" or "ship" and write down the letters for each sound they hear?

topics.ds: Write simple sentences from memory when dictated by the teacher, applying taught GPCs, spelling rules, and common exception words
topics.p: If you read a sentence out loud to {{name}} and ask them to write it down, can they spell the words correctly and put the letters in the right order?

topics.ds: Spell words with common suffixes (-s/-es for plurals and third person verbs, -ing, -ed, -er, -est) where no change to the root word is needed
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about more than one dog or talks about something that is happening now, do they add the right ending — like "dogs" or "jumping" — without making spelling mistakes?

topics.ds: Spell words using the prefix un- to change meaning; understand that un- creates opposites or reverses actions
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that adding "un-" to the front of a word like "happy" or "lock" flips its meaning, and can they spell those words correctly?

topics.ds: Spell common exception words from memory that do not follow regular phonic patterns, including the days of the week
topics.p: Can {{name}} spell tricky everyday words like "said," "were," "come," and the days of the week from memory without needing to sound them out?

topics.ds: Spell words using alternative grapheme choices for known phonemes, learning new spellings for sounds already encountered (e.g., /ɔ:/ as 'a' before ll, /ʌ/ as 'o', words ending -tion), including distinguishing common homophones
topics.p: When {{name}} writes and comes across a word where the same sound can be spelled different ways — like "see" and "sea" — do they know which spelling to use?

topics.ds: Use the possessive apostrophe with singular nouns to show ownership (e.g., the girl's book, the dog's bone)
topics.p: When {{name}} writes something belonging to one person or thing — like "the dog's lead" or "the girl's bag" — do they put the apostrophe in the right place?

topics.ds: Spell contracted forms correctly by placing the apostrophe where letters are omitted (can't, didn't, I'll, it's, etc.)
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a short form like "can't" or "didn't," do they put the apostrophe in the right place to show where letters are missing?

topics.ds: Apply suffix spelling rules that require changes to the root word: dropping final -e before vowel suffixes, changing -y to -i, doubling final consonants in short-vowel words; use suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful, -less, -ly
topics.p: When {{name}} adds an ending like "-ing" or "-ed" to a word, do they know when to drop a silent "e," double the last letter, or change a "y" to an "i" — for example, "running," "baked," or "happily"?

topics.ds: Use the possessive apostrophe accurately with both regular and irregular plural nouns (e.g., the girls' bags, the children's toys), distinguishing singular from plural possession
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about something belonging to a group — like "the children's coats" or "the teachers' cars" — do they put the apostrophe in the right place?

topics.ds: Distinguish and correctly spell common homophones and near-homophones encountered at Y3-4 level (e.g., accept/except, affect/effect, brake/break, grate/great), including using the /eɪ/ sound spelt ei, eigh, or ey
topics.p: When {{name}} writes, do they use the right spelling for words that sound the same but mean different things — like "brake" (on a bike) and "break" (snap something)?

topics.ds: Spell words with a range of prefixes (dis-, mis-, un-, re-, pre-, anti-, auto-, super-) understanding how each prefix modifies the root word's meaning without changing its spelling
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a word starting with "dis-," "mis-," or "pre-," can they work out what the word means and spell it correctly by thinking about the prefix?

topics.ds: Spell words from the statutory word list for Years 3 and 4, including commonly misspelt words that do not follow regular patterns
topics.p: Can {{name}} spell the tricky words on their school's Year 3 and 4 word list — like "enough," "believe," or "separate" — from memory when writing?

topics.ds: Spell words using productive suffixes (-ation, -ly, -ous) and less common sound-spelling correspondences (/ɪ/ as y, /ʌ/ as ou, endings sounding like /ʒə/, /tʃə/, /ʒən/, /ʃən/) introduced in the Year 3-4 programme
topics.p: Can {{name}} spell words with endings like "-tion," "-ous," or "-ly" correctly — for example, "nation," "famous," or "quietly" — without needing to look them up?

topics.n: Using a Dictionary to Check Spellings
topics.ds: Use the first two or three letters of a word to check its spelling in a dictionary; consult reference materials including beginning dictionaries to verify and correct spellings
topics.p: If {{name}} isn't sure how to spell a word, can they look it up in a dictionary by using the first two or three letters to find it quickly?

topics.n: Spellings from Greek, French and Latin
topics.ds: Spell words with etymological letter patterns from Greek (ch = /k/), French (ch = /ʃ/, -gue, -que), and Latin (sc = /s/) origins
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that some words have letter patterns from other languages — like "ch" making a "k" sound in "school" or "chorus" — and can they spell those words correctly?

topics.ds: Spell words using assorted Y5-6 conventions: doubling after -fer when the stress remains (referring but reference), using hyphens to join prefixes to root words (co-ordinate, re-enter), the /iː/ sound spelt ei after c (receive, ceiling), and the letter string ough representing different sounds (though, through, thought, thorough, plough)
topics.p: Can {{name}} correctly spell tricky words like "receive," "though," or "co-ordinate," including knowing when to use a hyphen or the "-ei" pattern after "c"?

topics.ds: Distinguish and correctly spell homophones and commonly confused words at Y5-6 level (e.g., affect/effect, practice/practise, advice/advise, complement/compliment, aisle/isle, led/lead), including confused words such as to/too/two and there/their/they're
topics.p: When {{name}} writes, do they use the right spelling for commonly mixed-up words — like "affect" vs "effect," "practice" vs "practise," or "there," "their," and "they're"?

topics.ds: Spell words containing silent letters that are remnants of earlier pronunciation or etymology, recognising common silent-letter patterns and using word origins to remember them
topics.p: When {{name}} writes words that have silent letters — like "knight," "wrap," or "lamb" — do they remember to include the silent letter even though you can't hear it?

topics.ds: Spell words ending in -able/-ible and the corresponding adverb forms -ably/-ibly, applying patterns to determine which suffix to use based on the root word
topics.p: When {{name}} needs to spell a word ending in "-able" or "-ible" — like "comfortable" or "visible" — can they choose the right ending and spell it correctly?

topics.ds: Spell words from the statutory word list for Years 5 and 6, including words with irregular or uncommon spelling patterns that must be learned individually
topics.p: Can {{name}} spell the challenging words on their school's Year 5 and 6 word list — like "accommodate," "conscience," or "prejudice" — from memory when writing?

topics.ds: Spell words with Latin and French suffix patterns: endings sounding like /ʃəs/ spelt -cious or -tious (e.g., precious, cautious), /ʃəl/ spelt -cial or -tial (e.g., official, essential), and words ending in -ant/-ance/-ancy vs -ent/-ence/-ency (e.g., observant/observance, confident/confidence)
topics.p: Can {{name}} spell words with tricky endings like "-cious," "-tious," or "-cial" — for example, "precious," "cautious," or "official" — without making mistakes?

topics.n: Applying Spelling Rules to Complex Words
topics.ds: Spell correctly and consistently, applying the spelling patterns and rules from KS1-2 to increasingly complex vocabulary encountered in KS3 reading and subject-specific study
topics.p: When {{name}} writes longer, more complex words in secondary school — like subject-specific vocabulary in science or history — do they spell them correctly without needing to check each time?

topics.ds: Ask and answer questions about unknown words in texts; discuss word meanings and link new vocabulary to words already known
topics.p: When {{name}} comes across a word they don't know in a book, do they try to figure out what it means from the other words around it and connect it to words they already know?

topics.ds: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs describing similar actions and among adjectives differing in intensity; make real-life connections between words and their use
topics.p: Does {{name}} notice the difference between similar words — for example, knowing that "scorching" is stronger than "warm," or that "trotted" is different from "sprinted"?

topics.ds: Sort common objects and words into categories to understand how concepts relate; demonstrate understanding of opposites (antonyms) for common verbs and adjectives
topics.p: Can {{name}} sort a group of words into categories — for example, separating fruits from vegetables — and tell you the opposite of common words like "hot" or "fast"?

topics.ds: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, being read to, and responding to texts in own speech and writing
topics.p: When {{name}} learns a new word from a book or conversation, do they try to use it themselves — in their writing or when they're talking?

topics.ds: Use knowledge of common inflections and affixes (-ed, -s, un-, -er) as clues to the meaning of unknown words; understand how the prefix un- changes meaning
topics.p: If {{name}} sees an unfamiliar word like "unhelpful" or "jumped," can they use the beginning or ending of the word to work out what it means?

topics.ds: Define words by category and by one or more key attributes (e.g., 'a duck is a bird that swims'), making real-life connections between words and their use
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain what a word means by saying what type of thing it is and what makes it special — for example, "a penguin is a bird that can't fly but is great at swimming"?

topics.ds: Identify frequently occurring root words and their inflectional forms (e.g., look/looks/looked/looking), using affixes as clues to word meaning and understanding how suffixes create nouns and adjectives
topics.p: When {{name}} sees words like "play," "plays," "played," and "playing," do they understand they all come from the same root word and can they use each form correctly?

topics.ds: Recognise and compare formal and informal uses of English, understanding that language choices vary based on audience, purpose and context
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand the difference between how they'd write a text to a friend versus a formal letter — and can they explain why the language would be different?

topics.ds: Explore word families based on common root words, understanding how words are related in form and meaning through shared roots, prefixes and suffixes (e.g., solve → solution, solver, dissolve, insoluble)
topics.p: If {{name}} knows the word "cycle," can they work out what related words like "recycle," "bicycle," or "cyclist" mean by thinking about the shared root?

topics.ds: Acquire and use accurately academic and domain-specific vocabulary relevant to grade-level topics, including words that signal precise meaning in informational texts across subject areas
topics.p: When {{name}} is studying a topic in science or history, do they pick up and correctly use the specific vocabulary for that subject — like "erosion," "parliament," or "habitat"?

topics.ds: Distinguish literal from nonliteral (figurative) language in context and interpret common idioms and phrases
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a phrase like "it's raining cats and dogs" or "she had butterflies in her stomach," do they know it doesn't mean what the words literally say?

topics.ds: Extend topic-specific and technical vocabulary and know that the same word can have different meanings in different contexts and learning areas (e.g. 'table', 'volume', 'power', 'scale')
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that a word like 'table' or 'volume' can mean different things in maths, science and at home — and work out which meaning fits?

topics.ds: Demonstrate understanding of words by relating them to their antonyms (opposites) and synonyms (words with similar meanings), using synonym and antonym relationships to refine vocabulary and improve precision in writing
topics.p: When {{name}} is writing, can they swap out a basic word for a more precise one — for example, replacing "happy" with "elated" or "said" with "whispered" — to make their meaning clearer?

topics.n: Greek and Latin Roots for Word Meaning
topics.ds: Use knowledge of Greek and Latin affixes (prefixes and suffixes) and roots as clues to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words, building a bank of common roots and their meanings
topics.p: If {{name}} comes across an unfamiliar word containing a Greek or Latin root they recognise — like "port" in "transport" or "bio" in "biology" — can they use that to work out the meaning?

topics.ds: Recognise and interpret common idioms (break the ice, hit the nail on the head), adages (actions speak louder than words), and proverbs (a stitch in time saves nine), understanding their figurative meanings and when to use them
topics.p: If {{name}} hears a saying like "don't judge a book by its cover" or "the early bird catches the worm," do they know what it really means and when you'd use it?

topics.ds: Understand and identify similes (comparisons using like or as) and metaphors (direct comparisons stating something is something else) in texts, explaining how each creates imagery and conveys meaning
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a description like "the moon was a silver coin" or "her smile was like sunshine," can they explain what image the author was trying to create?

topics.n: Using a Thesaurus to Choose Words
topics.ds: Use a thesaurus to find synonyms and extend vocabulary choices, selecting the most appropriate word based on context, connotation, and register
topics.p: When {{name}} is writing and wants a better word than the one they first thought of, can they use a thesaurus and pick the right synonym for the context — not just any word that means something similar?

topics.ds: Distinguish between formal and informal vocabulary, selecting words appropriate for formal speech and writing such as 'discover' instead of 'find out' and 'request' instead of 'ask for'
topics.p: When {{name}} is writing something formal — like a letter or a report — do they choose more sophisticated words, like "enquire" instead of "ask" or "sufficient" instead of "enough"?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the varieties of English used in stories, dramas, or poems, including dialects and registers, understanding how language varies by region, context, and purpose
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story with characters who speak in dialect or old-fashioned language, can they understand it and explain how it differs from the way we speak today?

topics.ds: Acquire and use accurately a broad range of general academic vocabulary and domain-specific words — drawing new vocabulary from reading and listening and deploying it consciously in writing and speech to achieve particular effects
topics.p: Does {{name}} pick up new words from books and lessons and actually use them in their own writing and conversation — not just understand them when someone else uses them?

topics.ds: Understand and interpret figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meaning — including allusion, irony, pun, oxymoron, and extended metaphor — and distinguish between connotation and denotation when analysing or choosing words
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a poem or novel and the author uses irony, a pun, or an unexpected comparison, can they explain what effect it creates and why the author chose those words?

topics.ds: Identify authors' use of vivid, emotive vocabulary, including metaphor, simile, personification, idiom, imagery and hyperbole, and explain the effect of each
topics.p: When {{name}} reads or hears 'I've told you a million times!' or 'the forest weeps', do they recognise the exaggeration or the human feelings given to things — and why writers use them?

topics.ds: Determine the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases using a flexible range of strategies — including context clues, Greek and Latin affixes and roots, reference materials, and verification of inferred meaning
topics.p: When {{name}} encounters an unfamiliar word in a book or article, can they work out its meaning using context clues, word roots, or a dictionary — and then check whether their guess was right?

topics.ds: Retell and adapt a familiar story by changing a character, the setting or the ending through play, performance, drawing or simple writing
topics.p: When playing with toys or puppets, does {{name}} retell a story they know but change it — like giving it a new ending or a different character?

topics.ds: With teacher guidance, re-read own writing aloud to check it sounds right; listen and respond to questions and suggestions from teacher or peers to add detail, clarify meaning, and strengthen writing — this is the scaffolded beginning of writing self-evaluation, not an independent skill
topics.p: When {{name}}'s teacher asks them to read their own writing aloud and then asks "does that bit make sense?", can {{name}} listen to the feedback and make a simple change to improve it?

topics.ds: Say out loud what is going to be written; compose sentences orally before writing them down as preparation for independent writing
topics.p: Before {{name}} starts writing a sentence, do they say it out loud first — testing how it sounds — before putting pen to paper?

topics.ds: Participate in shared research and writing projects; recall information from experiences or gather information from sources to answer a question
topics.p: When {{name}} is given a writing project that involves finding out about something — like an animal or a place — can they look up information and use what they find to write about the topic?

topics.ds: Read own writing aloud clearly enough to be heard by peers and the teacher; use digital tools to produce and publish writing
topics.p: Can {{name}} read their own writing aloud to the class clearly enough for everyone to hear and follow along — and have they ever typed or published a piece of writing using a computer or tablet?

topics.n: Simple Stories with Beginning and Ending
topics.ds: Write simple narratives by sequencing sentences to describe events in order; narrate a single event or linked events with a beginning, middle, and ending or reaction
topics.p: Can {{name}} write a short story about something that happened — with a clear beginning, middle, and end — so that someone who wasn't there could follow what happened and in what order?

topics.ds: Take part in shared writing and shared editing with the teacher: suggesting words and sentences for a class text and helping to fix capital letters, full stops and the spelling of simple CVC words
topics.p: When writing a card or list together, does {{name}} suggest what to write and help spot things to fix, like a missing full stop or capital letter?

topics.ds: Compose opinion pieces using drawing, dictating, or writing that name a topic or book and state a preference or opinion about it
topics.p: Can {{name}} write a sentence or two giving their opinion about something — like their favourite book or food — and explain why they feel that way?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of the writing process — compose, plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread, genre, audience, purpose, narrative, recount, instruction, paragraph, sequence, and detail — and understand that these words describe distinct steps and decisions that all writers make, not just tasks to tick off
topics.p: If you asked {{name}} to explain what they're doing when they write a story at school, could they walk you through each step using words like 'plan', 'draft', and 'revise' — showing they understand it's a process, not just one sitting?

topics.ds: Compose informative or explanatory texts using drawing, dictating, or writing that name a topic and supply some information about it
topics.p: Can {{name}} write a few sentences explaining something they know about — like how butterflies grow or how to make a sandwich — naming the topic and sharing some facts?

topics.ds: Compose informative or explanatory texts that introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section
topics.p: Can {{name}} write an explanatory or informative piece — like "How Volcanoes Work" — that introduces the topic clearly, develops it with facts and definitions, and ends with a conclusion?

topics.ds: Write about real events and for different purposes, developing stamina for sustained writing across genres beyond narrative (e.g., recounts, letters, instructions)
topics.p: Can {{name}} write in different styles for different purposes — for example, writing a recount of a school trip, a letter to a friend, or a set of instructions for a game?

topics.ds: Listen to and discuss poems, chants and songs, then imitate and invent sound patterns including alliteration and rhyme in their own lines and verses
topics.p: Can {{name}} make up a silly rhyme or a line where all the words start with the same sound — like 'Wiggly worms wriggle'?

topics.ds: Create and edit literary texts by deliberately adapting the structure and language features of familiar texts (e.g. repeated patterns, story openings, rhyme) through drawing, writing, performance and digital tools
topics.p: Can {{name}} write their own version of a favourite patterned book — keeping the pattern but changing the characters — and perform or record it?

topics.ds: Plan before writing by saying aloud or noting down what will be written, writing down ideas and key words, and encapsulating ideas sentence by sentence before composing
topics.p: Before {{name}} starts a piece of writing, do they spend a few minutes planning — jotting down ideas, key words, or a rough structure — rather than jumping straight into writing the first sentence?

topics.ds: Orally retell or adapt a familiar story, keeping its plot structure, characters and key vocabulary, through role-play, writing, drawing or digital tools
topics.p: Can {{name}} act out, or record on a tablet, a story they know — keeping the order of events but maybe changing a character?

topics.ds: Proof-read own writing to check for errors in spelling, grammar, and punctuation; evaluate and revise writing with teacher/peer support, re-reading to ensure meaning is clear and tense is consistent
topics.p: When {{name}} finishes a piece of writing, do they proofread it for spelling mistakes, missing punctuation, and errors in grammar — and make corrections before handing it in?

topics.ds: Compose opinion pieces that introduce a topic, state a clear point of view, provide organised reasons linked with connecting words, and include a concluding statement or section
topics.p: Can {{name}} write a persuasive piece — like arguing for a longer lunch break or why dogs are better pets than cats — with a clear viewpoint, organised reasons, and a conclusion?

topics.ds: Write poetry, exploring patterns of language, rhyme and rhythm, and learning poems by heart for recitation with appropriate intonation
topics.p: Has {{name}} tried writing a poem — playing with rhyme, rhythm, or repeating patterns — and can they recite one they've learned or written with expression?

topics.ds: Write narratives with developed settings, characters and plot, using dialogue and description to develop experiences and show character responses to situations
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they bring it to life with descriptions of the setting, details about the characters, and some dialogue — rather than just listing what happened?

topics.ds: Organise writing into paragraphs, grouping related material around a theme, and use simple organisational devices such as headings and sub-headings in non-narrative writing
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a longer piece — like a report or a story — do they organise it into paragraphs, with related ideas grouped together and, where appropriate, headings to help the reader navigate?

topics.ds: Compose and rehearse sentences orally before writing, progressively building varied and rich vocabulary and an increasing range of sentence structures including dialogue
topics.p: Does {{name}} try out a sentence aloud before writing it — experimenting with different words and structures to find the version that sounds best?

topics.ds: Evaluate and edit writing by assessing effectiveness, proposing changes to grammar and vocabulary for consistency, and proof-reading for spelling, grammar and punctuation errors at Y3-4 level
topics.p: When {{name}} revisits a draft piece of writing, can they improve it — changing word choices to be more precise, fixing inconsistent tenses, and correcting spelling and punctuation errors?

topics.ds: Create and edit imaginative texts by deliberately using or adapting language features, characters, settings, plot structures and ideas encountered in literary texts read
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they borrow good ideas from books they've read — like a great opening line or a story pattern — and make them their own?

topics.n: Choosing Form and Tone for Your Audience
topics.ds: Identify the audience for and purpose of writing before beginning, selecting the appropriate form, tone, and register to match the intended reader and communicative goal
topics.p: Before {{name}} starts a piece of writing, do they think about who will read it and why — adjusting their tone, vocabulary, and format accordingly, like writing more formally for a teacher than for a friend?

topics.ds: Plan, create, edit and publish multimodal texts that combine writing with visual features — images, labelled diagrams, captions, headings and layout — using digital or print tools, choosing visual features to suit the purpose and audience
topics.p: Can {{name}} make a poster or slide that combines writing with pictures, labels and captions — choosing a layout that suits what it's for?

topics.ds: Read back your own writing critically and independently — notice where meaning is unclear, where a word could be stronger, or where the reader might be confused; make revisions without needing teacher prompts, using your own judgment about what is and isn't working
topics.p: Can {{name}} read back something they've written — a story, a report, a letter — and spot a part that isn't quite right or could be better, all by themselves without you or a teacher pointing it out?

topics.ds: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge about a topic, gather information from print and digital sources, and take brief organised notes
topics.p: When {{name}} is given a research project at school, can they look up information from books or websites, take organised notes, and then write it up in their own words?

topics.ds: Choose precise and vivid words and phrases to create specific effects in writing
topics.p: When {{name}} writes descriptive or creative pieces, do they choose interesting and precise words — like "sprinted" instead of "ran", or "crimson" instead of "red" — to create a specific effect?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of writing craft and effect — form, structure, register, tone, voice, coherence, cohesion, argument, evidence, perspective, rhetoric, technique, formal, informal, and style — and understand that these words describe choices writers make intentionally to achieve a particular effect on the reader
topics.p: If {{name}} is writing a persuasive letter compared to a story, can they explain the difference in 'tone' and 'register' — and why they'd make different word choices for each one?

topics.ds: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organisation are appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience, maintaining a consistent style and structure throughout
topics.p: When {{name}} writes for school, does the piece feel well-organised and appropriate for its purpose — whether it's a formal essay, a creative story, or a persuasive argument — with a consistent tone throughout?

topics.ds: Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research in writing, applying grade-level reading standards to non-fiction
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a non-fiction piece — like a report on climate change — do they draw on specific facts and evidence from things they've read, weaving that information into their own writing?

topics.ds: Draw evidence from literary texts to support analysis, reflection, and research in writing, applying grade-level reading standards to literature
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about a book they've read — like an essay about a character or a theme — do they support their ideas with specific quotes or details drawn directly from the text?

topics.ds: Gather relevant information from print and digital sources, summarise or paraphrase information in notes and finished work, and provide a basic bibliography or list of sources
topics.p: If {{name}} is researching a topic for a school project, can they find information from books or websites, put it in their own words, and keep track of where they got it from?

topics.ds: Plan, create, edit and publish digital multimodal texts (e.g. slideshows, e-books, web pages, short videos) that combine paragraphs with images, captions, diagrams or graphs, layout and audio, choosing each visual and digital feature to suit purpose and audience
topics.p: Could {{name}} create a slideshow or short e-book on a topic — with writing, images, captions and maybe a voice recording — and explain why they laid it out that way?

topics.n: Layout and Formatting in Informational Writing
topics.ds: Use layout devices including headings, sub-headings, columns, bullets, and tables to structure text and guide the reader through informational and explanatory writing
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a non-fiction piece — like a guide or an explanation — do they use layout features like headings, bullet points, and columns to help the reader navigate the information easily?

topics.ds: Plan narrative writing by considering how authors have developed characters and settings, drawing on techniques observed in texts read, heard, or performed
topics.p: When {{name}} is about to write a story, do they think ahead about what their main character is like and where the story will take place before they start writing?

topics.ds: Create and edit literary texts, experimenting with figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification) and with storylines, characters and settings drawn from texts experienced
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they try out comparisons like 'as quiet as a mouse', or make objects act like people — 'the old house groaned'?

topics.ds: Precis longer passages by summarising the main ideas and key information concisely while maintaining the essential meaning and removing non-essential detail
topics.p: If {{name}} reads a long article about a topic they're studying, can they write a short summary in their own words that captures the key points without copying sentences?

topics.ds: Use varied transitions, cohesive devices, and paragraph-linking strategies to create coherence across a whole piece of writing — including temporal transitions, causal connectives, and techniques for signalling shifts in argument, time, or setting
topics.p: When {{name}} writes several paragraphs, do they use linking phrases like "however," "as a result," or "on the other hand" to connect ideas smoothly between sections?

topics.ds: Write informative and explanatory texts that examine a topic and convey ideas clearly — organising information logically with headings and formatting, developing the topic with relevant facts, definitions, details, and quotations, and using precise vocabulary
topics.p: Can {{name}} write a clear explanation of how something works — like how a volcano erupts or how bread is made — so that someone who's never learned about it would understand?

topics.ds: Create and edit literary texts that adapt plot structure, characters, settings and/or ideas from texts experienced, experimenting with literary devices such as flashback, foreshadowing, figurative language and symbolism
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they experiment with tricks like a flashback to a character's past, or an early hint about what's coming?

topics.ds: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence — including introducing claims, acknowledging counterclaims, organising reasons logically, maintaining a formal style, and providing a concluding statement
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to convince you to let them stay up later, can they write down clear reasons and examples to support their case rather than just saying "because I want to"?

topics.ds: Plan, revise, and edit writing to improve coherence and effectiveness — considering how the writing reflects its intended audience and purpose, amending vocabulary, grammar, and structure, and proofreading for accurate spelling, punctuation, and grammar
topics.p: After {{name}} finishes a first draft, do they go back and make real improvements — not just fixing spelling, but changing sentences or reorganising ideas to make it better?

topics.ds: Summarise and organise material from reading and research — gathering relevant information from multiple sources, assessing credibility, integrating evidence without plagiarising, and supporting ideas with factual detail
topics.p: If {{name}} is preparing for a school project, can they gather notes from several sources and organise them into a logical order before they start writing?

topics.ds: Write for a range of purposes and audiences beyond narrative — including scripts, poetry, personal and formal letters, notes for talks, and other forms — selecting the appropriate form, register, and conventions for each
topics.p: Can {{name}} write in different styles depending on the task — for example, a persuasive letter, a set of instructions, or a diary entry — and make each one sound appropriate?

topics.ds: Write narratives that develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique — including establishing context and point of view, developing characters through dialogue, pacing, and description, using varied transitions, and providing a reflective conclusion
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they use techniques like describing feelings, building suspense, or showing dialogue to make it interesting to read?

topics.ds: Apply growing knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, and text structure to writing — drawing on literary and rhetorical devices from reading (e.g., rhetorical questions, tricolon, anaphora, contrast) to enhance impact
topics.p: When {{name}} edits a piece of their writing, do they make choices about word order, sentence structure, or vocabulary to make the writing more powerful or clearer?

topics.ds: Record locations on pictorial maps or simple models of familiar places (classroom, playground, home), placing pictures or objects in the right positions
topics.p: Could {{name}} put stickers in the right places on a simple picture map of your street, home or their school — and tell you where things are using words like 'next to' or 'behind'?

topics.ds: Locate positions on a two-dimensional representation (simple map or plan) of a familiar space such as the classroom or playground, and move positions by following directions and pathways
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a simple drawing of the classroom or the backyard, can they find where things are on it and follow a path drawn on it?

topics.ds: Represent places at different geographical scales (local, regional and state, territory or national) on maps, and describe how people and places are interconnected across those scales (e.g. through food, jobs, services and transport)
