topics.p: Can {{name}} use tricks like breaking up a number — working out '6 × 14' as '6 × 10 + 6 × 4 = 60 + 24 = 84' — to make multiplication easier?

topics.ds: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers (e.g. 8 × ? = 48, ? × 6 = 42)
topics.p: If {{name}} sees '8 × ? = 48' or '? ÷ 6 = 7' written on paper, can they figure out what number goes in the blank?

topics.ds: Interpret whole-number quotients (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share or the number of equal groups)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that '56 ÷ 8' could mean 'if 56 things are shared between 8 people, how many does each person get?' — not just recite the answer '7'?

topics.ds: Interpret products of whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7)
topics.p: If {{name}} sees '5 × 7' written down, can they explain it means 5 groups with 7 in each group — not just recite the answer '35'?

topics.ds: Multiply two-digit and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out '347 × 6' by setting it out formally in a column — multiplying each digit separately and carrying where needed?

topics.ds: Solve multi-step word problems using the four operations with whole numbers, including interpreting remainders in context; represent with equations using a letter for the unknown; check with estimation
topics.p: If {{name}} reads 'a school buys 7 boxes of 24 pens and shares them equally between 8 classes', can they work through all the steps and decide sensibly what to do with any remainder?

topics.ds: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100; identify common factors and common multiples of two numbers; use these concepts to solve problems
topics.p: Can {{name}} list all the factor pairs for a number like 36 — (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9), (6, 6) — and find factors that two numbers share?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using knowledge of factors, multiples, squares, and cubes
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked to find all the square numbers less than 100, can they work through it systematically and give you the correct list: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81?

topics.ds: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using formal written methods including long multiplication; illustrate with area models
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out something like '2,346 × 7' or '43 × 28' using the formal column method — setting it out carefully and working through all the steps?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts, including related facts and place-value adjustments
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out things like '24 × 5' or '360 ÷ 8' in their head — using clever connections to known facts rather than needing to write anything down?

topics.ds: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison (e.g. 35 = 5 × 7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7); represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as equations
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at '35 = 5 × 7' and explain it as '35 is five times as many as 7' — understanding it as a comparison, not just a multiplication fact?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number
topics.p: If you say 'Maya has 4 times as many stickers as Tom, and Tom has 6 — how many does Maya have?', can {{name}} recognise this as a multiplication problem and solve it?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide whole numbers and those involving decimals by 10, 100, and 1000
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly work out '4.7 × 100' or '3,600 ÷ 1,000' — knowing that digits shift left or right in the place-value chart depending on whether they're multiplying or dividing?

topics.ds: Explain and use the properties of odd and even numbers when adding, subtracting and multiplying, e.g. odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd, and any whole number multiplied by an even number is even
topics.p: Without adding them up, can {{name}} tell you whether 347 + 129 will be odd or even — and explain why?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors, and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall prime numbers up to 19
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you what makes a number 'prime' — that it only divides exactly by 1 and itself — and give some examples like 7, 11, and 13?

topics.ds: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule; identify apparent features of the pattern not explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur
topics.p: If {{name}} is told 'start at 3 and multiply by 2 each time', can they write out the pattern — 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 — and spot any interesting features in how it grows?

topics.ds: Divide numbers up to four digits by a one-digit number using short division (and place-value/array strategies); interpret remainders appropriately for the context
topics.p: Can {{name}} use the short division ('bus stop') method to work out something like '2,457 ÷ 6', and decide what to do with any remainder left over?

topics.ds: Recognise and use square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared (²) and cubed (³)
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that '5²' means 5 × 5 = 25 and '3³' means 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 — and can they work out other squared and cubed numbers?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates
topics.p: If a recipe serves 4 and {{name}} wants to make it for 6, can they scale up each ingredient — for example, changing '2 cups of flour' to '3 cups'?

topics.ds: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions and evaluate expressions containing these grouping symbols
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at '3 × (4 + 5)' and work out the brackets first — getting '3 × 9 = 27' — rather than just multiplying left to right?

topics.ds: Use a calculator or spreadsheet where appropriate to multiply larger numbers and to divide, check results by estimation, and interpret a decimal calculator answer to a division in context as a whole number, a remainder, a fraction or a decimal
topics.p: If {{name}} divides 250 by 8 on a calculator and sees 31.25, can they work out what that means for the problem — like needing 32 buses, not 31.25?

topics.ds: Multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers (e.g. 3.47 × 6)
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out '3.47 × 6' — keeping the decimal point in the right place and carrying correctly through each column?

topics.ds: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal written short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to context
topics.p: Can {{name}} use short division to work out something like '2,184 ÷ 12' — keeping track of each digit and carrying any remainders into the next column?

topics.ds: Use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places; divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers
topics.p: Can {{name}} use a written method to calculate something like '17 ÷ 4 = 4.25' — carrying the division past the decimal point to get a decimal answer rather than a remainder?

topics.ds: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit divisor using formal written long division, interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate
topics.p: Can {{name}} use long division to work out something like '1,848 ÷ 24' — going through the steps of divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down until they reach the answer?

topics.n: Estimation to check answers to calculations
topics.ds: Use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy
topics.p: Before {{name}} works out a large multiplication or division, can they estimate what the answer should be roughly — and then check whether their final answer is in the right ballpark?

topics.ds: Create and use algorithms with steps and decisions, and digital tools such as spreadsheets, to experiment with factors, multiples and divisibility, and describe the patterns that emerge
topics.p: Can {{name}} set up a list or spreadsheet to find all the numbers that divide into 24 — and spot patterns, like which numbers have only two factors?

topics.ds: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers (up to 4 digits by 2 digits) using the formal written method of long multiplication
topics.p: Can {{name}} use long multiplication to work out something like '2,347 × 24' — setting it out in two rows, one for the units and one for the tens, then adding the results?

topics.ds: Perform mental calculations including with mixed operations and large numbers, using strategies such as partitioning, compensation, and derived facts
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out a mixed calculation like '(200 × 6) + 350 − 75' entirely in their head — keeping track of each step without writing anything down?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100, and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places, understanding that digits shift position in the place-value chart
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out '4.6 ÷ 1,000 = 0.0046' — knowing that each division by 10 shifts digits one place to the right, even past the decimal point?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, deciding which operations and methods to use and why; solve multi-step problems in contexts
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a multi-step problem mixing different operations — like working out the total cost of several items at different prices — can they plan and carry out each step correctly?

topics.ds: Understand and apply the conventional order of operations (PEMDAS/BODMAS) to carry out calculations involving the four operations
topics.p: If {{name}} sees '8 + 4 × 3', do they get 20 — not 36 — because they know to do the multiplication before the addition?

topics.ds: Solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy
topics.p: If {{name}} calculates an answer of 8.63 but the question asks for it to the nearest whole number, can they round it correctly to 9 — and explain why that level of precision matters in context?

topics.ds: Write simple numerical expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them (e.g. recognise that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921)
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at '4 × (5 + 3)' and say 'that's 4 times the result of adding 5 and 3' — reading the expression as a description of a calculation, without having to work it out first?

topics.ds: Use estimation and rounding to check the reasonableness of answers when multiplying and dividing decimals (including by multiples of powers of 10), identifying misplaced decimal points
topics.p: If {{name}} works out 4.87 x 30 and gets 1461, do they notice it can't be right because 5 x 30 is only about 150?

topics.ds: Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property
topics.p: Can {{name}} find the highest common factor of two numbers like 24 and 36 — working out the biggest number that divides exactly into both — and explain how they found it?

topics.ds: Use conventional notation for the priority of operations including brackets, powers, roots, and reciprocals; apply BIDMAS/BODMAS consistently to evaluate complex numerical expressions
topics.p: Can {{name}} evaluate a complex expression like '5 + 2³ ÷ 4' correctly — applying the right order of operations, handling the power before the division and division before the addition?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide with positive and negative integers and rational numbers, understanding the rules for the sign of the product or quotient
topics.p: If {{name}} knows that a negative times a negative makes a positive, can they use that rule to work out calculations like '−3 × −4 = 12' — and explain why it makes sense?

topics.ds: Recognise and use relationships between operations including inverse operations; use these relationships to check answers and simplify calculations
topics.p: If {{name}} works out '252 ÷ 7 = 36', can they immediately use the inverse to check — '36 × 7 = 252' — without having to redo the division?

topics.ds: Read and write number words from one to twenty
topics.p: Can {{name}} write number words like 'fourteen' or 'twenty' — and read them on a birthday card or in a story book without needing help?

topics.ds: Name, represent and order numbers from 0 to at least 20 using physical and virtual materials (number cards, on-screen ten frames and number tracks) and numerals
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a handful of number cards between 0 and 20 — like 14, 3, 19 and 8 — can they lay them out in order from smallest to biggest?

topics.ds: Read and write numerals from 0 to 100
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write any number up to 100 — both as a numeral and by saying what it means?

topics.ds: Read and write numerals from 0 to 20
topics.p: Can {{name}} read a number like '17' written on paper and write it themselves — and do they know what each digit means?

topics.ds: Understand that the teen numbers (11–19) are composed of ten ones and some further ones (early place value)
topics.p: If {{name}} has 14 building blocks, can they see it as one full tower of 10 and 4 left over — understanding 'teen' numbers as ten-and-some-more?

topics.ds: Mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a given two-digit number without counting
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly tell you what is 10 more than 43 or 10 less than 71 — without counting up or down one at a time?

topics.ds: Understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that ten single objects bundled together make 'one ten' — and that this is why we write 10 with a 1 in the tens place and a 0 in the ones place?

topics.ds: Compare and order two-digit numbers using the symbols >, =, and <, based on place value understanding
topics.p: If you show {{name}} the numbers 34, 67, and 21, can they put them in order from smallest to largest — and use the symbols > or < correctly?

topics.ds: Recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120, including 101 to 120, using physical materials (bundled straws, base-ten blocks), virtual materials (on-screen base-ten blocks, digital number charts), numerals, number lines and charts
topics.p: If {{name}} is counting a big jar of buttons past 100, can they keep going to 120, show a number like 112 with bundles of ten, and put 104, 98 and 111 in order?

topics.ds: Read and write numbers to at least 100 in words
topics.p: Can {{name}} write 'seventy-four' or 'one hundred and three' as number words — and read them correctly when they appear in a book or on a sign?

topics.n: Place value understanding and number facts
topics.ds: Use place value understanding and number facts to solve problems
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked 'which number is closest to 50 — 47 or 54?', can they use their number knowledge to answer quickly and explain why?

topics.ds: Count to 120 starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals to 120
topics.p: Can {{name}} start counting from any number up to 120 — for example, starting at 87 and counting up to 120 without losing track?

topics.ds: Partition and rename two-digit numbers in standard and non-standard ways (e.g. 34 = 3 tens 4 ones = 2 tens 14 ones) using physical and virtual base-ten materials, recognising that the total stays the same
topics.p: If {{name}} has 34 counters made up of 3 bags of ten and 4 loose ones, can they show the same number another way — like 2 bags of ten and 14 loose ones?

topics.ds: Identify, represent and estimate numbers to 100 using different representations: place a two-digit number on a 0–100 number line marked in tens, represent it with base-ten blocks (tens and ones), drawings, bead strings or hundred squares, and estimate 'about how many' objects in a set before counting to check
topics.p: If {{name}} has a number line from 0 to 100 marked in tens, can they point to roughly where 47 goes — and show 47 another way, such as 4 tens and 7 ones with blocks or a drawing?

topics.ds: Understand that the multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30 … 90) represent one to nine tens and 0 ones
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that 60 means 6 tens and no ones — and that this is why the ones column has a zero as a placeholder?

topics.n: The two digits of a two-digit number
topics.ds: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the number 47, can they tell you there are 4 tens (forty) and 7 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'four seven'?

topics.ds: Find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number up to 1000
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly work out '10 more than 342' or '100 less than 875' in their head — knowing which digit changes and which stays the same?

topics.ds: Understand that 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred'
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that ten full tens stacked together make one hundred — and that this is why 100 has a 1 in the hundreds place and zeros in the rest?

topics.ds: Represent and order numbers to at least 1000 using physical base-ten blocks and virtual materials (on-screen base-ten blocks and interactive number lines), connecting each representation to the numeral
topics.p: If {{name}} uses a maths app with hundreds, tens and ones blocks, can they build 347 on screen and with real blocks — and put 608, 680 and 860 in order on a number line?

topics.ds: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members
topics.p: If {{name}} has a group of 14 objects, can they tell you whether that number is odd or even — for example by pairing them up to see if any are left over?

topics.ds: Compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, and < symbols, based on place-value understanding
topics.p: If you give {{name}} a set of three-digit numbers like 456, 231, and 789, can they put them in order and use > and < correctly?

topics.ds: Solve number problems and practical problems involving place value of numbers up to 1000
topics.p: If {{name}} is told 'I have 4 hundreds, 3 tens, and 7 ones — what number is that?', can they put it together and tell you 437?

topics.ds: Read and write numbers to 1000 in numerals, number names, and expanded form
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 1,000 — both as numerals and in words — like reading '642' as 'six hundred and forty-two'?

topics.ds: Identify, represent and estimate three-digit numbers using different representations: place a number on a 0–1000 number line marked only in hundreds or unmarked, estimate the value of a marked point, and represent a number with base-ten blocks (hundreds, tens and ones), a place-value chart and a drawing, including numbers with a zero digit and non-standard partitions
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a number line from 0 to 1000 marked only in hundreds, can they point to roughly where 346 goes — and show 346 another way, such as hundreds, tens and ones blocks or a place-value chart?

topics.ds: Understand that the multiples of 100 (100–900) each represent a number of hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that 700 means 7 hundreds with no tens and no ones — and show what that looks like using base-ten blocks or a drawing?

topics.n: The three digits of a three-digit number
topics.ds: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the number 348, can they tell you there are 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 8 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'three four eight'?

topics.ds: Find 1000 more or less than a given number
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly work out '1,000 more than 3,456' or '1,000 less than 7,200' in their head — knowing only the thousands digit changes?

topics.ds: Order and compare numbers beyond 1000
topics.p: Can {{name}} put a set of four-digit numbers like 4,321, 1,876, and 9,045 in order from smallest to largest — comparing them digit by digit?

topics.ds: Count backwards through zero to include negative numbers
topics.p: Can {{name}} count backwards past zero into negative numbers — like 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3 — without hesitating at zero?

topics.ds: Identify, represent, and estimate numbers up to 10,000 using different representations
topics.p: Can {{name}} mark a number like 6,400 roughly in the right place on a number line that goes from 0 to 10,000 — and explain how they decided where to put it?

topics.ds: Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the number 5,347, can they tell you the value of each digit — that the 5 means 5,000, the 3 means 300, the 4 means 40, and the 7 means 7?

topics.ds: Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large positive numbers
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked 'what is the largest 4-digit even number you can make from the digits 3, 7, 1, and 8?', can they work through it systematically and give you an answer?

topics.ds: Read, write, order, and compare whole numbers up to at least 1,000,000 using base-ten numerals, number names, expanded form, and place-value understanding
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write numbers into the millions — like 1,340,000 — and put a set of large numbers in order correctly?

topics.ds: Read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and understand that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value
topics.p: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like XIV (14) or XLII (42) — and do they know why we stopped using Roman numerals for most things once zero and place value were invented?

topics.ds: Round any number to the nearest 10, 100, or 1000
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a number like 4,738 to the nearest 10 (4,740), 100 (4,700), or 1,000 (5,000) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

topics.ds: Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000, 10,000, 100,000) for any given number up to 1,000,000
topics.p: Can {{name}} count forwards and backwards in steps of 1,000 or 10,000 from any starting number — like 34,500, 44,500, 54,500 — without losing track?

topics.ds: Interpret negative numbers in context (temperature, sea level, bank balance); count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero
topics.p: If the temperature drops to −5°C overnight and rises to 3°C by day, can {{name}} place both on a number line and say how many degrees warmer the daytime temperature is?

topics.ds: Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (e.g. 700 ÷ 70 = 10)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that in 700, the 7 is worth 10 times more than in 70 — because moving one place to the left multiplies the value by 10?

topics.ds: Read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals
topics.p: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like MMXIX (2019) or CDXLIV (444) — and recognise the year a film or building was made when it's shown in Roman numerals?

topics.ds: Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, or 100,000 using place-value understanding
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a large number like 346,712 to the nearest 1,000 (347,000) or 10,000 (350,000) — identifying which digit to look at for each rounding?

topics.ds: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000
topics.p: If {{name}} is told the population of a city is 2,347,819, can they read that number aloud correctly and say roughly how many millions it is?

topics.ds: Round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a decimal like 3.748 to one decimal place (3.7) or two decimal places (3.75) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

topics.ds: Use negative numbers in context (temperature, finance, sea level); calculate intervals across zero
topics.p: If a bank account goes from −£45 to +£120, can {{name}} work out the total change — counting through zero to get £165?

topics.ds: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding, and negative numbers up to 10,000,000
topics.p: If {{name}} reads that the distance to the Moon is about 384,400 km, can they round it to the nearest 10,000 km and say whether it's closer to 380,000 or 390,000?

topics.ds: Explain patterns in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when multiplying/dividing by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10 (e.g. 10³ = 1000)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why 10² = 100 and 10³ = 1,000, and why multiplying by 10 just adds a zero — connecting the pattern of zeros to place value?

topics.ds: Recognise that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that in 4.56, the digit 5 is worth 5 tenths — ten times less than the 5 in 54, and ten times more than the 5 in 0.056?

topics.ds: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form; compare using >, =, < based on place-value meaning
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write decimals like 3.047 or 0.625, say what each digit means (3 ones, 0 tenths, 4 hundredths, 7 thousandths), and put a set of decimals in order?

topics.ds: Read, write, order, and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 10 million — like 4,302,617 — and say the value of any digit in the number?

topics.ds: Identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378, the 7 represents 7 hundredths)
topics.p: In the number 4.378, can {{name}} tell you that the 7 represents 7 hundredths — not 7 tenths or 7 thousandths?

topics.ds: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude in real-world contexts; distinguish absolute value comparisons from ordering statements
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you that the absolute value of −7 is 7 — because it's 7 steps from zero on a number line regardless of direction — and use this idea to compare distances?

topics.ds: Round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a measurement like 12.3746 km to 2 decimal places (12.37 km) or 3 significant figures (12.4 km) — and explain when each level of precision is appropriate?

topics.ds: Understand and use place value for decimals, measures, and integers of any size; extend the number system to include all positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a single number line
topics.p: Can {{name}} place a mix of numbers — like 3, −2, 0.5, −1.75, and ¼ — all on the same number line, in the right order?

topics.ds: Order positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values including negative numbers and mixed representations
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a mixed list like 2.5, −3, ¾, 0, and −0.5, can they put them in order from least to greatest using a number line if needed?

topics.ds: Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, and higher); recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, and 5; distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out that √25 = 5 and ∛27 = 3 — knowing these are the inverse of squaring and cubing — and say whether √50 is closer to 7 or 8?

topics.ds: Use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b; understand upper and lower bounds of rounded values
topics.p: If a length is measured as 7 cm to the nearest cm, can {{name}} say the actual length could be anywhere from 6.5 cm to 7.5 cm — understanding that rounding creates a range of possible values?

topics.ds: Interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer; convert between ordinary numbers and standard form
topics.p: Can {{name}} write 3,400,000 as 3.4 × 10⁶ and convert back — understanding that standard form is a shorthand for very large or very small numbers?

topics.ds: Appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, real numbers, and rational numbers; position integers on a number line and distinguish between rational and irrational numbers
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that numbers like √2 and π can't be written as exact fractions — and that their decimal expansions go on forever without repeating?

topics.ds: Use probability language to describe and compare the likelihood of everyday events using words such as certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible
topics.p: Does {{name}} use words like "certain," "likely," "unlikely," and "impossible" correctly — for example, knowing that rolling a 7 on a normal die is impossible but rolling an even number is likely?

topics.ds: Conduct simple probability experiments — flipping a coin, rolling a die, pulling coloured counters from a bag — record results, and compare experimental outcomes with expected theoretical outcomes
topics.p: Has {{name}} ever done an experiment like flipping a coin or rolling a die lots of times, recorded the results in a tally chart, and noticed any patterns in what came up?

topics.ds: Understand that 'equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance of occurring; identify whether a given situation has equally likely outcomes (a fair coin, a fair die, a spinner with equal sections) or unequally likely outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with unequal sections)
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell the difference between a fair situation — like rolling a normal die where every number has the same chance — and an unfair one, like a bag with many more of one colour than another?

topics.ds: Run repeated probability experiments and compare experimental (relative frequency) results with theoretical predictions; understand and demonstrate that as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends towards the theoretical probability — and that short runs can give very different results
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads, do they understand why this doesn't mean heads is "more likely" — and that the more times you flip, the closer the results get to 50:50?

topics.ds: Identify whether events in chance experiments and everyday situations are independent (one does not affect the other) or dependent (the first outcome changes the chances of the next)
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a coin and gets heads three times in a row, do they understand the next flip is still 50-50 — but that taking a lolly from a bag without putting it back does change what's left?

topics.ds: Compare the likelihood of different events and order them from least to most likely — including situations with unequal outcomes such as a bag with more of one colour than another, or a spinner with sections of different sizes — and explain reasoning using informal language
topics.p: If a bag has 8 red counters and 2 blue ones, does {{name}} understand that picking red is much more likely than picking blue — and can they put different events in order from least to most likely?

topics.ds: Describe the probability of simple equally-likely outcomes using unit fractions: the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, flipping heads is 1/2, picking one specific colour from three equally represented colours is 1/3; place these fractional probabilities on a 0-to-1 probability scale
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a fair coin, do they know the probability of getting heads is 1/2 — and can they express similar simple probabilities as fractions and place them on a 0-to-1 scale?

topics.ds: Calculate the probability of a simple event with equally likely outcomes using the formula: probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes; express the result as a fraction in its simplest form; apply to rolling dice, drawing from bags, and other simple chance situations
topics.p: If there are 3 red and 7 blue balls in a bag, can {{name}} work out the probability of picking a red one and express it as a fraction in its simplest form?

topics.ds: Understand that when all possible outcomes of a trial are listed, their probabilities must add up to 1; use this to find the probability of an event NOT happening: P(not A) = 1 − P(A); apply this shortcut to avoid counting all unfavourable outcomes directly
topics.p: If the probability of it raining tomorrow is 0.3, can {{name}} work out the probability of it NOT raining — and explain why all probabilities in a situation must add up to 1?

topics.ds: Understand probability as a measure expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain); place events on the probability scale; express probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percentages
topics.p: Can {{name}} write the same probability as a fraction, a decimal, and a percentage — for example, knowing that an even chance is ½, 0.5, and 50%?

topics.ds: Understand and apply the rule that probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to one; use this to find the probability of a complementary event (P(not A) = 1 − P(A))
topics.p: If a spinner has three sections and one has a probability of 0.4 and another has 0.35, can {{name}} work out the probability of landing on the third section without being told?

topics.ds: Record, describe, and analyse the frequency of outcomes from probability experiments to develop an understanding of relative frequency as an estimate of probability
topics.p: If {{name}} rolls a die 60 times and records the results, can they compare how often each number came up with what they'd expect in theory — and explain why they might not match perfectly?

topics.ds: Run chance simulations with an increasing number of trials using digital tools (spreadsheet random functions or online simulators), repeating each run size several times, and explain that relative frequencies tend to stabilise near the expected proportion as the number of trials grows, even though any single longer run need not be closer than a shorter one
topics.p: If {{name}} uses a computer to 'roll a dice' 10 times, then 1000 times, and repeats each a few times, can they notice that the 1000-roll results bunch more closely around one-sixth sixes — while knowing any single run can still be a bit off?

topics.ds: Understand probability as a measure on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); use the language of probability including likely, unlikely, certain, and impossible
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), place events on that scale as numbers, and tell you whether a game is fair or not?

topics.ds: Develop a probability model (a list of all the outcomes of a chance process with a probability for each, adding to 1) and use it to find probabilities of events: a uniform model gives every outcome the same probability (e.g. selecting a student at random from a class); a non-uniform model uses probabilities estimated from the observed frequencies of a chance process (e.g. how a tossed paper cup lands); compare a model's probabilities with observed frequencies and, when they disagree, explain whether the difference is plausibly chance variation or a sign that the model does not fit (e.g. a biased die or unequal spinner sections)
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a paper cup 50 times and records whether it lands on its side, open end up or open end down, could they turn the results into a probability for each way of landing — and say whether the three are equally likely?

topics.ds: Enumerate sets and their unions and intersections systematically using tables, grids, and Venn diagrams to organise and count outcomes
topics.p: Can {{name}} use a table or Venn diagram to systematically list all the possible outcomes of two events — like rolling two dice — and use it to count favourable outcomes?

topics.ds: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event: choose a random device (coins, dice, spinners, counters drawn with replacement, random-digit tables, or calculator or software random numbers) and a mapping whose probabilities match the situation; define one complete trial (what is generated and when the trial stops) and the event being counted; run many trials; and estimate the probability as the event's relative frequency. Explain why the model fits (each simulated outcome has the same probability as the real one, and successive outcomes are independent when the real ones are), and why different runs give different estimates that become more consistent as the number of trials grows; where a theoretical value can be found (e.g. with a tree diagram), compare it with the estimate
topics.p: If 40% of blood donors are type A, could {{name}} use random numbers or a spinner to act out lots of donor queues, estimate how often at least four donors are needed before the first type A — and explain why doing it again gives a slightly different answer?

topics.ds: Generate theoretical sample spaces for single and combined events using listing, tables, and tree diagrams, and calculate theoretical probabilities as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes
topics.p: Can {{name}} draw a tree diagram to map out all possible outcomes of a two-step probability situation — like flipping a coin and then rolling a die — and calculate the probability of any particular combination?

topics.ds: Construct and interpret Venn diagrams with two or three sets to organise and count outcomes; use systematic listing and the product rule for counting to enumerate all possible outcomes of combined events
topics.p: If {{name}} surveys a class about which sports they play and draws a Venn diagram to show the results, can they use it to find out how many students play both sports — and calculate the probability of picking one of those students at random?

topics.ds: Represent ratio and proportion problems using bar models (rectangular strips divided into equal parts labelled with quantities) and tape diagrams (segmented strips showing part-to-part and part-to-whole relationships); use these visual models to set up and solve unequal sharing, scaling, and percentage problems — drawing the diagram first, then reading off the answer
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to share 30 stickers between two friends in a 2:3 ratio, can they draw a bar model — splitting a strip into 5 equal boxes — and use it to work out each share without just guessing?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of ratio and proportion — ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, unequal, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole, and out of — and understand the difference between ratio (comparing parts to parts) and proportion (comparing a part to the whole)
topics.p: If {{name}} is sharing something 3 ways and 2 ways, can they explain the difference between a ratio (like 3:2) and a proportion (like 3 out of 5) — showing they know what each word means?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving the calculation of percentages of amounts (e.g. 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison
topics.p: If a jumper originally costs £40 and is 15% off, can {{name}} work out how much the discount is and what the sale price would be?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts
topics.p: If a recipe uses 3 eggs for every 200g of flour, can {{name}} work out how many eggs would be needed for 600g of flour?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found
topics.p: If {{name}} has a scale drawing where 1 cm represents 5 m, and a room measures 3.5 cm on the plan, can they work out the real length of the room?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples
topics.p: If three friends share a bag of 24 sweets so that one person gets twice as many as each of the others, can {{name}} work out how many each person receives?

topics.ds: Use compound units such as speed (distance ÷ time), unit pricing (cost ÷ quantity), and density (mass ÷ volume); solve problems involving compound units
topics.p: If a car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours, can {{name}} work out its average speed — and use the same idea to solve problems about price per kilogram or density of a material?

topics.ds: Divide a given quantity into two parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express the division as a fraction of the whole
topics.p: If £60 is shared between two people in the ratio 2:3, can {{name}} work out how much each person gets?

topics.ds: Express one quantity as a fraction of another where the result may be less than 1 or greater than 1, and interpret the meaning in context
topics.p: If there are 15 boys and 20 girls in a class, can {{name}} express the number of boys as a fraction of the whole class and say whether that fraction is less than or greater than a half?

topics.ds: Define percentage as 'number of parts per hundred'; interpret percentages and percentage changes as a fraction or a decimal; express one quantity as a percentage of another; compare quantities using percentages; work with percentages greater than 100%
topics.p: If a shop says a TV is 130% of its original price, does {{name}} understand what that means — and can they work out the new price from the original?

topics.ds: Know and use advanced vocabulary of multiplicative reasoning — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — accurately in problem-solving contexts
topics.p: If {{name}} is solving a problem about speed or density, can they explain what 'compound unit' means and tell the difference between direct proportion (more of one means more of the other) and inverse proportion (more of one means less of the other)?

topics.ds: Represent proportional relationships using double number lines (two parallel number lines aligned at 0) and ratio tables; recognise that equivalent ratios generate straight lines through the origin when graphed
topics.p: If {{name}} is comparing the cost of buying different numbers of cinema tickets, can they sketch a proportion graph — a straight line through zero — and use it to read off the cost of any number of tickets without recalculating each time?

topics.ds: Use ratio notation to describe the relationship between two or more quantities, simplify ratios to their simplest form, and convert between ratio and fraction representations
topics.p: If a smoothie recipe uses orange juice and mango juice in the ratio 3:2, can {{name}} simplify that ratio, express it as a fraction, and work out how much of each is needed for a given total amount?

topics.ds: Use a scale, given as a ratio (e.g. 1:50), as a statement such as '1 cm represents 2 m', or as a scale factor, to work out actual lengths from a scale drawing or map and drawing lengths from actual lengths; reproduce a scale drawing at a different scale by finding each new drawing length, either through the actual length or from the ratio of the two scales; and solve map, room-plan and design problems with consistent units, converting between mm, cm, m and km before or after scaling. Areas from scale drawings and the area factor are developed in the follow-on topic Area from scale drawings
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a house plan where 1 cm stands for 50 cm, could they work out how long a 9 cm wall really is — and redraw the plan half the size to fit a smaller sheet of paper?

topics.ds: Convert freely between related standard units of measurement (time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places where appropriate
topics.p: Can {{name}} convert between units confidently — for example, changing kilometres to metres, kilograms to grams, or hours and minutes to just minutes — including multi-step problems?

topics.ds: Find actual areas from a scale drawing or map, either by converting each drawing length to an actual length before multiplying or by using the area factor; explain why, when every length is multiplied by a scale factor k, areas are multiplied by k² (both dimensions are scaled), and avoid the mistake of applying the length factor to an area; convert between square units consistently (e.g. 1 m² = 10,000 cm²); and apply this to map, room-plan and design problems such as flooring, turf, paint or land area
topics.p: If a room is drawn 6 cm by 4 cm on a plan where 1 cm stands for 50 cm, could {{name}} work out how much carpet the real room needs — and explain why a room twice as long and twice as wide would need four times as much carpet, not twice as much?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving percentage increase, percentage decrease, finding the original value after a percentage change, and calculating simple interest
topics.p: If a bike originally costs £250 and its price goes up by 8%, can {{name}} work out the new price — and if a savings account earns 3% simple interest per year, how much interest would £500 earn in 4 years?

topics.ds: Recognise and solve problems involving direct proportion (as one quantity increases, the other increases at a constant rate) and inverse proportion (as one increases, the other decreases), including graphical and algebraic representations
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand the difference between quantities that grow together at the same rate (direct proportion) and ones where one goes up as the other goes down — like more workers meaning fewer days to finish a job (inverse proportion)?

topics.ds: Understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio; use ratio notation; simplify ratios
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why a ratio like 3:4 is really the same as the fraction ¾ — and show how that relationship connects to a straight-line graph through the origin?

topics.ds: Express their own feelings appropriately using words rather than actions — saying 'I feel angry because...' instead of hitting, shouting, or withdrawing
topics.p: When {{name}} is frustrated — say a sibling takes their toy — do they use words to say how they feel rather than snatching it back or crying?

topics.ds: Understand that everyone has feelings, that feelings change throughout the day, and that the same event can make different people feel different things
topics.p: If you and {{name}} watch the same film and you find it funny but {{name}} finds it scary, can they understand why you both felt differently?

topics.ds: Name and recognise basic emotions — happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, and surprised — in themselves and in others by looking at facial expressions and body language
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a friend crying at a birthday party, can they tell you what that friend might be feeling and name the emotion?

topics.ds: Understand that feelings have causes — something happens (a trigger) and that makes us feel a certain way — and begin to identify what triggers their own emotions
topics.p: When {{name}} gets upset about something at school, can they explain to you what happened that made them feel that way?

topics.n: How Emotions Feel in Your Body
topics.ds: Understand the connection between emotions and the body — recognising physical signals like butterflies in the stomach (nervous), clenched fists (angry), racing heart (scared or excited), and tight shoulders (stressed)
topics.p: Before a school performance or sports day, can {{name}} notice and tell you about the physical feelings in their body — like butterflies in their tummy — and connect them to being nervous or excited?

topics.ds: Use a wider vocabulary of emotion words beyond the basics — including frustrated, worried, anxious, embarrassed, jealous, proud, disappointed, grateful, and lonely — and distinguish between similar emotions
topics.p: If {{name}} doesn't get invited to a classmate's party, can they describe whether they feel disappointed, jealous, lonely, or a mix — rather than just saying 'sad'?

topics.ds: Recognise that people sometimes hide or mask their true feelings — smiling when they're actually sad, or saying 'I'm fine' when they're not — and understand why someone might do this
topics.p: If a friend at school says 'I'm fine' but looks upset and is being very quiet, can {{name}} recognise that the friend might not actually be fine?

topics.ds: Understand that emotions come in different intensities — from mild to strong — and that the same emotion can feel very different depending on how intense it is (e.g., annoyed → angry → furious, or nervous → anxious → panicked)
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell the difference between being a bit annoyed about losing a game and being truly furious — and explain that they're different levels of the same feeling?

topics.ds: Understand that emotional responses are shaped by personal experiences, culture, and context — the same situation triggers different emotions in different people because of their backgrounds and past experiences
topics.p: If one child in {{name}}'s class gets very scared during a thunderstorm while others think it's exciting, can {{name}} understand that the scared child might have had a frightening experience with storms before?

topics.ds: Reflect on their own emotional patterns over time — noticing recurring triggers, understanding their typical responses, and recognising how their emotional awareness has grown
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you something like 'I always get stressed before tests but I've learned that's normal for me' — showing they understand their own emotional patterns?

topics.ds: Understand how emotions influence thinking and decision-making — that strong feelings can cloud judgement, that we often make different choices when calm versus when upset, and that recognising this gives us more control
topics.p: If {{name}} sends an angry message to a friend during an argument and later regrets it, can they explain how their anger affected their decision and what they might do differently next time?

topics.ds: Understand that people can experience mixed or conflicting emotions at the same time — feeling excited and nervous about starting a new school, or happy for a friend who won but disappointed for yourself
topics.p: When {{name}}'s best friend gets picked for the team and they don't, can {{name}} explain that they feel happy for their friend AND disappointed for themselves at the same time?

topics.ds: Understand how the amygdala triggers emotional responses and how the prefrontal cortex (still developing in adolescence) regulates them; explain why stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) affect thinking and memory; understand that the adolescent brain's dopamine system makes feelings more intense; distinguish between emotion regulation (managing feelings effectively) and emotion suppression (pushing feelings down, which is counterproductive); introduce cognitive reappraisal as a research-backed technique for changing how we interpret a situation
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain, in basic terms, why teenagers tend to feel emotions more intensely than adults — what's happening in the developing brain that makes feelings so powerful during adolescence, and what's the difference between managing a feeling and suppressing it?

topics.ds: Understand that adolescence involves active construction of identity, leading to emotional complexity around questions of 'who am I?'; explore the emotional dynamics of belonging to multiple groups simultaneously (family, peer group, cultural or religious identity); understand social comparison and its intensification through social media; recognise that identity is not fixed and that uncertainty about identity is normal, not a sign of failure; develop language for navigating emotions tied to group membership and personal values
topics.p: If {{name}} goes through a phase of feeling unsure about who they are or where they belong, can they explain why this kind of uncertainty is a completely normal and even necessary part of adolescence — not a sign that something is wrong?

topics.ds: Introduce Goleman's emotional intelligence model (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills); develop vocabulary for complex emotional states (ambivalence, ennui, schadenfreude, awe, nostalgia, cognitive dissonance); understand the evidence linking emotional intelligence to wellbeing, relationship quality, and long-term life outcomes; reflect on personal emotional growth over the secondary school years; explore the relationship between emotional literacy and mental health, and know when to seek professional support
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe a real situation where being aware of their own emotions — knowing what they were feeling and why — helped them handle a difficult moment better than if they had just reacted automatically?

topics.ds: Show kindness and care towards others in simple everyday ways — comforting a friend who is upset, helping someone who has dropped their things, sharing without being asked, and saying kind words
topics.p: If a younger child at school falls over in the playground, does {{name}} go over to help or comfort them without being told to by an adult?

topics.ds: Understand that other people have their own feelings and thoughts, and that these might be different from your own — a foundational awareness that not everyone sees or feels things the same way
topics.p: If {{name}} loves dogs but their friend is scared of dogs, can {{name}} understand that their friend's fear is real even though they don't feel it themselves?

topics.ds: Notice and appreciate ways that people are similar to and different from each other — including appearance, family structures, languages spoken, foods eaten, and celebrations observed — and understand that differences make communities interesting
topics.p: Can {{name}} talk positively about how families in their class are different — some have two mums, some speak another language at home, some celebrate different holidays — and see this as interesting rather than strange?

topics.ds: Know and use the key vocabulary for understanding others — empathy, perspective, kind, fair, community, similar, different, and care — and understand that these words describe real habits of thinking and feeling
topics.p: When {{name}} sees someone who seems sad or left out, can they describe what that person might be feeling using words like 'empathy' or 'perspective' — showing they're thinking about the other person, not just themselves?

topics.ds: Understand that people's lives and experiences can be very different from their own — that some children face challenges like disability, poverty, family difficulties, or being new to a country — and develop compassion rather than judgement
topics.p: If a new child joins {{name}}'s class who doesn't speak much English or whose family situation is very different, does {{name}} show understanding and try to include them rather than avoiding them?

topics.ds: Understand what fairness means and why it matters — recognising that fair doesn't always mean equal (everyone getting the same) but can mean equitable (everyone getting what they need), and applying this understanding in group situations
topics.p: If a child with a broken arm gets extra time to finish a task at school, can {{name}} explain why that's fair even though other children don't get extra time?

topics.n: Seeing Someone Else's Point of View
topics.ds: Practise perspective-taking by imagining how someone else might feel in a given situation — using prompts like 'How would you feel if that happened to you?' and applying this when reading stories or during real interactions
topics.p: When reading a story together, can {{name}} pause and explain how a character might be feeling and why — putting themselves in the character's shoes?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of social awareness — including stereotype, prejudice, discrimination, equality, equity, bias, compassion, and fairness — and understand what distinguishes these closely related concepts
topics.p: If {{name}} hears a classmate say something that groups all people of a certain background together, can they explain why that's a stereotype and how it differs from a fact about an individual person?

topics.ds: Identify symbols and emblems important to Australia's identity and diversity — the Australian flag, the Aboriginal flag, the Torres Strait Islander flag, the Commonwealth Coat of Arms, the golden wattle and the national anthem — and what they represent
topics.p: When {{name}} sees the Aboriginal flag, the Torres Strait Islander flag or the golden wattle, do they know what they are and what they stand for?

topics.ds: Describe how stereotypes can influence people's choices and actions, such as the toys, activities, sports, careers or clothes people choose or avoid
topics.p: Does {{name}} notice when ideas like 'that's a boys' toy' or 'girls don't play that' might stop someone from doing what they enjoy?

topics.ds: Describe how religious and cultural festivals (e.g. Easter, Christmas, Diwali, Eid al-Fitr, Lunar New Year and Hanukkah) are celebrated in their community and country, and what each means to the people who celebrate it
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how a festival like Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year or Christmas is celebrated, and what it means to the families who celebrate it?

topics.ds: Understand the impact of prejudice and discrimination on individuals and communities — that treating people unfairly because of their identity causes real harm — and act on their responsibility to stand against it by carrying out a strategy that values diversity and includes others in their school or community, then reflecting on its effect
topics.p: If {{name}} notices a child at school being left out for being different — new to the country, or using a wheelchair — have they actually done something to include them, like inviting them to play, and can they tell you how it went?

topics.ds: Recognise stereotypes — oversimplified beliefs about groups of people based on gender, race, age, or other characteristics — and understand that stereotypes are unfair because they ignore individual differences
topics.p: If someone says 'boys don't cry' or 'girls aren't good at maths', can {{name}} explain why those statements are unfair stereotypes that don't apply to everyone?

topics.n: The world contains many cultures, traditions
topics.ds: Understand that the world contains many cultures, traditions, and belief systems, and that learning about others' perspectives enriches our own understanding — developing genuine curiosity about and respect for cultural diversity
topics.p: Does {{name}} show genuine interest when learning about how families from different cultures celebrate, eat, or worship — asking questions respectfully rather than dismissing things that are unfamiliar?

topics.ds: Describe the diversity of First Nations Australians — Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples, each made up of many distinct groups — including the more than 250 languages spoken before colonisation and the languages spoken and being revived today; their social organisation (family and kinship, Elders, roles and responsibilities); and their continuous connections to Country/Place, recognising that Aboriginal peoples have lived on the Australian continent for more than 60,000 years and that Torres Strait Islander peoples have their own distinct histories and connections to their islands and seas
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are distinct peoples with many groups and languages — and that Aboriginal peoples have lived on this continent for more than 60,000 years?

topics.ds: Describe the diversity of cultural, religious and social groups to which they and others in the community belong, and explain the importance of belonging to identity
topics.p: Can {{name}} list the groups they belong to — family, culture, faith, sport, school — and explain how they help make them who they are?

topics.ds: Reflect on their own assumptions and biases — recognising that everyone carries unconscious assumptions about others, and that actively questioning these assumptions is an ongoing practice that leads to greater fairness and empathy
topics.p: Can {{name}} catch themselves making an assumption about someone — like assuming a quiet child is unfriendly — and then question whether that assumption is fair?

topics.ds: Investigate how the portrayal of societal roles and responsibilities (e.g. in ads, TV, books and games) can be influenced by gender stereotypes, and how these portrayals can shape expectations
topics.p: When watching TV or ads, can {{name}} spot when jobs or chores are always shown being done by one gender — and explain how that might shape what people expect?

topics.ds: Move beyond 'treating everyone the same' to understand that structural advantages and disadvantages exist regardless of individual effort or intention; explore concrete examples of systemic inequality (educational attainment gaps, gender pay gap, representation in leadership); distinguish between individual prejudice and structural discrimination; understand intersectionality — how multiple aspects of identity interact; develop informed compassion rooted in evidence rather than pity; explore what being a genuine ally means in practice
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the difference between treating everyone 'the same' and actually making things fair — and give a real example of a structural barrier that means two people starting in different positions face unequal opportunities even if they try equally hard?

topics.ds: Distinguish sympathy ('I feel sorry for you') from empathy ('I understand what you're experiencing'); develop active listening skills: reflecting, paraphrasing, asking open questions, resisting the urge to problem-solve too quickly; understand empathic curiosity as genuine interest in another person's inner world; practise being present for someone in distress without trying to fix or minimise their experience; understand vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue, and how empathetic people can protect their own wellbeing while staying present for others
topics.p: When a friend is going through something really difficult, can {{name}} describe what makes a listener genuinely helpful — and explain the difference between empathy and sympathy, using an example of something that sounds supportive but actually isn't?

topics.ds: Understand what it means to be a citizen in an interconnected world where decisions in one place affect people elsewhere; explore global issues (climate justice, forced migration, global health, poverty) through an empathy lens, distinguishing facts from value judgements; engage with the ethical tension between obligations to those close to us and obligations to distant strangers; introduce evidence-based giving and effective altruism as one framework for thinking about global responsibility; develop a personal, reasoned stance on global citizenship that acknowledges complexity
topics.p: When {{name}} reads about a crisis happening in another country, can they describe how they think about their own responsibility — and name one practical thing young people can genuinely do about large-scale problems rather than just feeling helpless?

topics.ds: Ask for help when they need it — from a friend, teacher, or family member — and understand that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness
topics.p: If {{name}} is stuck on something at school or feeling worried about something, will they ask a teacher or friend for help rather than struggling in silence?

topics.ds: Seek permission respectfully before borrowing or touching other people's possessions or entering their personal space — asking clearly, waiting for the answer and accepting 'no'
topics.p: Does {{name}} ask before borrowing a sibling's toy or giving a friend a hug — and accept it calmly if the answer is no?

topics.ds: Listen to others when they are speaking — looking at the speaker, waiting until they finish, and showing they have heard by responding to what was said rather than just talking about their own ideas
topics.p: When a friend is telling {{name}} about their weekend, does {{name}} actually listen and ask questions about it — rather than immediately jumping in to talk about their own weekend?

topics.ds: Understand what makes someone a good friend — being kind, honest, reliable, and including others — and recognise behaviours that are not friendly, such as being bossy, leaving people out, or saying mean things
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe what makes a good friend and recognise when someone — including themselves — isn't being a good friend?

topics.ds: Give or deny permission respectfully when asked to share possessions or personal space, using clear words and body language, and know that it is OK to say no to sharing or touch that feels wrong
topics.p: If a friend wants a hug or to play with {{name}}'s special toy, can {{name}} say yes or no clearly and kindly?

topics.ds: Take turns, share materials, and play cooperatively with others — understanding that group activities work better when everyone gets a fair go and that waiting for your turn is part of being a good friend
topics.p: When {{name}} is playing a board game with friends or siblings, can they wait for their turn and share the pieces without grabbing or getting upset?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of working with others — cooperate, share, take turns, team, listen, agree, disagree respectfully, and include — and understand that these words describe habits that friendships and group work depend on
topics.p: When {{name}} is working on something with a friend or sibling, can they use words like 'cooperate' or 'take turns' to describe what they're doing — and actually practise those things?

topics.ds: Resolve simple disagreements with peers by talking it through — explaining how they feel, listening to the other person's side, and finding a compromise or solution that both can accept
topics.p: If {{name}} and a friend disagree about which game to play at break time, can they talk it through and find a compromise — rather than one person always getting their way or the argument escalating?

topics.ds: Understand different roles people play in groups — leader, supporter, mediator, idea-generator — and recognise that effective groups need a mix of roles, not everyone trying to be the leader
topics.p: In a group project, can {{name}} recognise that they don't always have to be in charge — and that sometimes the group works better when they support someone else's idea rather than pushing their own?

topics.ds: Work effectively as part of a small group — contributing their own ideas, listening to others' ideas, taking on a fair share of the work, and supporting the group to reach a shared goal
topics.p: When {{name}} has to do a group project at school, do they pull their weight — sharing ideas and doing their part — rather than sitting back or trying to take over?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of healthy communication and conflict — assertive, passive, aggressive, compromise, conflict, resolution, mediate, bystander, upstander, and peer pressure — and understand the difference between these contrasting approaches
topics.p: If {{name}} and a friend have a disagreement, can they describe it using words like 'conflict' or 'compromise' — and explain how assertive communication is different from aggressive or passive behaviour?

topics.ds: Understand that friendships change over time — that it's normal for friends to drift apart or for new friendships to form — and develop strategies for making new friends and handling friendship changes without feeling like something is wrong with them
topics.p: If {{name}}'s best friend starts spending more time with someone else, can they handle it without falling apart — understanding that friendships shift and they can make new friends too?

topics.ds: Use assertive communication — expressing needs, opinions, and boundaries clearly and respectfully without being aggressive (pushy/demanding) or passive (giving in/staying silent) — including saying no when something doesn't feel right
topics.p: If friends want {{name}} to do something they're uncomfortable with — like excluding another child or breaking a rule — can {{name}} say 'I don't want to do that' firmly but politely?

topics.ds: Rehearse and refine strategies for seeking, giving and denying permission respectfully, reflecting on how a request or response went and improving it
topics.p: If you role-play with {{name}} — asking to borrow something, or someone asking them for something they don't want to give — can they ask and answer respectfully and improve it when you give them tips?

topics.ds: Reflect on their own role and behaviour in relationships — recognising patterns in how they interact with others, understanding what they contribute to friendships, and identifying areas where they could improve as a friend or team member
topics.p: Can {{name}} honestly reflect on their friendships and say something like 'I think I sometimes take over in group work and I'm trying to listen more' — showing awareness of their own social patterns?

topics.ds: Apply and rehearse help-seeking in online and offline situations: telling a trusted adult, keeping on telling until someone helps, using a personal network of trusted adults, and knowing help services and online reporting tools (e.g. Kids Helpline and the eSafety Commissioner in Australia). Know that it is never too late to tell and never the child's fault, and that a trusted adult helps report an unwanted picture without anyone saving or forwarding it
topics.p: Does {{name}} have a list of trusted adults they could tell if something went wrong online or offline — and know about help services like Kids Helpline?

topics.ds: Describe situations when permission is required — borrowing things, touching or hugging, entering private spaces, taking or sharing photos and personal information online — and who can give it
topics.p: Does {{name}} know when they need to ask first — like before posting a photo of a friend or borrowing someone's phone?

topics.ds: Give and receive constructive feedback — telling someone what they did well and what could be improved in a way that is helpful rather than hurtful, and receiving feedback about their own work without becoming defensive
topics.p: If {{name}} reviews a classmate's story and finds mistakes, can they give feedback that's helpful — like 'I loved this part, and this bit could be clearer' — rather than just saying 'it's wrong'?

topics.ds: Mediate conflicts between others — helping two friends who are arguing by listening to both sides, helping them see each other's perspective, and guiding them toward a fair resolution
topics.p: If two of {{name}}'s friends are arguing and both come to {{name}} for support, can {{name}} help them talk it out fairly rather than just taking one side?

topics.ds: Describe strategies for seeking, giving or denying consent — asking clearly, checking for a freely given 'yes', noticing non-verbal cues, accepting 'no' and knowing consent can be changed — and rehearse communicating their intentions effectively and respectfully
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that a real 'yes' has to be freely given and can be changed — and can they ask, agree or refuse clearly, like before sharing a photo of a friend?

topics.ds: Understand subtext, indirect communication, and social cues in adolescent peer groups; analyse the psychology of in-group and out-group dynamics and why belonging can come at the cost of exclusion; understand gossip as a social bonding and status mechanism, and its costs; develop strategies for navigating social hierarchies without compromising values; distinguish between assertiveness and aggression in peer settings; understand how to respond to exclusion — whether experiencing it or witnessing it
topics.p: When {{name}} senses tension or unspoken 'undercurrents' in a group of friends, can they describe what social cues they pick up on and explain the difference between being assertive and being aggressive when they choose to address it?

topics.ds: Understand how to have honest, direct conversations that address problems without attacking the person; apply the principles of non-violent communication (observation, feeling, need, request); understand the repair process after significant conflicts: taking responsibility without defensiveness, offering a genuine apology (without blame-shifting), and rebuilding trust through consistent behaviour over time; distinguish between a real apology and a face-saving 'sorry'; understand how friendships survive and deepen through navigated conflict rather than avoidance
topics.p: When {{name}} falls out seriously with a friend, can they describe what makes an apology actually repair a relationship — and what the difference is between a genuine apology and just saying sorry to end the awkwardness?

topics.ds: Distinguish different leadership styles (directive, democratic, servant, transformational) and understand when each is appropriate; understand that influence in a group comes with responsibility, and explore the difference between leading through inspiration versus coercion; practise inclusive leadership: actively creating space for quieter voices and diverse perspectives; understand the ethics of influence and the boundary between persuasion and manipulation; explore concepts of consent and coercion in peer relationships; reflect on what kind of influence they want to have in their communities
topics.p: If {{name}} were leading a group project where one person was dominating all the decisions, can they describe two different leadership approaches they could take and explain why the most authoritative person in a group isn't always the best leader?

topics.ds: Understand that actions have consequences — that what you choose to do affects both yourself and other people — and begin to think about what might happen before they act
topics.p: Before {{name}} does something — like taking a toy from a sibling or running in the corridor — can they stop and think about what might happen as a result?

topics.ds: Recognise unsafe or uncomfortable situations and their body's early warning signs (e.g. butterflies in the tummy, a racing heart, sweaty hands), and tell the difference between safe surprises and unsafe secrets
topics.p: Does {{name}} know how their body feels when something isn't safe — like a funny tummy — and the difference between a fun surprise and a secret they should tell you?

topics.ds: Keep themselves safe in everyday situations — knowing basic safety rules about roads, strangers, water, and the internet — and understanding who their trusted adults are and when to tell them something
topics.p: Does {{name}} know their basic safety rules — like not going off with someone they don't know, looking both ways before crossing, and telling you if something online makes them uncomfortable?

topics.ds: Identify health and safety symbols, signs and messages in their community and what they tell people to do (e.g. poison and hazard symbols, hand-washing signs, sun-safe and 'no swimming' signs, the first aid cross)
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a poison symbol on a bottle or a hand-washing sign, do they know what it means and what to do?

topics.ds: Understand that their body belongs to them, name body parts including private parts using correct terms, and tell necessary care apart from touching that is not OK: a parent, carer, doctor or nurse may sometimes need to help wash or check their private parts, but should explain why and ask if it's OK first; nobody else should touch or look at their private parts, and nobody should ever ask them to touch or look at someone else's private parts
topics.p: Does {{name}} use the correct names for their body parts, and know that a doctor or carer who needs to check them should explain why and ask first — and that they should tell you if anyone else touches their private parts or asks them to touch someone else's?

topics.ds: Demonstrate and rehearse a protective response to unsafe situations: say 'no' clearly, get away, and tell a trusted adult — and keep telling until someone helps. Know that if someone hurts them or touches them in a way that is not OK, it is never their fault, even if they froze, couldn't say no or couldn't get away, and they can still tell
topics.p: If something felt unsafe, does {{name}} know to say 'no', get away and tell a trusted adult — and that it's never their fault and they can still tell, even if they froze or couldn't say no?

topics.ds: Know the difference between right and wrong in familiar everyday situations — understanding basic rules about honesty, not hurting others, respecting others' property, and being fair — and choose to do the right thing even when it's harder
topics.p: If {{name}} accidentally breaks something at a friend's house, do they tell the truth about it rather than hiding it or blaming someone else?

topics.ds: Understand why rules and agreements exist — that they help keep people safe, make things fair, and help groups work well together — and follow agreed rules willingly rather than only when being watched
topics.p: Does {{name}} follow the class rules or family agreements even when no adult is watching — not because they're scared of punishment but because they understand why the rules matter?

topics.n: Vocabulary: making decisions and keeping safe
topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of making decisions and keeping safe — choice, consequence, rule, safe, fair, honest, trusted adult, and right and wrong — and understand that naming these ideas clearly helps make better choices
topics.p: If {{name}} faces a situation where they need to make a choice — like whether to tell the truth about something that went wrong — can they talk through what might happen using words like 'consequence' and 'fair'?

topics.ds: Understand basic digital citizenship — being kind online, protecting personal information, recognising that people behind screens are real people with real feelings, and knowing what to do if something online makes them uncomfortable
topics.p: When {{name}} is chatting with friends online or playing multiplayer games, do they treat people kindly and know not to share personal details like their address or school name?

topics.ds: Understand the bystander role — that when someone witnesses unkind or unfair behaviour, they have a choice: they can be a passive bystander (doing nothing), join in, or be an upstander (speaking up or getting help) — and develop the confidence to be an upstander
