topics.p: If {{name}} sees a group of children being mean to someone at school, do they have the courage to say something, walk away with the person being targeted, or tell a teacher — rather than just watching?

topics.ds: Investigate a range of health messages and practices in their community (posters, ads, school and family routines) and discuss their purposes
topics.p: When you pass a health poster or ad — like 'Slip, Slop, Slap' — can {{name}} tell you what it wants people to do and why?

topics.ds: Understand what bullying is — repeated behaviour intended to hurt someone, including physical, verbal, social (exclusion, spreading rumours), and cyberbullying — and know that it is always wrong and what to do if they experience or witness it
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand the difference between a one-off argument and bullying, and do they know what to do if they see someone being bullied — rather than just ignoring it?

topics.ds: Use a simple decision-making process when faced with a choice — stopping to think, identifying the options, considering the consequences of each option, and then choosing — rather than acting impulsively
topics.p: When {{name}} faces a tricky choice — like whether to tell the teacher that a friend cheated — can they think through their options and the consequences rather than just reacting?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of ethics and citizenship — bullying, cyberbullying, bystander, upstander, peer pressure, digital citizenship, rights, responsibility, and ethical — and understand the distinctions between these closely related terms
topics.p: If {{name}} saw someone being treated unkindly online and you asked them about it, could they explain the difference between being a bystander and an upstander — and what 'digital citizenship' means?

topics.ds: Understand their rights and responsibilities as a member of a community — that everyone has a right to be treated with respect and to feel safe, and that with rights come responsibilities to treat others the same way
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that they have a right to feel safe at school AND a responsibility to help make school safe for others — understanding that rights and responsibilities go together?

topics.ds: Understand peer pressure — the influence friends and peers can have on your choices and behaviour — and develop strategies for resisting pressure to do something they know is wrong or that makes them uncomfortable
topics.p: If {{name}}'s friends dare them to do something risky or unkind — like shoplifting a sweet or posting an embarrassing photo of someone — can they resist the pressure and explain why they won't do it?

topics.ds: Propose actions or responses to a community or environmental issue or challenge, considering the possible effects of each action on different people and places
topics.p: If {{name}} notices a problem in your area — like litter or a dangerous crossing — can they suggest a couple of solutions and think about how each would affect different people?

topics.ds: Interpret the nature and intention of health information and messages (to inform, persuade or sell) and reflect on how they influence personal health decisions and behaviours
topics.p: When {{name}} sees an ad for a sugary drink and a sun-safety campaign, can they explain what each is trying to get people to do — and whether an ad has ever changed what they chose?

topics.ds: Describe and apply protective behaviours in a range of online and offline situations (e.g. an unknown person messaging in a game, being asked to share a photo, feeling unsafe at a park or event), choosing safe responses: offline, say no, get away and tell; online, don't reply, block, and get a trusted adult's help to report. Never save, screenshot or forward a naked or sexual picture of a child; a trusted adult can help keep a safe record of an ordinary mean or threatening message
topics.p: If someone they don't know messages {{name}} in a game, or sends a rude picture, do they know not to reply, save or share it, and to come to you so you can block and report it together — and, offline, to get away and tell you?

topics.ds: Identify who makes rules in the school and local community (e.g. the principal, school council, student representative council, families, local council), why rules are important and the consequences of rules not being followed
topics.p: Does {{name}} know who makes the rules at school and in your community — like the principal, the student council or the local council — and why they matter?

topics.ds: Explain why people participate within communities (e.g. to help others, to belong, for enjoyment, to improve a place) and how students can actively participate and contribute
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand why people volunteer or join clubs — and have they found a way to help out at school or in the community themselves?

topics.ds: Understand that ethical decisions are not always black and white — that sometimes there is no perfect answer and reasonable people can disagree — and practise weighing up competing values when making difficult choices
topics.p: If {{name}}'s friend tells them a secret but the secret involves something dangerous, can {{name}} think through the tension between loyalty to their friend and the need to keep someone safe?

topics.ds: Evaluate the ethical dimensions of real-world issues they encounter — such as environmental responsibility, fairness in sport, digital ethics, or social justice — considering multiple perspectives and forming a reasoned personal position
topics.p: Can {{name}} discuss a real issue — like whether it's fair that some children have more than others, or whether animals should be kept in zoos — considering different viewpoints and explaining their own position thoughtfully?

topics.ds: Distinguish rules from laws: laws apply to everyone in a state, territory or the nation and can be enforced by police and courts, while rules made by families, schools and clubs apply only to their members. At primary level, recognise that parliaments make statute laws (Acts) and that courts also develop common law through their decisions, and explain why laws are important and how they affect people's lives
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the difference between a family or school rule and a law — like wearing a seatbelt — and that laws come from parliaments and from decisions in courts?

topics.ds: Describe the roles of local government (councils) and how members of the community use and contribute to local services
topics.p: Does {{name}} know what your local council does — like bins, parks and libraries — and how people help by paying rates, volunteering or giving their ideas?

topics.ds: Analyse online and offline situations for risk — who is involved, warning signs, possible consequences and tricks people may use to gain trust (e.g. gifts, flattery, asking for secrecy) — and rehearse protective responses, knowing that if someone tricks or pressures a child it is never the child's fault, even if they went along with it at first or couldn't get away
topics.p: Can {{name}} spot the warning signs if a new online 'friend' offers gifts and asks them to keep chats secret — and do they know it would never be their fault and they could tell you at any time, even if they'd already gone along with it?

topics.ds: Describe key values and features of Australia's democracy, including free and fair elections, the secret ballot and compulsory voting, and the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives
topics.p: When there's an election, does {{name}} understand why voting is secret and compulsory in Australia, and what the person we elect is supposed to do?

topics.ds: Describe how citizens with shared beliefs and values work together to achieve a civic goal, through actions such as petitions, campaigns, advocacy and volunteering
topics.p: Does {{name}} know how people work together to change things in the community — like starting a petition for a new crossing — and could they plan a campaign of their own?

topics.ds: Investigate different sources and types of health information — health professionals, product labels, government websites, apps and social media — judge their reliability and apply them to their own and others' health choices
topics.p: At the supermarket, can {{name}} use the food label to pick the healthier snack — and do they know which health websites or people to trust?

topics.ds: Describe the key institutions of Australia's system of government (the Parliament, the Governor-General, the Prime Minister and Cabinet, and the High Court), how it is based on the Westminster system, and the key values and beliefs of Western democracies
topics.p: When the news mentions Parliament, the Senate or the High Court, can {{name}} explain what each one does?

topics.ds: Distinguish between risk (decisions with known probabilities) and uncertainty (decisions with unknown outcomes); identify cognitive biases that distort risk assessment: availability heuristic (judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind), present bias (overvaluing the immediate over the future), optimism bias (underestimating personal risk), and groupthink; understand why adolescent brains are biologically calibrated toward higher risk tolerance; apply a structured decision-making framework to real choices; understand the role of personal values in decisions where facts alone cannot determine the answer
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why taking a risk isn't always irrational — and describe one cognitive bias that causes people to misjudge risk in their everyday decisions, such as why teenagers tend to underestimate certain dangers?

topics.ds: Describe the roles and responsibilities of the three levels of government in Australia — federal, state/territory and local — and how some responsibilities are shared
topics.p: If there's a pothole on your street, a problem at the local hospital, or a passport to renew, does {{name}} know which level of government looks after each?

topics.ds: Understand the ethics of online identity and the importance of consistency between who you are online and offline; explain how recommendation algorithms and filter bubbles narrow information exposure; evaluate the psychology of misinformation: why it spreads, why smart people believe it, and how to apply source evaluation (lateral reading, checking evidence, recognising emotional manipulation); understand digital consent around sharing images or personal information; explore the ethics of AI, surveillance, and data privacy as they affect everyday life; reflect on responsible content creation and online influence
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a convincing claim shared on social media, can they describe their process for deciding whether to believe or share it — and explain why even intelligent people are regularly misled online?

topics.ds: Introduce the three main ethical frameworks: consequentialism (judge actions by outcomes and overall welfare), deontology (judge actions by adherence to rules and duties regardless of consequences), and virtue ethics (judge actions by the character they reflect); apply each framework to real-world moral dilemmas: climate responsibility, AI ethics, civil disobedience, wealth inequality, healthcare rationing; understand the strengths and limitations of each framework; develop the capacity for careful moral reasoning — the ability to think through ethical questions systematically rather than relying only on intuition or group opinion
topics.p: Can {{name}} take a real ethical dilemma — like whether it's ever right to break a rule to help someone — and explain how a consequentialist, a deontologist, and someone focused on virtue ethics would each think about it differently, and which approach they find most persuasive?

topics.ds: Investigate who they are — their likes, strengths, family background and what makes them special — and the important people in their world (family, carers, friends, teachers, community helpers)
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you about themselves — what they like and are good at — and name the important people in their life and what each one does for them?

topics.ds: Notice what you are feeling and put a name to it — being able to label an emotion is the first step to understanding and managing it
topics.p: When {{name}} seems upset, excited, or frustrated, can they stop and tell you what emotion they're feeling — even if they can't fully explain why?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of self-reflection — self-awareness, reflect, pattern, trigger, assumption, impact, perspective, and notice — and understand that having precise words for these inner experiences makes them easier to understand and talk about
topics.p: After a difficult moment — a falling-out with a friend or a frustrating task — can {{name}} talk about what happened using words like 'trigger' or 'reflect', showing they're thinking about their own reactions rather than just what the other person did?

topics.ds: Understand that feelings and actions are separate — you can feel something strongly without having to act on it straight away
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that feeling angry, scared, or jealous doesn't mean they have to act on it immediately — that there's a gap between the feeling and what they choose to do next?

topics.ds: Describe their own personal qualities (e.g. kind, brave, funny, curious) and those of others, and explain how these qualities contribute to developing who they are (their identity)
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe what kind of person they are — kind, brave, curious — with an example, and say what they admire in someone else?

topics.ds: Notice patterns in your own reactions — 'I tend to respond like this when I'm tired, left out, or put on the spot'
topics.p: Has {{name}} ever noticed a pattern in how they react — for example, that they get more upset at certain times of day, or that a particular type of situation reliably triggers a strong feeling?

topics.ds: Investigate how experiences of success, challenge, setbacks and failure in different contexts (school, sport, friendships, hobbies) strengthen resilience and shape identity
topics.p: Can {{name}} talk about something hard they got through — like a tough game or a test — and explain how it changed how they see themselves?

topics.ds: Reflect on how your behaviour lands on others — consider not just what you intended but what the actual impact was on the other person
topics.p: Can {{name}} think about how something they said or did might have felt to the other person — not just what they meant by it, but what the impact actually was?

topics.ds: Notice when your first reading of a social situation might be wrong — your assumptions about why someone acted a certain way are not always facts
topics.p: If {{name}} felt sure someone was being unfair or unkind, could they pause and consider whether there might be another explanation for what happened?

topics.ds: Explain how identities can be influenced by people (family, friends, cultural and community groups, role models, media) and places (home, a family's Country/Place or homeland, community), and use strategies to create a positive self-identity
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how the people and places in their life — family, friends, where they grew up — have shaped who they are, and name something that helps them feel good about themselves?

topics.ds: Reflect on your own growth over time — the things that challenge you now are not fixed, and noticing how you have already changed builds genuine self-knowledge
topics.p: Can {{name}} look back over the past year or two and point to something they used to find really difficult that they now handle better — and explain what changed?

topics.ds: Understand that change is a normal part of life — such as starting school, getting a new teacher, a new baby arriving, or moving house — and identify simple strategies that help them cope with changes
topics.p: When something changes in {{name}}'s life — like getting a new teacher at school — can they talk about how it makes them feel and think of ways to help themselves adjust?

topics.ds: Understand that making mistakes is a normal part of learning and that everyone — including adults — makes mistakes, and begin to see mistakes as opportunities to learn rather than reasons to give up
topics.p: If {{name}} gets an answer wrong in class or messes up during a game, do they bounce back and keep trying rather than shutting down or saying 'I can't do it'?

topics.ds: Wait for things they want without becoming very distressed — practising patience and delayed gratification in everyday situations like waiting their turn, waiting for a treat, or waiting for help
topics.p: If {{name}} has to wait their turn for something they really want — like a go on the iPad or being served dinner — can they wait without a big fuss?

topics.ds: Use simple calming strategies when feeling upset or overwhelmed — such as taking deep breaths, counting to ten, or going to a quiet space — and understand that these help the body and mind settle down
topics.p: When {{name}} gets really upset — say they lose a game or argue with a sibling — can they use a strategy like deep breaths to calm themselves down rather than staying in meltdown mode?

topics.ds: Know and use the key words for managing big feelings — calm, strategy, cope, settle, patience, overwhelmed, and breathe — and understand that having words for these ideas is the first step to using them
topics.p: When {{name}} is feeling really upset or frustrated, can they use words like 'I need to calm down' or 'I'm feeling overwhelmed' instead of just acting out?

topics.ds: Break a challenging task into smaller, manageable steps rather than feeling overwhelmed by the whole thing — and celebrate progress along the way
topics.p: If {{name}} has a big school project that feels overwhelming, can they break it down into smaller steps — like 'first I'll research, then I'll write the introduction' — rather than panicking about the whole thing?

topics.ds: Understand that different situations require different coping strategies — what works for anger might not work for sadness, and what helps at school might be different from what helps at home
topics.p: Can {{name}} recognise that when they're angry they need to do something physical like walk around, but when they're worried they need to talk it through — rather than using the same approach for every difficult feeling?

topics.ds: Understand the concept of a growth mindset — that abilities and intelligence can grow with effort, practice, and good strategies — as opposed to a fixed mindset where you believe you're either good at something or you're not
topics.p: When {{name}} finds something difficult like learning to ride a bike or mastering times tables, do they say 'I can't do it YET' rather than 'I'm just not good at this'?

topics.ds: Use positive self-talk to manage difficult situations — replacing unhelpful thoughts like 'I'm stupid' or 'I'll never be able to do this' with encouraging ones like 'This is hard but I can keep trying' or 'I've done hard things before'
topics.p: When {{name}} is struggling with homework and starts saying 'I'm rubbish at this', can they catch that thought and replace it with something more helpful like 'I just need to try a different approach'?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of resilience and self-management — including regulate, resilience, growth mindset, fixed mindset, self-talk, trigger, setback, persevere, and distress — and understand what each word means in practice
topics.p: If {{name}}'s team loses a match or they fail a test, can they talk about what happened using words like 'resilience' or 'growth mindset' — showing they understand the difference between giving up and bouncing back?

topics.ds: Reflect on which self-regulation and coping strategies work best for them personally, building a 'toolkit' of approaches they can draw on in different situations and sharing what works with others
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you 'When I'm stressed about exams I go for a walk and that helps, but when I'm sad I need to talk to someone' — showing they know their own coping toolkit?

topics.ds: Plan, rehearse and reflect on strategies to cope with changes and transitions they experience, such as a new class or school, moving house, family changes or the changes of puberty
topics.p: Before a big change — a new class, moving house or body changes — can {{name}} make a plan for coping, practise it, and talk afterwards about what helped?

topics.ds: Understand resilience as the ability to recover from setbacks, adapt to difficult circumstances, and keep going — recognising that resilience is a skill that develops through experience, not a trait you either have or don't
topics.p: After a real disappointment — like not getting a part in the school play or failing a test they studied for — can {{name}} feel upset but then pick themselves up and figure out what to do next?

topics.ds: Set realistic personal goals, create a simple plan to achieve them, monitor their own progress, and adjust their approach when things aren't working
topics.p: Can {{name}} set themselves a goal — like improving their swimming or finishing a book series — and actually work towards it step by step, adjusting their plan if needed?

topics.ds: Manage their own time and attention effectively — prioritising tasks, minimising distractions, and maintaining focus on important work even when it's not the most exciting option
topics.p: When {{name}} has homework to finish but also wants to play a game, can they manage their time — doing the homework first or setting a timer — rather than always needing you to enforce it?

topics.ds: Investigate resources and strategies to manage changes and transitions, including puberty and moving to secondary school: trusted adults, school counsellors, health services and reliable information sources
topics.p: Does {{name}} know who and where to go to with questions about puberty or starting high school — and which information sources to trust?

topics.ds: Distinguish between eustress (the productive, motivating kind of stress) and distress (harmful, overwhelming stress); explain the physiological stress response (fight-flight-freeze, HPA axis) and how chronic stress affects the body and mind; identify common adolescent stressors (academic pressure, social comparison, physical change, uncertainty about the future); evaluate evidence-based coping strategies (exercise, sleep, mindfulness, social support, expressive writing); recognise warning signs that stress has crossed into anxiety or depression and know where to get help
topics.p: When {{name}} is under pressure from exams or social situations, can they name two or three strategies that genuinely help them manage the stress — and explain why each one actually works, not just that it 'makes them feel better'?

topics.ds: Understand habit formation through the cue-routine-reward loop and how to design new habits intentionally; distinguish intrinsic motivation (doing something for its own value) from extrinsic motivation (rewards/punishments) and understand when each is more effective; understand procrastination as primarily an emotion regulation problem (avoiding discomfort) rather than a time management failure; apply self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness) to boost intrinsic motivation; design environments that reduce friction for desired behaviours
topics.p: If {{name}} keeps meaning to do something important but finds themselves putting it off, can they explain the real reason people procrastinate — it's not laziness — and describe one practical change they could make to their environment to make starting easier?

topics.ds: Understand that facing serious challenges can lead to genuine growth in three domains: new perspectives on life, improved relationships, and a strengthened sense of personal capability (post-traumatic growth); distinguish genuine growth from toxic positivity ('everything happens for a reason') and from denial; understand that resilience does not mean being unaffected by adversity but recovering and growing through it; develop a personal philosophy for handling setbacks based on meaning-making; explore how to support others going through serious difficulty without minimising their experience
topics.p: Has {{name}} ever come through something genuinely hard and found it changed them in a meaningful way? Can they explain what post-traumatic growth means and how it differs from just 'getting over it' or pretending something difficult was fine?

topics.ds: Know that many animals use camouflage — colours and patterns that help them blend into their surroundings — to hide from predators or to sneak up on prey, like a leaf insect that looks like a leaf or an Arctic hare that turns white in winter
topics.p: If {{name}} tries to spot a grasshopper in the garden, can they explain that it's hard to see because its green colour helps it hide in the grass — and give other examples of animals that use camouflage?

topics.ds: Know that animals make or find many different kinds of homes — birds build nests, rabbits dig burrows, bees live in hives, hermit crabs use empty shells, spiders spin webs — and that these shelters protect them and their young
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} where different animals live, can they describe several animal homes — like a bird's nest, a rabbit's burrow, or a bee's hive — and say why animals need shelter?

topics.ds: Know some of the world's animal record-holders — the blue whale is the largest animal ever, the cheetah is the fastest land animal, the bee hummingbird is the smallest bird, the giraffe is the tallest — and compare their sizes to familiar objects
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} which animal is the fastest or the biggest in the world, can they name some record-holders like the cheetah or blue whale and compare their size to something familiar, like 'a blue whale is as long as three buses'?

topics.ds: Know that animals live all over the world — on land, in water, and in the air — and that every continent, even icy Antarctica, is home to animals, each suited to the conditions where they live
topics.p: If you show {{name}} pictures of a polar bear, a parrot, a camel, and a penguin, can they tell you that animals live in all sorts of different places around the world?

topics.ds: Know that different animals have their babies in different ways — some lay eggs (birds, reptiles, fish, insects), some give birth to live young (most mammals) — and that babies may look like miniature adults or look very different from their parents
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a nest with eggs in a nature programme, can they explain that birds lay eggs and the babies hatch out, but dogs and cats have their babies born alive?

topics.ds: Know that some animals are nocturnal — active at night and sleeping during the day — and that nocturnal animals often have special features like big eyes (owls, tarsiers), large ears (bats, fennec foxes), or sensitive whiskers to help them find food in the dark
topics.p: If {{name}} hears an owl hooting at bedtime, can they explain that owls are nocturnal — meaning they sleep during the day and come out at night — and that their big eyes help them see in the dark?

topics.ds: Understand the difference between wild animals, farm animals, and pets — wild animals find their own food and shelter in nature; farm animals are kept by people for food, wool, or eggs; pets are animals people keep for companionship — and know that wild animals should be observed from a distance
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a fox in the garden, can they explain that it's a wild animal — different from their pet cat or a farm sheep — and that wild animals look after themselves and shouldn't be touched?

topics.ds: Understand that animals communicate in many different ways — birds sing to attract mates and defend territory, whales call across vast ocean distances, bees dance to show other bees where food is, wolves howl to keep the pack together, and fireflies flash light signals — and that communication is essential for survival
topics.p: If {{name}} hears birds singing in the morning, can they explain that birdsong is a way of communicating — and describe at least two other ways different animals send messages to each other?

topics.ds: Know that many animals make incredible journeys called migrations — Arctic terns fly from pole to pole, monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles across North America, wildebeest cross the Serengeti following rain, and humpback whales swim between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters — and that these journeys are linked to food, breeding, and seasons
topics.p: If {{name}} learns about the monarch butterfly's journey, can they explain what migration means and name at least two other animals that make long journeys — and say why they travel?

topics.ds: Explore animals of the desert — camels, fennec foxes, scorpions, rattlesnakes, meerkats — and understand how desert animals survive extreme heat and lack of water through being active at night, storing water or fat, burrowing underground during the day, and having large ears to lose heat
topics.p: If {{name}} reads about camels in a desert, can they explain at least two ways desert animals cope with the heat and lack of water — like being active at night or having special body features?

topics.ds: Explore animals of the Arctic and Antarctic — polar bears, Arctic foxes, and walruses in the north; penguins, seals, and albatrosses in the south — and understand how polar animals survive extreme cold through thick fur or blubber, huddling behaviour, and seasonal changes like white winter coats
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a nature programme about the Arctic, can they explain how polar bears stay warm in freezing temperatures and name at least two differences between Arctic animals (north) and Antarctic animals (south)?

topics.ds: Understand that predators have evolved hunting strategies — wolves hunt in packs, chameleons use their long tongues, spiders build webs, crocodiles ambush at water's edge — and prey animals have evolved defences — porcupine spines, skunk spray, poison dart frog toxins, zebra stripes confusing predators, playing dead
topics.p: If {{name}} watches a nature programme showing a lion hunting, can they describe at least two different ways predators catch food and two ways prey animals defend themselves?

topics.ds: Explore animals of the tropical rainforest — the most species-rich habitat on Earth — learning that the forest has layers (canopy, understory, forest floor) with different animals at each level: toucans and monkeys in the canopy, jaguars and frogs on the floor, and that rainforests are found near the equator
topics.p: If {{name}} watches a documentary about rainforests, can they describe at least three animals that live there and explain that different animals live at different heights in the forest — some in the treetops and some on the ground?

topics.ds: Explore animals of the grasslands and savanna — lions, zebras, wildebeest, elephants, cheetahs in African savanna; bison and prairie dogs in American grasslands — understanding why large herds form on open grasslands and how predators and prey interact in these wide-open spaces
topics.p: If {{name}} sees pictures of the African savanna, can they name at least four animals that live there and explain why some animals like zebras live in large herds?

topics.ds: Know that insects and other minibeasts (spiders, worms, snails, centipedes) are the most numerous and diverse group of animals on Earth — there are more species of beetle than any other animal — and that they play vital roles as pollinators (bees, butterflies), decomposers (woodlice, worms), and food for other animals
topics.p: If {{name}} spots a bee in the garden, can they explain why bees are important — and name at least two other jobs that insects and minibeasts do that help the natural world?

topics.ds: Explore animal intelligence and complex behaviour — chimpanzees and crows use tools, dolphins recognise themselves in mirrors, octopuses solve puzzles and escape enclosures, elephants mourn their dead, meerkats teach their young to handle scorpions — understanding that many animals think, learn, and have social lives more complex than once believed
topics.p: If {{name}} watches a video of a crow using a stick to get food from a tube, can they explain that this shows animal intelligence and give other examples of animals that use tools, solve problems, or show complex behaviour?

topics.ds: Understand that biodiversity — the variety of different species in an ecosystem — is essential for healthy ecosystems, and that keystone species (like wolves in Yellowstone, sea otters in kelp forests, or bees as pollinators) have an outsized impact on their ecosystem, so that losing one key species can cause a cascade of changes affecting many others
topics.p: If {{name}} learns about how wolves were brought back to Yellowstone and the whole ecosystem changed, can they explain what a 'keystone species' is and why having many different species in an area matters?

topics.ds: Understand why some animal species become endangered or go extinct — habitat destruction, hunting/poaching, pollution, climate change, and invasive species — and know examples like the giant panda, mountain gorilla, Amur leopard, and the now-extinct dodo and thylacine, using the IUCN Red List as the system scientists use to track threatened species
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a news story about an endangered animal, can they explain what 'endangered' means and describe at least three reasons why some animals are at risk of disappearing forever?

topics.ds: Understand that invasive species are animals (or plants) that have been introduced to a place where they don't naturally belong — like grey squirrels outcompeting red squirrels in the UK, cane toads poisoning native predators in Australia, or rabbits devastating ecosystems in Australia — and that they can cause serious harm to native wildlife by competing for food, spreading disease, or having no natural predators
topics.p: If {{name}} learns that grey squirrels were brought to the UK from America, can they explain why introduced animals can be a problem for the animals that were already living there?

topics.ds: Know how people work to protect endangered animals — through national parks and marine reserves, captive breeding programmes (like those that saved the California condor and Arabian oryx), anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors connecting habitats, and laws banning trade in endangered species — and understand that children can contribute through habitat-friendly choices
topics.p: If {{name}} visits a zoo with a breeding programme, can they explain how zoos help save endangered species and describe at least two other ways people protect wildlife?

topics.ds: Understand that animals have structural adaptations (body features like the giraffe's long neck, eagle's talons, dolphin's streamlined shape), behavioural adaptations (migration, hibernation, tool use), and physiological adaptations (antifreeze in Arctic fish blood, echolocation in bats) — and that these developed over many generations through natural selection
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a woodpecker pecking a tree, can they explain that its strong beak, long tongue, and shock-absorbing skull are all adaptations — and describe what the word 'adaptation' means with other examples?

topics.ds: Understand symbiosis — close relationships between different species — including mutualism (both benefit, like clownfish and anemones), commensalism (one benefits without harming the other, like remora fish riding sharks), and parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense, like ticks on deer) — and recognise these relationships in nature
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a nature programme showing a small bird picking insects off a buffalo's back, can they explain that both animals benefit from this relationship and name the type of symbiosis?

topics.ds: Introduce the Red Queen hypothesis — species must keep evolving just to maintain fitness relative to co-evolving partners; describe predator-prey arms races (cheetah speed vs gazelle speed, bat echolocation vs moth hearing jamming) and parasite-host co-evolution (myxomatosis in rabbits); explain Darwin's hawk moth and orchid as a classic example of mutualistic co-evolution predicting an unknown species; understand that co-evolution is a major driver of biological diversification
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the idea of an evolutionary arms race — how a predator and its prey keep evolving better attack and defence strategies in response to each other, never quite getting ahead?

topics.ds: Explain how deep-sea animals cope with crushing pressure (no gas-filled spaces, flexible proteins, pressure-adapted enzymes); describe thermoregulation extremes — antifreeze glycoproteins in Antarctic fish, supercooling in wood frogs; introduce tardigrades and cryptobiosis (surviving desiccation, extreme temperatures, radiation, vacuum); survey other extremophiles (thermophiles at hydrothermal vents, halophiles in salt flats); consider what these organisms tell us about the limits of life
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe an animal that can survive being frozen solid, completely dried out, or exposed to the vacuum of space — and explain roughly how it manages to survive conditions that would kill almost any other living thing?

topics.ds: Explain sexual selection as a form of natural selection: runaway selection for peacock tails, bird of paradise displays, and frog calls; explain kin selection and altruistic behaviour — why worker bees die to protect the hive, why meerkats stand guard at personal risk (Hamilton's rule, inclusive fitness); introduce game theory in animal behaviour using the hawk-dove model; define cognitive ethology and survey evidence for animal emotions, play, and culture
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why a worker bee dying to protect the hive actually makes evolutionary sense — even though the bee never has its own offspring? What's the logic that makes this a successful strategy?

topics.ds: Quantify the current biodiversity crisis: extinction rates 100-1000x the background rate; explain methods for measuring biodiversity loss (species-area relationship, population viability analysis, IUCN Red List categories); evaluate rewilding case studies — Yellowstone wolf reintroduction triggering a trophic cascade that changed river courses; Iberian lynx recovery; describe minimum viable population theory and conservation triage; examine ethical debates in deciding which species to prioritise
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe what happened to Yellowstone National Park after wolves were reintroduced — what unexpected changes rippled through the whole ecosystem, including effects on rivers, as a result of one predator coming back?

topics.ds: Explain cladistics: organisms are grouped by shared derived characters, not just similarity; how phylogenetic trees are built using molecular data (DNA sequence alignment) and the molecular clock; explain why birds are technically a group within dinosaurs (crown Avemetatarsalia); distinguish convergent evolution (unrelated species evolving similar traits) from parallel evolution; introduce horizontal gene transfer and why the tree of life is more accurately a web; explain why classification systems keep changing as new data emerge
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why biologists now say that birds ARE a type of dinosaur — not just their descendants but literally within the dinosaur family tree? What does that tell us about how scientists classify animals?

topics.ds: Use simple materials and equipment (child-safe scissors, glue sticks, tape, play dough tools) to make a solution for a purpose, following safety rules such as carrying scissors closed and pointing down and keeping the work area tidy
topics.p: When {{name}} makes something at home with scissors, glue and tape, do they cut carefully, carry the scissors safely and clean up afterwards?

topics.ds: Explore how familiar products (toys, lunchboxes, chairs), services (a library, a bus route) and environments (a playground, a classroom) are designed by people for a purpose
topics.p: At the playground, can {{name}} tell you why someone designed it that way — like soft ground under the swings to reduce the risk or severity of injury if someone falls?

topics.ds: Use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions: measuring and cutting, joining with tape, glue, split pins or staples, and folding, rolling and shaping card, fabric or recycled materials
topics.p: When building a model from boxes and card, can {{name}} cut, fold and join the parts — with tape, glue or split pins — safely and neatly?

topics.ds: Identify how familiar products, services and environments are designed and produced by people to meet personal or local community needs (e.g. a school garden, a bus shelter, a pedestrian crossing, a lunchbox)
topics.p: On a walk, can {{name}} explain how something in your neighbourhood — like a crossing or bus shelter — was designed to help people in the community?

topics.ds: Sequence the steps for making a designed solution cooperatively, agreeing with a partner or group what to do first, next and last and who does each step
topics.p: When making something with a friend or sibling, can {{name}} agree on the steps — what to do first, next and last — and share the jobs?

topics.ds: Select and use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions — e.g. a junior hacksaw with a bench hook, a hand drill, a low-temperature glue gun, a needle and thread — following safety procedures under supervision
topics.p: If {{name}} was building a model car, could they choose the right tools — like a small saw for the axles and a glue gun for the frame — and use them safely with an adult?

topics.ds: Examine occupations in design and technologies — architects, engineers, product and fashion designers, landscape designers, food technologists, farmers and builders — and what each designs or produces to meet community needs
topics.p: Does {{name}} know what jobs like architect, engineer or food technologist involve — and could they tell you what one of them designs to help people?

topics.ds: Examine factors that influence the design of products, services and environments to meet community needs — sustainability (materials, energy, waste), cost, safety, function and appearance
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why a park bench might be made from recycled plastic — and what else designers had to think about, like cost and safety?

topics.ds: Sequence the production steps to make designed solutions individually and collaboratively — ordering measuring, cutting, joining, assembling and finishing, with checkpoints and shared roles
topics.p: Before building a school project, does {{name}} write the steps in order — measure, cut, join, finish — and stick to the plan or adjust it sensibly?

topics.ds: Explore needs or opportunities for designing, and test components, tools, equipment and processes before making — trialling different joins, wheels and axles or techniques to find out which works best
topics.p: Before building, does {{name}} try out a few ways of joining or making a part — like tape versus glue — to see which works best?

topics.ds: Explain how people in design and technologies occupations weigh competing factors — sustainability, cost, function, safety, appearance, time and the needs of different users — when designing products, services and environments
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why designers can't always choose the 'greenest' material — because cost, strength or safety matter too — using an example like a new building?

topics.ds: Explain how the characteristics and properties of tools and equipment (blade type, teeth size, power source, precision, safety features) affect their use when producing designed solutions
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why you'd use a saw with fine teeth for thin wood and a different one for metal — how a tool's features suit the job?

topics.ds: Investigate the components, tools, equipment and processes needed to create a designed solution — comparing mechanisms, joining methods or production processes through research and testing
topics.p: When planning a project, does {{name}} research and test which parts and methods to use — like comparing gears and pulleys for a moving toy?

topics.ds: Select and use suitable materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make a quality designed solution, planning safety controls and finishing the product accurately
topics.p: When {{name}} makes a project like a moving toy or a sewn bag, do they pick the right materials and tools, follow safety steps and finish it neatly to match their plan?

topics.ds: Develop project plans that consider resources — materials, tools, equipment, time, cost and people — to individually and collaboratively make designed solutions
topics.p: For a bigger project, can {{name}} make a plan with a timeline, a list of materials and costs, and who does what — and keep track as they go?

topics.ds: Compare dinosaur sizes to familiar things — some dinosaurs were as tall as a house, others were as small as a chicken — and understand that dinosaurs came in a huge range of sizes
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you that some dinosaurs were enormous and others were tiny — maybe using comparisons like 'as tall as a building' or 'as small as a cat'?

topics.ds: Understand that dinosaurs were real animals that lived on Earth a very long time ago and are now extinct — none are alive today
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a dinosaur toy, can they tell you that real dinosaurs lived long ago but aren't alive any more?

topics.ds: Recognise and name common well-known dinosaur species: Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and Brachiosaurus/Diplodocus, describing a basic feature of each
topics.p: If {{name}} sees pictures of different dinosaurs, can they name at least three — like T. rex, Triceratops, and Stegosaurus?

topics.ds: Understand that fossils are the remains of ancient living things preserved in rock, and that scientists called palaeontologists study fossils to learn about dinosaurs
topics.p: If {{name}} found a fossil-shaped rock on a beach or at a museum, could they explain what a fossil is and who studies them?

topics.ds: Sort dinosaurs into plant-eaters (herbivores) and meat-eaters (carnivores) by looking at clues like tooth shape — flat teeth for plants, sharp teeth for meat
topics.p: If you showed {{name}} a picture of a dinosaur's teeth, could they guess whether it ate plants or meat?

topics.ds: Distinguish real dinosaurs from fictional or commonly confused creatures — pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) were not dinosaurs, and movie dinosaurs are not always accurate
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a flying reptile in a dinosaur book, can they tell you it's actually not a dinosaur but a different kind of prehistoric animal?

topics.ds: Understand that different dinosaurs lived on different continents and that fossil discoveries around the world show dinosaurs were a global phenomenon, with some species found only in certain regions
topics.p: If you showed {{name}} a world map, could they tell you that dinosaur fossils have been found on every continent — and maybe name a place where a famous dinosaur was discovered?

topics.ds: Describe what coprolites are (fossilised dinosaur dung) and how palaeontologists analyse them to discover what dinosaurs ate, including plant fragments, bones, and seeds
topics.p: Does {{name}} know what a coprolite is? Can they explain — with a giggle — how fossilised poo helps scientists figure out what a dinosaur ate?

topics.ds: Understand that fossils tell us not only about ancient animals but also about ancient environments — for example, marine fossils found on a mountaintop show that area was once underwater
topics.p: If {{name}} heard that seashell fossils were found on a mountain, could they explain what that tells us about what the area used to be like?

topics.ds: Explain in simple terms how fossils form: an organism dies and is quickly buried in sediment; over millions of years minerals replace the remains and the sediment turns to rock, preserving the shape
topics.p: If {{name}} made a salt-dough fossil at school, could they explain how real fossils form underground over millions of years?

topics.ds: Know who Mary Anning was — a pioneering fossil hunter from Lyme Regis, England, who discovered ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons in the early 1800s and contributed to our understanding of prehistoric life
topics.p: Has {{name}} heard of Mary Anning? Can they tell you who she was and why she was important to the study of fossils?

topics.ds: Use dinosaur trackways (fossilised footprints) to make inferences about a dinosaur's size, speed, and behaviour — widely spaced prints suggest running, closely spaced suggest walking
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a line of dinosaur footprints at a museum, could they figure out whether the dinosaur was walking or running based on how far apart the prints are?

topics.ds: Place the three periods of the Mesozoic Era — Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous — in order and understand that different dinosaurs lived in different periods, not all at the same time
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that T. rex and Stegosaurus didn't actually live at the same time — and can they name the three dinosaur time periods in order?

topics.ds: Distinguish body fossils (preserved bones, teeth, shells) from trace fossils (footprints, trackways, eggs, burrows, coprolites) and explain what each type can tell scientists
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a dinosaur footprint in rock at a museum, could they explain how it's different from a fossil bone and what scientists can learn from it?

topics.ds: Analyse and interpret data from fossils to provide evidence of organisms and environments that existed long ago
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a fossil of a fish in a rock on a hillside, can they explain that the area must have been underwater millions of years ago?

topics.ds: Understand that modern birds evolved from a group of small feathered theropod dinosaurs, using evidence such as the fossil Archaeopteryx, feathered dinosaur fossils from China, and shared skeletal features
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why scientists say birds are actually living dinosaurs — and point to evidence like feathered dinosaur fossils?

topics.ds: Evaluate competing scientific explanations about dinosaurs by weighing fossil evidence — understanding that scientific knowledge changes as new fossils are discovered and new methods of analysis are developed
topics.p: If {{name}} read two different explanations for why dinosaurs went extinct, could they discuss what evidence supports each idea and why scientists sometimes change their minds?

topics.ds: Classify dinosaurs into the two major groups based on hip structure: Saurischia (lizard-hipped, including theropods and sauropods) and Ornithischia (bird-hipped, including Triceratops and Stegosaurus)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that scientists divide dinosaurs into two big groups based on their hip bones — and tell you which group includes T. rex?

topics.ds: Describe how palaeontologists work in the field and lab: prospecting for exposed fossils, careful excavation with hand tools, plaster jacketing for transport, preparation in the lab, and scientific description and publication
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe the steps a palaeontologist goes through from first spotting a fossil in a cliff to it ending up on display in a museum?

topics.ds: Understand that palaeoart — scientific illustrations and models of dinosaurs — is based on fossil evidence but involves informed speculation about skin colour, feathers, and soft tissues that don't usually fossilise
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that pictures of dinosaurs are educated guesses? Can they explain what parts are based on evidence and what parts scientists have to imagine?

topics.ds: Read and create simple cladograms (branching diagrams) that show how groups of dinosaurs are related based on shared features, understanding that species sharing more features are more closely related
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a branching tree diagram showing dinosaur relationships, could they explain which dinosaurs are most closely related by looking at where the branches split?

topics.ds: Understand that rock layers (strata) form in sequence with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest at the top, and that fossils found in deeper layers are older — this is the principle of relative dating
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a cliff with layers of rock, could they explain that the bottom layers are the oldest and that fossils found deeper down lived longer ago?

topics.ds: Describe the Cretaceous–Palaeogene (K-Pg) extinction event approximately 66 million years ago, including the asteroid impact theory and its evidence (iridium layer, Chicxulub crater), and understand that this ended the reign of non-avian dinosaurs
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain what scientists think caused the dinosaurs to go extinct — and describe at least one piece of evidence for the asteroid theory?

topics.ds: Recognise that living things have changed over time and that fossils provide information about organisms that inhabited the Earth millions of years ago
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that the animals and plants alive today are different from those that lived millions of years ago, and that we know this from fossils?

topics.ds: Trace the evidence for the dinosaur-to-bird transition in depth: feathered theropods from the Liaoning Formation (China), the mix of dinosaur and bird features in Archaeopteryx, and the competing ground-up versus trees-down hypotheses for the origin of flight
topics.p: If {{name}} was told that a sparrow is technically a living dinosaur, could they explain the chain of fossil evidence that supports this — naming at least one key transitional fossil and describing what makes it part dinosaur, part bird?

topics.ds: Explain how radiometric dating works — radioactive isotopes decay at a known rate (half-life), so measuring the ratio of parent to daughter isotope in a rock or fossil gives an absolute age; distinguish between carbon-14 (useful up to ~50,000 years) and uranium-lead (useful for millions to billions of years)
topics.p: If {{name}} was told a dinosaur bone was dated using uranium-lead radiometric dating, could they explain what that means — what is decaying, why the rate of decay is useful, and roughly why scientists don't use carbon-14 for 70-million-year-old bones?

topics.ds: Compare the five major mass extinction events in Earth history (End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, K-Pg), describe proposed kill mechanisms for each (glaciation, oceanic anoxia, volcanic mega-eruptions, asteroid impact), and explain why mass extinctions, while catastrophic, also open ecological space for subsequent evolutionary radiations
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs was actually the fifth mass extinction in Earth history — and describe what happened in the worst one, which killed over 90% of all species?

topics.ds: Reconstruct an ancient ecosystem using multiple independent lines of evidence: isotope analysis of teeth to infer diet and migration, bone histology (growth rings) to estimate age and growth rate, coprolite chemistry for diet, and palaeobotany for habitat — understanding that palaeontology is an evidence-synthesis discipline
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked how scientists know a large dinosaur migrated hundreds of kilometres every year, could they explain what kind of evidence they look for and how they rule out alternative explanations?

topics.ds: Evaluate the debate over what drove Pleistocene megafauna to extinction — human overkill, climate change, or a combination — using evidence from fossil records, ancient DNA, and archaeological sites; connect to the present-day sixth mass extinction and consider the ethics and feasibility of de-extinction using ancient DNA
topics.p: If {{name}} heard that scientists are trying to bring back the woolly mammoth using ancient DNA, could they explain what ancient DNA is, what challenges exist, and why some scientists think reviving extinct species might actually help ecosystems?

topics.ds: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how plants and animals can change the environment to meet their needs
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how a beaver builds a dam that changes a river into a pond, or how tree roots can crack rocks apart?

topics.ds: Use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time, recording temperature, rainfall, and other conditions
topics.p: Has {{name}} kept a weather diary for a week or more, recording whether it was sunny, rainy, or windy, and noticed any patterns?

topics.ds: Observe changes across the four seasons and describe weather associated with each season, including how day length varies
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe what happens in each season — like leaves falling in autumn, snow in winter — and notice that days are shorter in winter and longer in summer?

topics.ds: Develop a model to represent the shapes and kinds of land (mountains, valleys, plains) and bodies of water (rivers, lakes, oceans) in an area
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a map or build a model showing mountains, rivers, and oceans, and explain what each type of land or water feature is?

topics.ds: Name and use vocabulary for the water cycle — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection, transpiration, water vapour, runoff, groundwater — and describe each stage of the cycle using these terms in the correct sequence
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain where the puddle goes after it stops raining — using words like 'evaporation' or 'water vapour' rather than just 'it dries up'?

topics.ds: Describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock over millions of years
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how a shell or bone from an ancient creature ended up preserved inside a rock?

topics.ds: Compare multiple solutions designed to slow or prevent wind or water from changing the shape of the land
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a sandcastle being washed away by waves, can they think of ways to protect it — like building a wall or planting grass to hold the sand?

topics.ds: Compare and group different kinds of rocks based on their appearance and simple physical properties such as hardness, texture, and colour
topics.p: Can {{name}} examine a collection of rocks and sort them by whether they're hard or crumbly, rough or smooth, and light or dark?

topics.ds: Recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter, and that different soils have different properties
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that soil isn't just dirt — it's made from tiny broken-down bits of rock mixed with dead leaves and other organic material?

topics.n: Where water is found on Earth
topics.ds: Identify where water is found on Earth and understand that water can exist as solid (ice) or liquid, recognising water in oceans, rivers, glaciers, and underground
topics.p: Can {{name}} name the different places water is found on Earth — in oceans, rivers, ice caps, and even underground — and explain that ice is just frozen water?

topics.ds: Analyse and interpret data from maps to describe patterns of Earth's features, recognising that many features result from processes that occur over long periods
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a map and notice patterns like mountains running in lines, rivers flowing to the sea, or deserts clustered near the equator?

topics.ds: Compare the observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals (colour, lustre, hardness, texture, grain size) and investigate why they are important Earth resources (building materials, growing food, metals, salt)
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a rock or crystal collection, can they compare things like shininess and hardness — and explain how rocks, soils and minerals are used, like clay for bricks?

topics.ds: Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season
topics.p: Can {{name}} collect weather data over several weeks, put it in a chart, and use it to describe what weather is typical for that time of year?

topics.ds: Obtain and combine information to describe climates in different regions of the world, distinguishing between weather and climate
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the difference between weather and climate, and describe why the Arctic is always cold while tropical areas are always warm?

topics.ds: Make observations and measurements to provide evidence of the effects of weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, or vegetation
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a crumbling cliff or a river bank and explain how water, wind, or ice has slowly worn away the rock or soil over time?

topics.ds: Describe and graph the amounts of salt water and fresh water in various reservoirs to provide evidence about the distribution of water on Earth
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that most of Earth's water is salty ocean water, and only a tiny fraction is the fresh water we drink, and show this on a graph?

topics.ds: Use vocabulary for Earth's geological processes and rock types — igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic, erosion, weathering, deposition, fossil, sediment, strata, permeable, impermeable — and apply these when explaining how rocks form and how landscapes change over time
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain the difference between a rock being weathered and being eroded — those are actually two different things?

topics.ds: Develop a model to describe ways the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere interact as connected Earth systems
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how rain (atmosphere) falls on mountains (geosphere), flows into rivers (hydrosphere), and provides water for plants and animals (biosphere)?

topics.ds: Describe how weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition cause slow or rapid change to Earth's surface, including transportation of sediment by water, wind and ice, and rapid changes such as floods, landslides and storm erosion
topics.p: After a big storm, can {{name}} explain how wind and water carried sand or soil away and dropped it somewhere else — and how that can change land quickly or slowly?

topics.ds: Interpret cross-section diagrams of the Earth's interior, geological strata, and rock cycle; read and label layers (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core); understand that deeper layers in sedimentary sequences are older
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a cut-away diagram of the Earth, can they point to and name the different layers — and if shown stacked rock layers, can they say which layer formed first?

topics.n: Plants and animals in their habitats
topics.ds: Use a model to represent the relationship between the needs of different plants and animals and the places they live, connecting organism needs to habitat features
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why a fish needs to live in water but a cactus can live in a desert, by matching what each living thing needs to where it lives?

topics.ds: Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air, and other living things in the local environment
topics.p: Can {{name}} suggest ways people can help the environment — like recycling, not littering, saving water, or planting trees?

topics.ds: Identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how habitats provide for basic needs and how organisms depend on each other
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why a polar bear lives in the Arctic and not in a desert, and how the animals and plants in a habitat help each other?

topics.ds: Name and use vocabulary for where living things are found — habitat, environment, microhabitat, conditions, woodland, ocean, desert, rainforest, pond — and use terms to describe what animals need to survive: food, water, shelter, space, and suitable conditions
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why a polar bear couldn't survive in a rainforest — using the word 'habitat' or 'conditions' rather than just 'it's too hot'?

topics.ds: Explore and compare the differences between things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive
topics.p: If you show {{name}} a rock, a fallen leaf, and a caterpillar, can they tell you which is alive, which was once alive, and which was never alive?

topics.ds: Identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including microhabitats such as under a log or in a pond
topics.p: If you turn over a log in the garden with {{name}}, can they name the little creatures they find and explain why they live there?

topics.ds: Describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify different sources of food
topics.p: Can {{name}} draw a food chain showing how a caterpillar eats a leaf and then a bird eats the caterpillar?

topics.ds: Construct an argument that some animals form groups that help members survive, such as herds, packs, or colonies
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why wolves hunt in packs or why fish swim in schools, and how being in a group helps them survive?

topics.ds: Recognise that environments can change and that this can sometimes pose dangers and challenges to living things
topics.p: Can {{name}} give examples of how changes like pollution, building, or drought can make it harder for animals and plants to survive?

topics.ds: Explore and use classification keys to identify, group, and name living things in local and wider environments
topics.p: Can {{name}} use a simple yes/no key chart to work out the name of an insect or plant they've found outside?

topics.ds: Use vocabulary for feeding relationships and ecological roles — producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer, food chain, food web, nutrient cycle — and describe how energy and matter flow through ecosystems using these terms
topics.p: Can {{name}} draw a food chain from a plant to a top predator and label each animal as a producer, consumer, predator, or prey?

topics.ds: Construct and interpret food chains identifying producers, predators, and prey, and understand energy transfer between trophic levels
topics.p: Can {{name}} build a food chain for a woodland and point out which organisms are producers, which are predators, and which are prey?

topics.ds: Recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways based on observable features
topics.p: Can {{name}} sort a set of animals or plants into groups using their own criteria, like 'has wings' or 'lives in water'?

topics.ds: Use vocabulary for human impact on the environment — pollution, habitat destruction, deforestation, biodiversity, conservation, renewable energy, non-renewable energy, fossil fuel, carbon footprint, sustainability, endangered, extinct — and apply these when discussing environmental issues and human choices
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain what a carbon footprint is — not just that it's about pollution, but what it actually measures?

topics.ds: Read and interpret food web diagrams — identify producers, primary and secondary consumers, and decomposers; trace energy flow along food chains within the web; predict the effect of removing or adding a species
topics.p: If {{name}} is shown a diagram with arrows connecting plants, insects, frogs, and hawks, can they trace which animals eat which and explain what would happen if the frogs disappeared?

topics.ds: Describe differences in the life cycles of mammals, amphibians, insects, and birds, comparing metamorphosis with direct development
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how a butterfly's life cycle (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly) is completely different from how a puppy grows into a dog?

topics.ds: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth's resources and environment
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe real examples of how communities protect the environment — like using solar panels, creating nature reserves, or cleaning up rivers?

topics.ds: Describe the life process of reproduction in some plants and animals, including sexual and asexual reproduction in plants
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain different ways plants reproduce — not just from seeds but also from cuttings or runners — and how animals reproduce by having babies or laying eggs?

topics.ds: Describe how living things are classified into broad groups (micro-organisms, plants, animals) according to common observable characteristics, similarities, and differences
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain the big groups that scientists sort all living things into — like plants, animals, and tiny micro-organisms — and give examples of each?

topics.ds: Give reasons for classifying plants and animals based on specific characteristics, using evidence to justify classification decisions
topics.p: If {{name}} finds an unusual creature, can they explain step by step how they'd work out what group it belongs to based on its features?

topics.ds: Develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers, and the environment in an ecosystem
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain what happens to a fallen leaf on the forest floor — how tiny organisms break it down and the nutrients go back into the soil to help new plants grow?

topics.ds: Explain how energy is transferred between trophic levels in a food chain, why energy is lost at each stage, and use pyramids of biomass/numbers to represent this
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked why there are so many more plants than foxes in a field, could they explain how energy gets lost at every step of a food chain and what that means for the size of each population?

topics.ds: Construct and interpret food webs showing the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem, explaining how a change in one population affects others
topics.p: If {{name}} was shown a diagram with lots of animals connected by arrows, could they explain what it means — tracing what eats what — and predict what would happen if one animal disappeared from the web?

topics.ds: Investigate the physical conditions of a habitat (light, temperature, moisture, wind) by measuring them, and analyse data from fair tests (changing one condition, keeping others the same) on how the growth and survival of living things are affected by changing physical conditions
topics.p: Could {{name}} set up a fair test — the same seedlings, soil and water, with one in sun and one in shade — measure them over two weeks, and use the results to explain which grew better and why?

topics.ds: Explain the importance of insect pollination for plant reproduction and human food security, and discuss the consequences of pollinator decline
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a news story about bees dying out, could they explain what that would actually mean for the food in your kitchen — which foods would be affected and why?

topics.ds: Describe the water cycle, tracing water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff, and transpiration in plants, explaining how the sun drives the cycle
topics.p: If {{name}} watched rain falling outside and was asked where that water had been before it fell, could they trace its journey through the water cycle from the sea to the clouds to the rain and back?

topics.ds: Explain what biodiversity means, why high biodiversity makes ecosystems more resilient, and describe the ways human activity threatens biodiversity (habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species, climate change)
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked why it matters if a rainforest is cut down even if lots of species survive elsewhere, could they explain what biodiversity means and why losing it makes whole ecosystems more fragile?

topics.ds: Describe the relationship between chromosomes, genes, and DNA in heredity, including the double helix structure of DNA and the historical roles of Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Wilkins
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked what DNA actually is and where it is in the body, could they explain the relationship between DNA, genes, and chromosomes — and say roughly how many chromosomes a human cell has?

topics.ds: Describe the main types of evidence for evolution: the fossil record (change over time), comparative anatomy (homologous structures), and the geographic distribution of related species
topics.p: If {{name}} visited a natural history museum and saw fossils and skeletons of different animals, could they explain how scientists use those to build up evidence that species change over time — and that different animals are related?

topics.ds: Explain how environmental change can outpace a species' ability to adapt through natural selection, leading to extinction, using historical and contemporary examples
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked why woolly mammoths no longer exist while other large mammals survived, could they explain what conditions led to the mammoth's extinction — and connect it to what's happening with endangered species today?

topics.ds: Explain genetic mutation as a random change in DNA sequence, describe causes of mutation (e.g. radiation, chemicals, copying errors), and explain that most mutations are neutral, some harmful, and a few beneficial
topics.p: If {{name}} heard that DNA can get damaged or changed, could they explain what a mutation is, what might cause one, and why most mutations don’t actually cause problems — but occasionally one leads to something new?

topics.ds: Explain natural selection as the mechanism of evolution: heritable variation + competition for resources + differential survival and reproduction = change in allele frequency over generations
topics.p: If {{name}} heard about bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics, could they explain how that happened using natural selection — without the bacteria ‘choosing’ to change?

topics.ds: Explain how environmental change (climate change, habitat loss, pollution) affects the distribution of species, including range shifts, local extinction, and invasive species
topics.p: If {{name}} heard that wild plants in the UK are now flowering weeks earlier than they did 50 years ago, could they explain why that happens and what problems it might cause for the other animals that depend on those plants?

topics.ds: Describe the carbon cycle, tracing carbon through photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, and combustion, and explain the role of each process
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked where the carbon in a wooden table came from originally, could they trace its journey through the carbon cycle — from the atmosphere, through a plant, into the tree, and back out again?

topics.n: Toxins Building Up in Food Chains
topics.ds: Explain how organisms affect and are affected by their environment, including the bioaccumulation of toxic materials (e.g. pesticides, heavy metals) through food chains
topics.p: If {{name}} heard that large fish like tuna can contain more mercury than small fish, could they explain why that is — even though the tuna didn’t encounter mercury directly?

topics.ds: Explain variation within and between species, distinguishing between continuous variation (e.g. height) and discontinuous variation (e.g. blood group), and between genetic and environmental causes
topics.p: If {{name}} looked around a classroom and noticed that everyone has slightly different heights, hair colours, and eye colours, could they explain why these differences exist — and which ones are inherited, which are down to the environment, and which are both?

topics.ds: Explain how alleles are inherited in sexual reproduction and use Punnett squares to predict the probability of offspring inheriting a characteristic, including dominant and recessive alleles
topics.p: If {{name}} was asked why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child, could they explain what dominant and recessive alleles are and show how it works using a Punnett square?

topics.ds: Use tools and materials to design and build a structure that will reduce the warming effect of sunlight on an area, such as a shade or shelter
topics.p: Can {{name}} design and build a simple shade — like an umbrella or canopy — and test whether it keeps an area cooler in the sun?

topics.ds: Make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth's surface, noticing that sunlight warms the ground, water, and objects
topics.p: Can {{name}} feel the difference between a sunny pavement and a shady one, and explain that sunlight warms up surfaces it shines on?

topics.ds: Name and use vocabulary for types of energy and energy transfer — kinetic energy, potential energy, heat energy, light energy, sound energy, electrical energy, chemical energy, stored energy, energy transfer, energy transformation — and describe energy changes in familiar situations using these terms
topics.p: If {{name}} stretches a rubber band and lets it go, can they name what type of energy it had when stretched — and what it changed into?

topics.ds: Construct a simple series electrical circuit, identifying and naming its basic parts: cells, wires, bulbs, switches, and buzzers
topics.p: Can {{name}} build a working circuit with a battery, wires, and a light bulb, and name each part they're using?

topics.ds: Recognise some common conductors and insulators, and associate metals with being good conductors of electricity
topics.p: Can {{name}} test objects in a circuit and explain why metal objects let electricity through but rubber and plastic don't?

topics.ds: Identify sources of heat energy (sun, fire, heaters, friction, bodies) and examine how the temperatures of two objects change as heat energy moves from the hotter to the cooler one until they reach the same temperature
topics.p: If {{name}} puts a warm drink into a bowl of cold water, can they predict and measure that the drink cools down while the cold water warms up?

topics.ds: Observe and provide evidence that energy can be transferred from place to place by sound, light, heat, and electric currents
topics.p: Can {{name}} give examples of how energy moves around — like heat from a radiator warming a room, light from a lamp reaching your eyes, or electricity flowing through a wire?

topics.ds: Recognise that a switch opens and closes a circuit, controlling whether a lamp lights or a buzzer sounds
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain what happens inside the wall when they flip a light switch — that it completes or breaks the electrical loop?

topics.ds: Draw and read simple circuit diagrams using standard symbols for cells, bulbs, switches, buzzers, and wires; identify whether a circuit is complete or broken from a diagram; match circuit diagrams to physical circuits
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a circuit diagram with symbols for a battery, switch, and light bulb, can they tell you whether the bulb would light up — and draw the diagram for a simple circuit you describe?

topics.ds: Identify common appliances that run on electricity and understand that electricity is a form of energy that powers devices in everyday life
topics.p: Can {{name}} walk around the house and point out which things use electricity to work, like the fridge, TV, and lights?
